Each group has different information needs, frequency requirements, and preferred channels. What should the communication plan specify for each group?

answers.text: Send all communications to all groups simultaneously — consistency eliminates gaps
Only communicate with the executive sponsors — they will relay information to other groups

The communication plan should specify for each group: what information they receive (content tailored to their role and decisions); frequency (weekly for the project team; monthly for executives; milestone-triggered for store managers); format (executive dashboard; team status meeting; store manager briefing); channel (email; project portal; town halls); sender/owner (PM to executives; PM to IT ops; change manager to stores; PM to vendor); and escalation threshold (what triggers an unscheduled communication)
Communication planning is not needed — the team will naturally communicate the right information to the right people

explanations.a: Identical communications to all groups creates information overload for executives and information gaps for technical teams. Executive dashboards and technical status reports serve different purposes for different audiences.
explanations.b: Executive sponsor relay is unreliable, introduces interpretation bias, creates communication delays, and deprives each group of direct, accurate information tailored to their needs.
explanations.c: STAKEHOLDER-SPECIFIC COMMUNICATION PLAN: EXECUTIVE SPONSORS: WHAT: budget vs. actual, milestone status (RAG), top 3 risks, go-live forecast; FREQUENCY: monthly steering committee + ad hoc for critical decisions; FORMAT: 1-page executive dashboard; CHANNEL: steering committee meeting + email; OWNER: PM. PROJECT TEAM: WHAT: sprint status, blockers, decisions needed, action items; FREQUENCY: weekly status meeting + daily stand-up; FORMAT: team meeting + project tool status; CHANNEL: video conference + Jira/Azure DevOps; OWNER: PM + Scrum master. IT OPERATIONS: WHAT: infrastructure readiness, integration milestones, deployment windows; FREQUENCY: biweekly technical status; FORMAT: technical status report; CHANNEL: email + technical review meeting; OWNER: PM + technical lead. STORE MANAGERS (END USERS): WHAT: what's changing for them, training schedule, go-live timeline, support resources; FREQUENCY: monthly change management update + pre-go-live weekly; FORMAT: newsletter + training materials + town hall; CHANNEL: intranet + email + in-store briefings; OWNER: change manager + PM. ERP VENDOR: WHAT: project status, open issues, change requests, milestone achievements; FREQUENCY: weekly technical sync + monthly formal status; FORMAT: meeting + formal status report; CHANNEL: video conference + email; OWNER: PM.
explanations.d: Without a communication plan, each group receives inconsistent information at random intervals — critical stakeholders are missed; executives are surprised; store managers don't prepare for changes; operational disruptions occur at go-live.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — detailed scope statement; acceptance criteria; exclusions
questions.text: A project manager is writing the detailed scope statement for a healthcare portal project. She includes deliverables, acceptance criteria, and a list of what's in scope. Her sponsor reviews it and says: 'This looks good, but I've seen scope disputes in past projects about unclear exclusions — what should we add?' What elements should be added?

answers.text: Add explicit exclusions (what the project will NOT deliver), out-of-scope items that stakeholders might assume are included, and boundary conditions; add assumptions that the scope is based on; add constraints that limit the solution choices; and note that any work beyond this scope statement requires a formal change request
Nothing — the scope statement is complete with deliverables and acceptance criteria
Add a detailed budget breakdown — scope and budget are the same document
Add the vendor's contact information — scope disputes are resolved by contacting vendors

explanations.a: COMPLETE SCOPE STATEMENT ELEMENTS: DELIVERABLES AND ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: what will be built and how we know it's done (already included); EXPLICIT EXCLUSIONS — MOST CRITICAL: list specific items that are NOT in scope even though stakeholders might assume they are; examples for a healthcare portal: 'Payment processing is NOT included — billing through existing patient accounting system'; 'Mobile native apps (iOS/Android) are NOT included — web-responsive only'; 'Integration with third-party insurance verification systems is NOT included — Phase 2'; the rule: if a reasonable stakeholder might think it's included, it should appear in the exclusions list if it's not; OUT-OF-SCOPE FUTURE PHASES: items explicitly deferred to Phase 2 or future projects; ASSUMPTIONS: conditions assumed to be true for this scope (e.g., 'Assumes patient data will be migrated from the legacy system in a pre-validated format provided by the data team'); CONSTRAINTS: limitations on the solution (e.g., 'Must use the existing Microsoft Azure cloud environment'; 'Must integrate with the Epic EHR system'); CHANGE REQUEST REQUIREMENT: 'Any work beyond this scope requires a formal change request submitted through the change control process'; WHY EXPLICIT EXCLUSIONS MATTER: prevents 'scope creep by assumption' where stakeholders later claim 'I assumed payment processing was included'; provides the PM with contractual authority to reject out-of-scope requests without a change request.
explanations.b: Deliverables and acceptance criteria define what will be built — but without explicit exclusions and assumptions, stakeholders can claim that unstated features were 'implied' in the scope. This is the source of most scope disputes.
explanations.c: Budget is documented in the cost management plan and cost baseline — not in the scope statement. Scope defines WHAT is delivered; budget defines HOW MUCH it costs.
explanations.d: Vendor contact information is a procurement/communication plan artifact — not a scope statement component.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — maintain communication plan; updating when circumstances change
questions.text: Four months into a 12-month ERP project, three new stakeholder groups are identified (data privacy compliance team, external auditors, and a newly formed user experience committee). The communication plan was created in planning and hasn't been updated. What should the project manager do?

answers.text: No action needed — the communication plan created in planning applies for the full project duration
Replace the entire communication plan — partial updates are unreliable

Update the communication plan to incorporate the three new stakeholder groups: identify their information needs (data privacy: compliance status and data handling decisions; auditors: formal audit trail documentation; UX committee: design decisions and user research findings); determine appropriate communication frequency and format; assign an owner for each new communication; add to the existing plan without replacing what works
Ask the new stakeholders to self-identify their communication needs — they will request what they need

explanations.a: Communication plans are living documents. New stakeholders who are not in the plan receive no structured communications — they will surface as disengaged, uninformed stakeholders who later raise objections about being excluded from decisions.
explanations.b: Replacing the entire plan destroys the existing framework that is working well for 8+ stakeholder groups. A targeted update incorporating the 3 new groups is far more efficient.
explanations.c: COMMUNICATION PLAN MAINTENANCE for new stakeholders: DATA PRIVACY COMPLIANCE TEAM: NEEDS: any design decisions affecting data handling; data breach notification procedures; compliance testing results; data retention and deletion procedures; FREQUENCY: monthly compliance update; ad hoc for decisions requiring their review; FORMAT: compliance status memo; CHANNEL: email + review meeting. EXTERNAL AUDITORS: NEEDS: formal audit documentation access; milestone completion confirmations; change control records; FREQUENCY: triggered by audit schedule (quarterly or as-needed); FORMAT: formal written documentation packages; CHANNEL: secure document repository access + formal letter/email. UX COMMITTEE: NEEDS: user research findings; design mockups for review; usability testing results; FREQUENCY: biweekly design review meetings; FORMAT: design review presentations; CHANNEL: design review meeting + shared design tool access. PROCESS: add these three new rows to the existing communication plan matrix; brief the new stakeholders on the communication cadence; assign communication owners; update the stakeholder register to reflect their inclusion.
explanations.d: Waiting for new stakeholders to 'self-identify' their communication needs places the burden on stakeholders who may not know what information exists or what they should ask for. Active communication management is the PM's responsibility.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — WBS; 100% rule; scope completeness
questions.text: A project manager reviews the WBS for a mobile app development project and realizes it doesn't include: Change Management, Documentation, User Training, or App Store Submission activities. The development team says: 'Those aren't really part of the app development — they're separate.' Is the development team correct, and what WBS principle applies?

answers.text: The development team is correct — WBS should only include technical development activities
The WBS is complete — those activities are implied even if not listed

The development team is incorrect — the WBS must include ALL project scope under the 100% Rule: change management (helping users adopt the new app), documentation (user guides, API documentation, maintenance manuals), user training (educating end users on app features), and app store submission (submitting and managing the app through the store review process) are ALL project work; if they're not in the WBS, they're not in the budget, not in the schedule, and have no owner — creating delivery gaps and cost overruns when someone eventually does the work
The development team is correct — those activities are the client's responsibility by default

explanations.a: A mobile app project doesn't 'finish' when the code is written. The app must also be: documented so users and future developers understand it; submitted to the app store (which has its own review process, typically 1-7 days for Apple App Store); delivered with user training so adoption is successful; accompanied by change management if users are shifting from a different tool or process.
explanations.b: Implied scope is a project management anti-pattern. If something is 'implied' but not in the WBS, it: has no budget allocation; has no owner; has no schedule time; will either not be done (delivery gap) or done as unplanned work (cost overrun).
explanations.c: 100% RULE APPLICATION: the WBS must include 100% of the project scope — ALL work required to deliver the project, INCLUDING: CHANGE MANAGEMENT: plan for user adoption; communications to end users about the app; resistance management; behavioral adoption support; typically represents 5-15% of project effort on enterprise apps; DOCUMENTATION: user guides; API documentation for integration; technical documentation for maintenance; app store description and marketing content; TRAINING: training material development; training session delivery; possibly video tutorials; help system content; APP STORE SUBMISSION: submission preparation (screenshots, descriptions, privacy policy); submission process management; responding to Apple/Google review feedback; monitoring post-submission status. EACH OF THESE: needs to be scheduled; needs to be budgeted; needs an owner; would be missed if not in the WBS. CORRECTED WBS: add Level 2 entries for Change Management, Documentation, Training, and Distribution (app store submission); decompose each into work packages with estimates.
explanations.d: These are project deliverables, not client responsibilities. Unless the contract explicitly assigns documentation, training, and change management to the client, these are the project team's responsibilities.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — product backlog; initial backlog creation; epic and story structure
questions.text: A product owner is creating the initial product backlog for a new HR system implementation during the planning phase. The scope includes: employee data management, payroll processing, benefits administration, and performance management. Each area has 20-30 features. How should the initial backlog be structured?

answers.text: Create all 80-120 features as individual user stories immediately — more detail in planning produces better sprints
Create the stories alphabetically — systematic ordering improves sprint planning efficiency
Create only 1 backlog item: 'Build the HR system' — broad items allow more flexibility

Create 4 Epics (one per HR area) and add high-level stories for the most critical features in each epic; leave future sprints' stories as rough backlog items to be refined as the project progresses — this 'just enough' planning approach provides direction without over-specifying work that may evolve

explanations.a: Creating 80-120 detailed user stories in planning is premature specification. Requirements evolve through stakeholder feedback on delivered increments; stories written 6+ months before they'll be developed will need significant revision when their sprint arrives. Over-specification in planning creates 'analysis paralysis' and wastes time writing detailed stories that will change.
explanations.b: Alphabetical ordering ignores business value, risk, technical dependencies, and stakeholder priorities. Backlog prioritization is a substantive judgment about what should be built first — not an alphabetical exercise.
explanations.c: A single backlog item 'Build the HR system' provides no basis for sprint planning, estimation, velocity tracking, or progress reporting. The backlog must be granular enough for sprint-sized selection and estimation.
explanations.d: INITIAL BACKLOG STRUCTURE — 'JUST ENOUGH' PLANNING: EPICS (4 top-level): Employee Data Management Epic; Payroll Processing Epic; Benefits Administration Epic; Performance Management Epic; NEAR-TERM STORIES (next 2-3 sprints): break the highest-priority features in each epic into specific user stories; these should be in 'ready' state: clearly defined; acceptance criteria written; story points estimated; dependencies identified; FAR-TERM ITEMS (sprint 4+): remain as rough backlog items (epics and features without full story-level detail); will be refined in backlog grooming sessions as they approach the sprint planning horizon; PRIORITIZATION: product owner orders all items by business value, risk, and dependencies; highest priority items at the top; PRINCIPLE: plan in detail only what you're about to build; leave future items at summary level to avoid wasted specification work on items that will change; this is called 'progressive elaboration' in Agile planning.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — detailed scope statement; managing stakeholder expectations through clear boundaries
questions.text: A project sponsor reviews the draft scope statement and asks: 'Why do we need to document what's NOT in scope? If it's not listed as a deliverable, it's obviously not included.' How should the project manager respond?

answers.text: 'You're right — we only need to document what is in scope; exclusions are obvious'
'We document exclusions because the PMO requires it — no practical benefit exists'
'Exclusions are only needed for government contracts — private sector projects can use informal scope management'

'Explicit exclusions prevent the most common type of scope creep — 'scope by assumption.' Stakeholders frequently assume that related capabilities are included even when they're not listed; without explicit exclusions, a VP can say 'I assumed payroll was included' after 6 months of planning; explicit exclusions create contractual clarity: anything not in the scope statement requires a change request to add; this protects both the team and the organization'

explanations.a: 'Obviously not included' is the PM's perspective — but stakeholders rarely have the same boundary clarity. Many scope disputes begin with 'I assumed...' or 'I thought it was obvious that...'
explanations.b: The practical benefit is substantial: explicit exclusions prevent scope disputes, protect the project budget, and give the PM contractual authority to manage change requests.
explanations.c: Scope creep affects all projects regardless of sector — private sector projects are equally affected by 'I assumed it was included' disputes.
explanations.d: EXCLUSIONS IN SCOPE STATEMENT — BUSINESS CASE: 'SCOPE BY ASSUMPTION' PREVENTION: stakeholders build mental models of the project that include related capabilities even when they're not explicitly described; example: if the scope says 'Build a customer portal,' many stakeholders will assume it includes: mobile app (not just web); integration with CRM (not specified); multi-language support (not specified); payment processing (not specified); if none of these are in scope, the PM will receive change requests for all of them — the alternative is to explicitly exclude them; COMMON EXCLUSIONS PATTERN: the scope statement lists what IS included; the exclusions list items that stakeholders would reasonably assume are included based on context, but are actually NOT included; CONTRACTUAL CLARITY: for vendor-delivered projects, explicit exclusions protect both parties from disputes about what was agreed; PM AUTHORITY: when a stakeholder requests an excluded item, the PM can point directly to the scope statement: 'Per Section 3.2 of the scope statement, payment processing is explicitly excluded — this requires a change request'; without the explicit exclusion, the PM has weaker authority to push back; the PM and sponsor are better protected from scope creep with explicit exclusions.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — staff training plan; training timing; knowledge application windows
questions.text: A project manager plans team training for a 9-month project. She has three training needs: AWS cloud fundamentals (needed for Month 3 infrastructure work), advanced data modeling (needed for Month 5 design work), and security compliance training (required for ALL work before any work begins due to data classification requirements). How should training be sequenced in the project schedule?

answers.text: Conduct all three trainings in Month 1 — front-load training to get it done early
Skip training — allow team members to use online resources when they need specific knowledge
Conduct all trainings in Month 8 — training should happen after work is complete for reflection

Schedule training just before it is needed: security compliance training in Month 1 (required before any work begins — non-negotiable prerequisite); AWS cloud fundamentals in Month 2 (4 weeks before Month 3 infrastructure work begins — allows learning + brief practice time); advanced data modeling in Month 4 (4 weeks before Month 5 design work) — this 'just in time' approach maximizes retention and minimizes the gap between learning and application

explanations.a: Front-loading all training in Month 1 creates: FORGETTING CURVE PROBLEM — skills learned 4-7 months before use are substantially forgotten by the time they're needed; PRODUCTIVITY IMPACT — team is in training rather than productive project work for all of Month 1; WASTED INVESTMENT — AWS knowledge learned in Month 1 that isn't applied until Month 3 will be partially forgotten.
explanations.b: 'Use online resources when needed' (self-study without structured training) is appropriate for supplemental knowledge but insufficient for: complex technical skills (AWS, data modeling) that require structured learning with labs; mandatory compliance training that requires certification of completion.
explanations.c: Training after work is complete has no application value — training for skills you've already used (or tried to use) produces post-hoc certification, not capability development. This sequencing makes no practical sense.
explanations.d: JUST-IN-TIME TRAINING SEQUENCING: SECURITY COMPLIANCE TRAINING — MONTH 1 (immediate, non-negotiable): data classification requirements mean NO WORK can begin without compliance training; this is a legal/regulatory prerequisite; schedule as the first project activity; everyone on the team completes it in Week 1-2; APPLY JUST-IN-TIME PRINCIPLE: training should occur close enough to the work that knowledge is fresh, but early enough to allow: completion of the training itself; brief practice/lab work; ramp-up to productive contribution; 4-6 weeks lead time is typically optimal for technical training. AWS CLOUD FUNDAMENTALS — MONTH 2 (6 weeks before Month 3 infrastructure work): team completes training; spends 2 weeks in practice environment; begins productive infrastructure work in Month 3 with fresh knowledge; ADVANCED DATA MODELING — MONTH 4 (4-6 weeks before Month 5 design work): fresh knowledge applied immediately; SCHEDULE IMPACT: each training period reduces productive project output during training (typically 60-80% of normal productivity during training weeks); factor into resource planning and schedule.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — communication plan; distributed teams; asynchronous-first approach
questions.text: A project team spans three time zones: Chicago (UTC-6), London (UTC+0), and Singapore (UTC+8). The communication plan must account for only a 1-hour overlap window available for all three locations simultaneously. How should the communication plan structure synchronous vs. asynchronous communication?

answers.text: Hold all meetings during Chicago business hours — the sponsor is in Chicago
Eliminate all synchronous communication — the time zone gap is too large

Design an asynchronous-first communication plan: use the 1-hour overlap window (approximately 8-9 AM London / 2-3 PM Singapore / 1-2 AM Chicago) sparingly for only the most critical synchronous decisions; document all decisions in writing immediately; leverage async tools (video recordings of updates, written status reports, Slack/Teams threads with clear response windows) as the primary communication mechanism; rotate meeting times monthly to share the inconvenient early/late hours equitably
Hire a communication coordinator in each city to relay messages — intermediaries solve time zone problems

explanations.a: Scheduling all meetings during Chicago business hours means London attends until midnight and Singapore attends at 3 AM. Consistently imposing inconvenient hours on two of three locations creates: burnout for overseas team members; resentment; reduced participation quality (people attending 3 AM meetings are not at their best); team disengagement.
explanations.b: Some synchronous communication is genuinely valuable — critical decisions, complex problem-solving, team relationship building. Complete elimination loses these benefits. The solution is to be SELECTIVE about synchronous communication.
explanations.c: ASYNCHRONOUS-FIRST COMMUNICATION DESIGN for distributed teams: SYNCHRONOUS (use the 1-hour overlap sparingly — 2× per week maximum): weekly project status meeting (most critical status update; all three cities attend once per week; rotate the inconvenient time monthly); emergency decision calls (when a decision cannot wait for async response); team check-in/relationship building meeting (monthly, shorter). ASYNCHRONOUS (primary communication mechanism): DAILY UPDATES: each location posts a brief async status at the end of their workday (Slack/Teams); next location sees the update when they start their day → handoff model; DECISIONS: document in writing with a 24-hour response window; decisions are async by default unless truly time-sensitive; STATUS REPORTS: written, published to project portal; each location reads at their own time; VIDEO RECORDINGS: complex technical explanations recorded and shared; teams watch at their convenience; STRUCTURED RESPONSE WINDOWS: 'Chicago team posts by 5 PM CT; London team responds by 12 PM GMT next day; Singapore team responds by 5 PM SGT the day after' — creates predictable async rhythm. TOOLS: asynchronous project tools (Jira, Confluence, SharePoint) as the source of truth; video recording tools (Loom) for explanations; clear written documentation of all decisions.
explanations.d: Relay intermediaries add communication delays, interpretation errors, and create bottlenecks. Modern async communication tools make intermediaries unnecessary.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — WBS; scope baseline; change control connection
questions.text: A signed WBS and scope statement constitute the project's scope baseline. Three months into execution, a stakeholder asks the team to 'quickly add' a small feature outside the documented scope. A developer agrees and begins work. What principle has been violated and what should have happened?

answers.text: No principle was violated — small features don't require formal change control
Small features don't need change control if they take less than 4 hours — a 4-hour threshold is standard
The developer should have asked the PM's permission via email — informal approval is sufficient

The SCOPE BASELINE INTEGRITY principle was violated: the WBS and scope statement define the authorized scope; any work outside the scope baseline — regardless of size — requires a formal change request; the developer should have declined and directed the stakeholder to submit a change request through the change control process; 'scope creep' occurs precisely this way — many small unauthorized additions accumulate into significant unplanned work

explanations.a: Size does not determine whether change control applies. The WBS represents the totality of authorized scope — any work outside it is unauthorized regardless of effort. Many scope creep incidents begin with 'small' features that cumulatively consume 20-30% of unplanned capacity.
explanations.b: There is no universal '4-hour threshold' for change control. Organizations may define thresholds for change review complexity (e.g., changes under $5K assessed by PM alone; larger changes go to CCB) — but the threshold is for REVIEW LEVEL, not whether change control is needed.
explanations.c: Informal email approval is not formal change control — it lacks: proper impact assessment; authority validation; WBS and schedule update; cost baseline update; audit trail.
explanations.d: SCOPE BASELINE INTEGRITY: THE VIOLATION: the developer began working on unauthorized scope; the stakeholder bypassed the change control process; neither the PM, sponsor, nor CCB was informed or consulted; NO IMPACT ASSESSMENT: even 'small' features have impacts: developer time = schedule impact; potential integration testing additions = testing impact; documentation updates needed = additional scope; potential ripple effects into dependent features; THE CORRECT PROCESS: stakeholder asks developer for a feature addition; CORRECT developer response: 'That sounds like it might be valuable. Let me direct you to the change request process — if it's approved, we can include it in a future sprint (or work package)'; developer does NOT begin work without approval; PM receives the change request; PM assesses impact (effort, schedule, budget, risk); change is presented for approval (PM/sponsor/CCB depending on size); if approved: WBS updated, schedule updated, budget adjusted, stakeholder informed; if rejected: stakeholder notified with rationale. CUMULATIVE SCOPE CREEP: a project with 20 'small' unauthorized additions, each taking 8 hours = 160 developer hours = 1 FTE month of unplanned work = significant schedule and budget impact unaccounted for.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — team assignments in Agile; cross-functional team structure; T-shaped skills
questions.text: An Agile project manager is forming a Scrum team for a new product. Available team members include: 3 Java developers, 1 UI/UX designer, 1 QA engineer, 1 DevOps engineer, and 1 data analyst. The product owner is already identified. How should team assignment be approached differently for Agile than for a traditional Waterfall team?

answers.text: Assign team members to specific feature work streams — each person owns their feature exclusively
Rotate the team every sprint — variety prevents burnout in Agile teams
Only assign senior team members — junior developers don't contribute in Agile

In Agile, the team is cross-functional and collectively owns all sprint work: all members contribute to sprint goals regardless of specialty; the assignment emphasis is on: ensuring the team COLLECTIVELY has all skills needed to deliver a potentially shippable increment (cross-functional); encouraging T-shaped skills (each person has deep expertise + broad awareness of adjacent skills); creating a stable team that builds relationships and improves velocity over time; the Scrum master facilitates; the product owner represents stakeholders

explanations.a: Feature-exclusive ownership creates silos in Agile: the QA engineer can't help a developer when QA has no sprint work; the developer can't help the DevOps engineer during deployment; this creates queue bottlenecks and idle capacity at different sprint phases. Agile team assignment promotes COLLECTIVE OWNERSHIP.
explanations.b: Team rotation every sprint destroys the benefits of team stability in Agile: velocity is established by stable teams; rotating teams produce unpredictable, lower velocity; relationship trust (essential for high-performing Scrum teams) takes months to develop — not sprints.
explanations.c: Junior developers are valuable in Agile teams — they contribute implementation capacity, ask clarifying questions that surface assumptions, and learn through pairing with senior members. Excluding juniors reduces capacity and eliminates development opportunities.
explanations.d: AGILE TEAM ASSIGNMENT PRINCIPLES: CROSS-FUNCTIONAL DESIGN: the team in the scenario collectively has: backend development (3 Java); UI/UX design (1); quality assurance (1); infrastructure/deployment (1); data analysis (1); product owner (business perspective); this team CAN deliver a complete product increment because all needed skills are present; COLLECTIVE OWNERSHIP: in Scrum, the development team collectively commits to sprint goals; individual team members self-assign to stories based on their skills and the sprint's needs; STABLE TEAM: Agile teams improve through experience together — velocity, trust, communication patterns, shared understanding of the codebase all develop over time; rotating teams constantly would reset this; T-SHAPED SKILLS ENCOURAGEMENT: the PM/Scrum master should encourage: the UI/UX designer to develop some front-end coding skills; Java developers to understand basic testing (writing unit tests); QA engineer to understand basic test automation; this creates resilience when team members are unavailable; TEAM SIZE: Scrum recommends 5-9 developers (this team has 7); optimal for communication while maintaining enough capacity; TEAM CAPACITY: plan sprint capacity accounting for all 7 team members' available hours per sprint.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — WBS; resource assignment; integration of WBS and resource planning
questions.text: A project manager has created the WBS for a network infrastructure upgrade with 12 work packages. She now needs to assign resources and estimate effort. Work Package 3 (Network Design) requires a network architect (12 days estimated), Work Package 7 (Security Configuration) requires the same network architect (10 days) and a security engineer (8 days), and Work Package 9 (Cutover Planning) requires the network architect (5 days). The network architect is available 4 days per week (concurrent project commitment). Work Packages 3, 7, and 9 are each dependencies of each other (sequential). What resource loading issue exists and how should the PM address it?

answers.text: No resource loading issue exists — the architect is available 4 days per week and the work packages are sequential
Assign the work to a different resource — never assign the same person to multiple work packages
The architect is over-allocated — 27 days total exceeds 4 days/week capacity

The network architect is required for 27 total days (12+10+5) across three sequential work packages; at 4 days/week availability, the work packages together require 27/4 = 6.75 weeks of calendar time; no over-allocation exists per week (only 4 days needed per week); but the DURATION IMPACT must be reflected in the schedule: WP3 = 3 weeks (12 days ÷ 4 days/week); WP7 = 2.5 weeks (10 days ÷ 4 days/week); WP9 = 1.25 weeks (5 days ÷ 4 days/week); total sequential duration = 6.75 weeks minimum; PM must ensure the schedule reflects this — not 27 calendar days assuming full-time availability

explanations.a: While there is no weekly over-allocation (the architect works 4 days/week on this project consistently), the DURATION CALCULATION is where the issue lies. The PM must correctly calculate that 12 days of work at 4 days/week = 3 calendar weeks (not 12 calendar days), and build this into the schedule.
explanations.b: Assigning the same expert to multiple sequential work packages is normal and appropriate — this is exactly what specialized resources do. The PM's job is to calculate realistic durations based on part-time availability.
explanations.c: Over-allocation occurs when someone is assigned more than 100% capacity (e.g., 4 days/week on this project + 3 days/week on another = 7 days in a 5-day week). Working 4 days/week consistently is NOT over-allocation — it's part-time assignment. The issue is duration calculation, not over-allocation.
explanations.d: RESOURCE LOADING CALCULATION: NETWORK ARCHITECT AVAILABILITY: 4 days/week (80% allocation; 1 day/week on another project). WORK PACKAGE DURATIONS (accounting for availability): WP3 (Network Design): 12 days of effort ÷ 4 days/week = 3 calendar weeks; WP7 (Security Configuration): 10 days of effort (architect) ÷ 4 days/week = 2.5 calendar weeks; CONCURRENT WORK: the security engineer (8 days) can work on WP7 while the architect works their 4 days/week; security engineer's 8 days = 1.6 calendar weeks at full time; WP7 DURATION = max(architect 2.5 weeks, security engineer 1.6 weeks) = 2.5 weeks (architect is the constraint); WP9 (Cutover Planning): 5 days of effort ÷ 4 days/week = 1.25 calendar weeks. TOTAL SEQUENTIAL DURATION: 3 + 2.5 + 1.25 = 6.75 calendar weeks; PM SCHEDULE IMPACT: a schedule that shows WP3 as 12 days, WP7 as 10 days, WP9 as 5 days would underestimate the calendar duration by approximately 2 weeks (27 days ÷ 5 days/week = 5.4 calendar weeks vs. actual 6.75 calendar weeks); CORRECT APPROACH: schedule shows realistic calendar durations based on resource availability (not effort-only); if the 6.75-week duration is too long, the PM may: negotiate to increase architect allocation on this project; add a second architect for WP7 (parallelism reduces WP7 architect constraint); accept the longer duration and manage stakeholder expectations.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — training plan; end-user training; change management integration
questions.text: A project manager is planning the end-user training component for a new ERP system. 500 employees across 5 departments will need training before go-live (3 months away). Each department has different ERP module responsibilities. What should the training plan include?

answers.text: Send all 500 employees to one all-day training session one week before go-live

A role-based, phased training plan: identify roles and their ERP module usage; develop role-specific training curricula (accounts payable clerks don't need warehouse management training); sequence training 4-6 weeks before go-live (enough time to practice but close enough to retain); use multiple training modalities (instructor-led for complex workflows; e-learning for system navigation; job aids and quick reference cards for post-go-live support); conduct train-the-trainer for department training leads; schedule practice sessions in a sandbox environment; measure training completion before go-live authorization
Only train the department heads — they will train their teams informally
Training can happen post-go-live — users learn best from live systems

explanations.a: One all-day session for 500 employees one week before go-live: lacks enough lead time for practice (users need 3-6 weeks of practice time between training and go-live to build confidence); can't differentiate by role (accounts payable and warehouse staff need completely different training); produces a training event rather than a learning experience.
explanations.b: COMPREHENSIVE END-USER TRAINING PLAN: ROLE-BASED CURRICULUM: identify all ERP user roles (accounts payable, accounts receivable, procurement, warehouse, HR, finance management, etc.); map each role to the specific ERP modules and workflows they'll use; develop role-specific training guides and exercises; 500 employees × 5 roles ≈ 100 employees per role on average; PHASED TRAINING TIMELINE (3 months, go-live in Month 3): Month 1 — develop training materials + set up sandbox environment; Month 2 — train-the-trainer sessions for department leads; Month 2-3 — role-based training groups (2-3 weeks per batch); 4-6 weeks before go-live is the optimal window: close enough to retain knowledge; enough time for supervised practice in sandbox; TRAINING MODALITIES: instructor-led: complex process workflows; group Q&A; e-learning: system navigation; reference data setup; job aids: quick reference cards, step-by-step checklists for common transactions; video tutorials: available for post-go-live support; SANDBOX PRACTICE: schedule supervised sandbox sessions after each training module; users practice their actual job workflows on test data; COMPLETION TRACKING: training attendance and completion are gate criteria for go-live authorization; departments below 90% completion trigger go-live escalation review.
explanations.c: Department heads training their teams informally produces: inconsistent training quality; missing critical system nuances; no documentation of training content; no way to measure readiness. Formal training provides consistency and accountability.
explanations.d: Go-live with untrained users produces: high volume of support tickets; errors in live transactions; user frustration and ERP rejection; potential financial reporting errors (for finance modules). Training before go-live is essential for ERP adoption success.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — WBS; WBS dictionary; work package numbering; WBS code
questions.text: A project manager creates the WBS for an IT security assessment project with this structure: 1.0 IT Security Assessment; 1.1 Discovery & Scoping; 1.2 Vulnerability Assessment; 1.3 Penetration Testing; 1.4 Reporting; 1.5 Remediation Support; 1.2.1 Network Vulnerability Scan; 1.2.2 Application Vulnerability Scan; 1.2.3 Database Scan. A team member asks: 'What is the WBS dictionary and why do we need it?' How should the PM explain?

answers.text: 'The WBS dictionary is just a glossary of technical terms used in the project'

'The WBS dictionary provides the detailed description for each WBS element: for each work package (like 1.2.1 Network Vulnerability Scan), it defines: what work will be performed; who is responsible; what resources are needed; duration estimate; cost estimate; acceptance criteria; predecessor/successor relationships; quality standards; contractual implications — turning each WBS element from a label into a fully defined work package that can be estimated, assigned, and tracked'
'The WBS dictionary lists all team members assigned to the project'
'The WBS dictionary is a legal document required for all government contracts only'

explanations.a: A technical glossary is a separate document. The WBS dictionary is a scope management tool that provides the detailed definition of each work package.
explanations.b: WBS DICTIONARY CONTENT FOR EACH WORK PACKAGE: For Work Package 1.2.1 (Network Vulnerability Scan), the WBS dictionary entry would include: CODE AND TITLE: 1.2.1 Network Vulnerability Scan; DESCRIPTION: 'Automated and manual scanning of all identified network components (IP range: [defined list]) using [specific tool]. Includes: open port scanning; service enumeration; OS identification; known vulnerability identification against NVD database.'; ACCOUNTABLE PERSON: Lead Security Engineer; RESOURCES: 1 Senior Security Engineer (3 days); 1 scanning tool license; DURATION ESTIMATE: 3 working days (includes scan execution + data analysis); COST ESTIMATE: $2,400 labor + $500 tool license = $2,900; ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: Scan covers 100% of IP range; Report includes all CVSS 7.0+ vulnerabilities; False positive review completed; PREDECESSOR: 1.1.3 (Network mapping complete); SUCCESSOR: 1.4.1 (Reporting begins after all scans); QUALITY REQUIREMENTS: Scan performed with [specific scanner] at [specific sensitivity settings]; peer review of findings required; WHY THE DICTIONARY MATTERS: the WBS element label ('1.2.1 Network Vulnerability Scan') is just a label — the dictionary turns the label into an actionable, estimable, assignable work definition. Without it, two team members will interpret '1.2.1' differently.
explanations.c: Team assignments are in the resource assignment matrix — not the WBS dictionary.
explanations.d: WBS dictionaries are a best practice for all projects of appropriate complexity — not a legal requirement specific to government contracts.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — preliminary scope statement to detailed scope; requirements as scope input
questions.text: A project manager notes that the planning phase begins with a 'preliminary scope statement' (from the charter) and produces a 'detailed scope statement.' What activities in the planning phase transform the preliminary scope into the detailed scope?

answers.text: The scope statement is automatically detailed once the project charter is signed — no additional activity is needed

Requirements gathering and analysis: through workshops, interviews, and prototyping with stakeholders, the project team elicits detailed requirements that define specifically what each deliverable must do; these requirements are documented, analyzed for completeness and consistency, prioritized, and validated — they form the detailed specification that transforms the high-level scope description into a detailed, measurable scope statement
The vendor proposes the detailed scope — the project team only approves it
The project manager writes the detailed scope alone based on their professional judgment

explanations.a: The charter's scope is intentionally high-level (written before detailed requirements are known). Transforming it into a detailed, executable scope requires active requirements elicitation work — it does not happen automatically.
explanations.b: REQUIREMENTS GATHERING as the transformation activity: PRELIMINARY SCOPE (from charter): 'Implement a cloud-based customer portal covering account management and order tracking'; REQUIREMENTS GATHERING ACTIVITIES: WORKSHOPS: structured sessions with business stakeholders (3-5 sessions with 8-12 participants); JAD sessions: joint business/IT sessions to co-design requirements; INTERVIEWS: one-on-one conversations with key users, SMEs, and technical stakeholders; SURVEYS AND QUESTIONNAIRES: for larger user populations; PROTOTYPE REVIEW: showing early wireframes or mockups to elicit requirements; DOCUMENT ANALYSIS: reviewing existing system documentation, process flows, business rules; OBSERVATION: watching users work with existing systems to discover undocumented requirements; REQUIREMENTS OUTPUT: functional requirements (what the system must do); non-functional requirements (performance, security, usability standards); business rules (how the system must behave in specific conditions); data requirements (what data must be managed, its structure, retention); SCOPE TRANSFORMATION: with detailed requirements, the scope statement can specify: specific portal features (account management includes: view profile, update contact info, view order history, download invoices, manage payment methods — 5 specific capabilities); performance standards (page load <2 seconds at 1,000 concurrent users); integration requirements (must integrate with SAP for order data, Salesforce for customer profile); exclusions become specific ('mobile native app is NOT included; web responsive only').
explanations.c: For internal projects, the project team elicits and defines the requirements with business stakeholders. Vendors may propose a solution in competitive procurement — but the organization defines its requirements first.
explanations.d: A PM writing scope alone (without stakeholder input) produces: incomplete requirements (the PM doesn't know all business nuances); incorrect requirements (PM assumptions about business needs); stakeholder rejection (they weren't consulted); scope disputes (stakeholders claim requirements were wrong).

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — resource pool review vs. team assignment; distinction and sequence
questions.text: What is the DIFFERENCE between 'reviewing the resource pool' and 'developing team assignments' during the planning phase, and why are they separate activities?

answers.text: They are the same activity with different names — no meaningful distinction

Reviewing the resource pool assesses what's AVAILABLE (inventory of skills, current commitments, availability windows, capacity); developing team assignments determines HOW available resources are ALLOCATED to specific project work packages (who does what, when, at what percentage); the pool review comes first to understand what's possible before assigning what's needed
Resource pool review is done by HR; team assignment is done by the PM — they involve different departments with no connection
Resource pool review happens after team assignment — first assign the team, then check if they're available

explanations.a: The two activities have different purposes, different inputs, different outputs, and different stakeholders. Treating them as identical misses the distinct analytical value of each.
explanations.b: RESOURCE POOL REVIEW vs. TEAM ASSIGNMENT: RESOURCE POOL REVIEW (first): QUESTION: 'What do we have to work with?'; INPUT: organizational resource directory, current project allocations, skills inventory; ACTIVITIES: catalog all potential resources (internal + external); assess each resource's: current commitments (when are they available?), skills and experience (match to project needs?), cost (internal rate vs. external contractor); identify gaps between what the project needs and what's available; OUTPUT: resource availability matrix — who is available, when, at what capacity; RESULT: the PM knows the constraints within which team assignment must work. TEAM ASSIGNMENT (second): QUESTION: 'How do we allocate available resources to project work?'; INPUT: resource availability matrix (from pool review); WBS work packages (what needs to be done); skill requirements per work package; ACTIVITIES: match skills to work packages; assign specific people to specific work packages; determine allocation percentages; check for conflicts (same person assigned to concurrent conflicting work packages); create resource assignments in the project management tool; OUTPUT: responsibility assignment matrix; updated project schedule with specific resources assigned; SEQUENCE LOGIC: you cannot meaningfully assign resources to work packages without first knowing who is available and when — pool review enables informed assignment decisions.
explanations.c: Both activities are performed by the project manager (with input from functional managers for the pool review). They are sequential activities within the same planning process, not separate departmental functions.
explanations.d: Resource pool review must come BEFORE team assignment — you cannot assign resources effectively without first understanding their availability, skills, and current commitments. Assigning first and checking availability second produces assignments that must be completely redone.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — scope baseline; scope management plan; preventing scope creep
questions.text: A project manager has created the detailed scope statement and WBS. She wants to formally establish the scope baseline. What constitutes the scope baseline and why is baselining the scope important?

answers.text: The scope baseline is just the project charter — no additional documentation is needed

The scope baseline consists of: the approved project scope statement + the approved WBS + the WBS dictionary; it is the approved, controlled reference that defines project scope against which all scope changes are measured; baselining is important because: (1) it creates a performance measurement reference point; (2) any change from the baseline requires a formal change request; (3) it prevents unauthorized scope additions; (4) it provides the basis for measuring project success
The scope baseline is established after the project is complete — you baseline the final delivered scope
Only the WBS is needed for the scope baseline — the scope statement is redundant

explanations.a: The project charter has a high-level scope description — insufficient for execution-phase scope management. The detailed scope statement and WBS are the execution-phase documents that constitute the scope baseline.
explanations.b: SCOPE BASELINE — THREE COMPONENTS: APPROVED SCOPE STATEMENT: the detailed description of what is in and out of scope, including deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions, constraints, and assumptions; APPROVED WBS: the hierarchical decomposition of all authorized scope into work packages; APPROVED WBS DICTIONARY: the detailed description of each work package; TOGETHER THESE THREE constitute the complete, detailed definition of the project's authorized scope. WHY BASELINING MATTERS: PERFORMANCE MEASUREMENT: the scope baseline is the 'what we planned to deliver'; actual deliveries are measured against it; CHANGE CONTROL TRIGGER: any request to add, remove, or modify scope is measured against the baseline; deviations require a formal change request; DISPUTE RESOLUTION: when a stakeholder claims 'this feature should have been included,' the scope baseline provides the definitive reference; BUDGET AND SCHEDULE ALIGNMENT: the schedule and cost estimates are built FROM the WBS; changes to the WBS invalidate the associated schedule and cost estimates — hence scope changes require integrated change control (updating scope, schedule, AND cost baselines together). BASELINING PROCESS: scope statement, WBS, and WBS dictionary are reviewed and approved by the sponsor; once approved: documents are version-controlled; changes require formal change request and re-approval; the approval date marks when the baseline is established.
explanations.c: Baselining after project completion defeats the purpose of a baseline. A baseline must be established BEFORE execution so that execution performance can be measured against the planned scope.
explanations.d: The scope statement provides the narrative and acceptance criteria context that makes the WBS meaningful. The WBS alone (a list of numbered deliverable titles) is incomplete without the scope statement's description and acceptance criteria.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — all planning elements integrated; planning quality assessment
questions.text: A PMO director reviews the planning phase deliverables for a $6M data platform project before authorizing execution. She finds: WBS has 45 work packages but is missing training and change management; the communication plan covers the project team but not the 200 end users or the regulatory compliance team; the resource assignments show 3 developers at 120% capacity in Months 4-6; and the scope statement has deliverables but no explicit exclusions or acceptance criteria. Score each problem by severity and prescribe corrections.

answers.text: All four problems are minor — proceed with execution and fix as you go
All four are equally severe — delay execution indefinitely until all are resolved

(1) WBS missing training/change management: HIGH severity — these omissions will cause cost and schedule overruns when the work is eventually done; corrective: add work packages for training and change management with effort estimates; (2) Communication plan gaps: HIGH — 200 end users and compliance team without communication creates adoption failure and compliance violations; corrective: add stakeholder-specific communication tracks; (3) Developer over-allocation at 120%: CRITICAL — unsustainable; will cause burnout, quality issues, and schedule slippage; corrective: resource level before execution begins; (4) Scope statement without exclusions/acceptance criteria: HIGH — will cause scope disputes and unclear completion criteria; corrective: add explicit exclusions and measurable acceptance criteria for each deliverable; ALL four must be corrected before execution authorization
Only the resource over-allocation matters — the other three can be resolved during execution

explanations.a: These are material planning deficiencies on a $6M project. 'Fix as you go' means discovering training and change management work mid-execution (scope addition, unplanned cost), missing end-user communications (adoption failure), burning out developers (quality drops, attrition risk), and having scope disputes about what 'done' means. Not minor problems.
explanations.b: The four problems have different remediation timelines — the resource over-allocation is most urgent (cannot begin execution at 120%); the others can be corrected quickly (1-2 weeks of focused work each). 'Indefinitely delay' is an overcorrection.
explanations.c: SEVERITY AND REMEDIATION: (1) WBS MISSING TRAINING AND CHANGE MANAGEMENT (HIGH): IMPACT: 200 users will be untrained at go-live → adoption failure; change management vacuum → resistance without facilitated transition; estimated unplanned cost: $200-400K (training program + change manager + materials); CORRECTIVE: add WBS entries for: User Training Program (curriculum development, delivery, sandbox environment); Change Management (impact assessment, communications, training coordination, resistance management); estimate effort and cost; update schedule and budget. (2) COMMUNICATION PLAN GAPS (HIGH): 200 end users with no communication plan → users unaware of changes → go-live disruption, negative adoption; compliance team without communication → regulatory findings post-deployment; CORRECTIVE: add communication tracks for end users (monthly newsletter + pre-go-live training comms) and compliance team (compliance milestone updates + audit trail access). (3) 120% DEVELOPER OVER-ALLOCATION (CRITICAL — fix before execution): a developer working 120% for 3 months produces: reduced quality (tired developers make more mistakes); burnout risk (medical issues, resignations mid-project); schedule slippage as productivity drops; CORRECTIVE: resource level BEFORE execution; options: reduce scope in Months 4-6 (MVP approach); add a contractor developer for the overloaded period; extend the schedule; (4) MISSING EXCLUSIONS AND ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA (HIGH): without acceptance criteria, project cannot be objectively closed ('done' is in the eye of the beholder); without exclusions, scope disputes arise mid-project; CORRECTIVE: for each deliverable: add at least 2-3 measurable acceptance criteria; add an explicit exclusions section listing 5-10 items stakeholders might assume are included.
explanations.d: All four are critical for a successful $6M project execution. The resource issue is the MOST critical (cannot begin at 120%), but the others are equally important for project outcomes.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — training plan; training vs. change management distinction
questions.text: A project sponsor asks: 'What's the difference between the training plan and the change management plan? They both seem to be about helping people use the new system.' How should the project manager clarify the distinction?

answers.text: 'They are the same thing — training and change management both involve teaching people new things'

'Training plan: focuses on SKILLS — teaching users HOW to use the new system (where to click, how to navigate, how to complete tasks); Change management plan: focuses on BEHAVIOR AND ADOPTION — addressing WHY people should change (making the case for change), managing RESISTANCE (addressing fears and concerns), and supporting the TRANSITION of people from current state behaviors to new behaviors; both are needed because training without change management produces technically competent but unmotivated resistors; change management without training produces motivated users who don't know how to operate the system'
'Training is for junior staff; change management is for senior leadership — they target different audiences'
'Training is more expensive so it is more important — change management is nice-to-have'

explanations.a: The two disciplines address fundamentally different aspects of user adoption. 'Teaching people new things' oversimplifies the distinction — training teaches skills; change management addresses the psychological and cultural dimensions of change.
explanations.b: TRAINING vs. CHANGE MANAGEMENT — COMPLEMENTARY DISCIPLINES: TRAINING PLAN — SKILLS FOCUS: WHAT: how to use the new system functionally; QUESTIONS ANSWERED: How do I submit a purchase requisition? How do I process a vendor invoice? How do I run the accounts payable aging report?; OUTCOME: USER COMPETENCE — users can perform required tasks in the new system; METHODS: instructor-led sessions; e-learning modules; sandbox practice; job aids; MEASURED BY: training completion rate; post-training assessment scores. CHANGE MANAGEMENT PLAN — ADOPTION FOCUS: WHAT: why change is needed and how to navigate the transition; QUESTIONS ADDRESSED: Why are we changing? What's wrong with the current system? (awareness); What does this mean for me? (understanding); How does it affect my role? (acknowledgment); How do I successfully transition? (adoption); Why is this better for me and the organization? (commitment); OUTCOME: USER WILLINGNESS — users are motivated to use the new system; METHODS: leadership communications; stakeholder engagement sessions; resistance management; success stories; MEASURED BY: adoption rate post-go-live; user satisfaction scores; reduction in workarounds. WHY BOTH ARE NEEDED: training without change management → users know HOW but resist WHY → low adoption, workarounds, shadow systems; change management without training → users want to change but don't know HOW → frustration, errors, low productivity; both together → competent AND motivated users → successful adoption.
explanations.c: Both training and change management address all levels of the organization — though the content and approach differ by seniority and role.
explanations.d: Adequate change management can prevent entire project abandonment due to resistance — it is not a nice-to-have. Many ERP project failures are attributed to insufficient change management, not technical failures.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — sequencing all planning activities; interdependencies between plans
questions.text: A project manager is sequencing the planning phase activities for a 9-month project. She identifies dependencies between planning deliverables: the WBS cannot be created before scope is defined; the schedule cannot be built before the WBS; resource assignments cannot be finalized before the schedule shows when each work package happens; the budget cannot be finalized before resource assignments; the risk register needs WBS and resource assignments as context. Which planning sequence is MOST logical?

answers.text: Start with the budget — financial constraints define everything else

Correct sequence: (1) Requirements gathering → (2) Detailed scope statement → (3) WBS + WBS dictionary → (4) Activity sequencing and schedule → (5) Resource pool review → (6) Team assignments + training plan → (7) Resource loading and leveling → (8) Detailed budget (cost estimates by work package) → (9) Risk register → (10) Communication plan → (11) Quality plan → (12) Procurement plan → (13) Integrated project management plan review and baseline
All planning activities can be done simultaneously — dependencies don't matter in planning
Start with the risk register — risks define everything else in the plan

explanations.a: Starting with the budget before scope is defined produces a budget disconnected from actual project requirements. Budget authority ($X million) comes from the charter; the DETAILED budget by work package requires the WBS to exist first.
explanations.b: PLANNING PHASE SEQUENCE WITH RATIONALE: (1) REQUIREMENTS GATHERING: collects the detailed information that defines what will be built; transforms the charter's high-level scope into specific deliverables; (2) DETAILED SCOPE STATEMENT: documents what is in/out of scope with acceptance criteria; requires completed requirements; (3) WBS + WBS DICTIONARY: decomposes the approved scope into work packages; requires completed scope statement (100% rule); (4) ACTIVITY SEQUENCING AND SCHEDULE: sequences WBS work packages into a timeline; identifies dependencies; calculates critical path; requires WBS; (5) RESOURCE POOL REVIEW: assesses available resources; must happen after schedule shows WHEN resources are needed; (6) TEAM ASSIGNMENTS + TRAINING PLAN: assigns specific people to work packages; identifies training needs; requires resource pool review and schedule; (7) RESOURCE LOADING AND LEVELING: checks for over-allocations; adjusts schedule based on resource constraints; requires team assignments; (8) DETAILED BUDGET: rolls up work package costs; requires finalized resource assignments (who works how long at what rate); (9) RISK REGISTER: identifies risks in the context of the full plan; meaningful risk identification requires knowing scope, schedule, resources, and cost; (10-12) COMMUNICATION, QUALITY, PROCUREMENT PLANS: can proceed in parallel once the core scope/schedule/resource/budget framework is established; (13) INTEGRATED PLAN REVIEW AND BASELINE: all plans reviewed together; inconsistencies resolved; baselines established.
explanations.c: Planning activities have real dependencies — you cannot meaningfully build a schedule before the WBS exists; you cannot finalize the budget before resource assignments are made. Ignoring dependencies produces plans that are internally inconsistent.
explanations.d: Risks are identified in the context of the project's scope, schedule, and resource plan. A risk register created before these elements exist produces generic risks ('scope may change; schedule may slip') rather than specific, actionable risk assessments.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — develop project schedule; schedule components; Gantt chart
questions.text: A project schedule is developed during the planning phase. Which elements are required to create a meaningful project schedule?

answers.text: Activities (tasks derived from WBS work packages), duration estimates for each activity, dependencies between activities, resource assignments, milestone dates, and the project start and end dates — together these produce a time-phased schedule that can calculate critical path and float
Only a list of tasks — tasks are sufficient for a project schedule
Only the project start date and end date — everything else is calculated automatically
Only team members' names — the schedule should be organized by person, not by task

explanations.a: PROJECT SCHEDULE ELEMENTS: ACTIVITIES: derived from WBS work packages; the lowest-level tasks that can be estimated and tracked; DURATION ESTIMATES: how long will each activity take? (using PERT, analogous, or parametric estimating); DEPENDENCIES: which activities must precede which others? (FS, SS, FF, SF relationships); RESOURCE ASSIGNMENTS: who does each activity? at what capacity?; together with duration, this determines the calendar timeline; MILESTONES: significant events (deliverable completion, phase gates, contractual deadlines) with zero duration; START AND END DATES: anchors for the schedule calculation; PROJECT SCHEDULE OUTPUTS: network diagram showing dependencies; Gantt chart showing time-phased activities; critical path (longest path determines project end date); float/slack for non-critical activities; resource histogram showing resource utilization over time; SCHEDULE DEVELOPMENT PROCESS: (1) define activities (from WBS); (2) sequence activities (determine dependencies); (3) estimate durations; (4) assign resources; (5) develop schedule (calculate dates); (6) optimize (level resources, compress where needed); (7) baseline the schedule.
explanations.b: A list of tasks without durations, dependencies, or resource assignments is a work inventory, not a schedule. It cannot answer 'when will this be done?' or 'what happens if Task X is delayed?'
explanations.c: Start and end dates alone cannot produce a schedule — the schedule must derive the end date from the sequenced, estimated, resourced activities (or verify that given start/end dates are achievable).
explanations.d: Person-centric schedules (Gantt charts organized by person) are resource histograms, not project schedules. Schedules organize work by deliverable and timeline, not by the individual performing it.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — schedule baseline; approved schedule plan; performance measurement
questions.text: What is a SCHEDULE BASELINE and why is it important in project management?

answers.text: The schedule baseline is the approved, fixed version of the project schedule against which actual performance is measured; it is retained throughout the project and updated only through formal change control; it enables the PM to calculate schedule variance (SV = EV − PV) and identify when the project is ahead of or behind plan
The schedule baseline is the original estimated schedule; it is deleted once work begins and replaced by the actual schedule
The schedule baseline is the project manager's personal estimate of how long the project should take
The schedule baseline is updated automatically every week to reflect actual progress — it always shows the current plan

explanations.a: SCHEDULE BASELINE: the approved version of the schedule model that can only be changed through formal change control procedures. WHAT IT IS: the time-phased plan of ALL project activities with start dates, end dates, and milestone dates; represents the plan as of the moment of approval; PERFORMANCE MEASUREMENT: by comparing actual progress to the baseline, the PM calculates: Schedule Variance (SV = Earned Value − Planned Value): SV negative = behind schedule; Schedule Performance Index (SPI = EV / PV): SPI < 1.0 = behind schedule; BASELINE INTEGRITY: the baseline should NOT be changed to match actual performance — doing so destroys the measurement reference point; the only legitimate baseline changes are through formal change control when: authorized scope changes affect the schedule; approved risk responses change the timeline; external events force recognized changes to the delivery date. VISUAL: on a Gantt chart, the baseline appears as a separate line showing the original planned dates; actual dates are shown differently (often as a percentage complete bar); RELATIONSHIP TO OTHER BASELINES: together with scope baseline and cost baseline, the schedule baseline forms the PERFORMANCE MEASUREMENT BASELINE.
explanations.b: The baseline is never deleted — it is the permanent reference point. Deleting it would make it impossible to measure whether the project performed as planned.
explanations.c: The schedule baseline reflects the team-developed, sponsor-approved schedule — not any individual's personal estimate.
explanations.d: A baseline that automatically updates to reflect actual progress would be an actual schedule, not a baseline. A baseline by definition remains fixed for comparison purposes.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — minimum viable product (MVP); feature prioritization
questions.text: In the planning phase, a product owner develops a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) definition. What is the MVP?

answers.text: The MVP is the smallest version of the product that delivers sufficient value to be useful, allows the team to test key assumptions with real users, and can be deployed to gather feedback for future development — containing only the core features necessary for it to work as intended
The MVP is the final, most complete version of the product with all features
The MVP is a prototype or mock-up that is never deployed to production
The MVP is the version with only the cheapest features — cost minimization defines the MVP

explanations.a: MINIMUM VIABLE PRODUCT (MVP): a version of a product with JUST ENOUGH features to: DELIVER VALUE: be genuinely useful to early adopters; TEST KEY ASSUMPTIONS: validate that the product addresses the intended problem; GATHER FEEDBACK: enable real users to interact with the product and provide actionable feedback. MVP CHARACTERISTICS: minimum = the smallest scope that achieves the value goal; viable = actually deployable and usable (not a prototype); product = a real, functioning system (not a concept); MVP IN PLANNING: during planning, the product owner defines which features constitute the MVP — separating must-have (MVP) from nice-to-have (future releases); this MVP scope defines the first release target; EXAMPLES: MVP of a ride-sharing app: users can request a ride, drivers can accept, payment processes — NO surge pricing, NO scheduled rides, NO luxury options; these come after the MVP validates that the core concept works; MVP VALUE: reduces risk by getting real user feedback before building a full-featured product; if the core concept doesn't work, you learn this with minimum investment; if it works, subsequent features are validated against a functioning foundation.
explanations.b: The MVP is the MINIMUM, not the maximum. It is by definition the smallest useful version, designed to enable learning with the least investment.
explanations.c: An MVP is deployed to real production users — it is not a prototype. A prototype or mock-up demonstrates design; an MVP demonstrates actual functionality in the real environment.
explanations.d: The MVP is defined by VALUE and VIABILITY, not by cost. The cheapest features may not be the most critical. MVP prioritization is based on which features are essential for the product to be useful at all.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — QA plan; quality management planning
questions.text: A Quality Assurance (QA) plan is developed during the planning phase. What is the PRIMARY purpose of the QA plan?

answers.text: To define how quality will be PLANNED, MEASURED, and CONTROLLED throughout the project — including quality standards, testing approaches, acceptance criteria, audit schedules, and quality improvement processes
To create the list of defects found during testing — the QA plan tracks bugs
To replace the test plan — the QA plan is identical to the test plan
To evaluate team member performance — the QA plan grades each developer's code quality

explanations.a: QA PLAN PURPOSE AND CONTENT: QUALITY STANDARDS: what standards the project's deliverables must meet (industry standards, regulatory requirements, organizational quality benchmarks); QUALITY OBJECTIVES: specific, measurable quality targets (e.g., defect density <2 defects/1,000 LOC; test coverage ≥90%; customer satisfaction ≥4.0/5.0); QUALITY ACTIVITIES: planned quality assurance activities throughout the project: code reviews; design reviews; process audits; testing cycles (unit, integration, regression, UAT); TESTING APPROACH: test strategy; types of testing; testing tools and environments; ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: measurable criteria each deliverable must meet to be accepted; QUALITY ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES: who is accountable for quality at each level?; QUALITY METRICS: how will quality be measured and reported?; QUALITY IMPROVEMENT PROCESS: how will quality issues be identified, tracked, and resolved?; QA vs. QC DISTINCTION: QA Plan = quality PROCESS planning (proactive, preventive); QC activities = quality PRODUCT inspection (reactive, detective); both are needed; the QA plan governs both.
explanations.b: A defect list/bug tracker is a quality control execution artifact — it is created during execution, not during planning. The QA plan defines the strategy; the defect tracker tracks results.
explanations.c: The QA plan and test plan serve different scopes: QA plan governs ALL quality activities across the entire project lifecycle; test plan governs the specific testing activities for a particular release or phase; the test plan is a subset of the QA plan's testing section.
explanations.d: Developer performance management is an HR activity — not a QA plan function. QA plans focus on product and process quality, not individual performance evaluation.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — develop risk assessment; risk register; probability and impact
questions.text: The risk assessment developed during planning produces a risk register. What information should the risk register capture for each identified risk?

answers.text: Risk ID, risk description, risk category, probability of occurrence, impact if it occurs, risk score (probability × impact), risk response strategy, risk owner, trigger events, contingency plan, and current status
Only the risk description — a brief description of each risk is sufficient
Only financial risks — the risk register tracks only budget-related risks
Only the risks that have already occurred — the risk register tracks historical events

explanations.a: COMPREHENSIVE RISK REGISTER CONTENT: RISK ID: unique identifier for tracking and reference; DESCRIPTION: clear statement of the risk condition and potential impact ('If [uncertain condition occurs], then [impact on project objectives]'); CATEGORY: schedule, cost, scope, quality, resource, technical, external, organizational; PROBABILITY: likelihood of the risk occurring (High/Medium/Low or numerical %; common scale: H=70-100%, M=30-70%, L=0-30%); IMPACT: severity of effect on project objectives if the risk occurs (H/M/L or 1-10 scale; varies by objective: schedule impact, cost impact, scope impact); RISK SCORE: probability × impact = risk priority ranking; RISK RESPONSE STRATEGY: Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate, Accept (for negative risks); Exploit, Share, Enhance, Accept (for positive risks/opportunities); RISK OWNER: specific person responsible for monitoring the risk and executing the response; TRIGGER EVENTS: what conditions indicate the risk is about to materialize?; CONTINGENCY PLAN: what actions will be taken if the risk materializes?; CURRENT STATUS: Active, Monitoring, Occurred, Closed; THE VALUE OF COMPLETENESS: a complete risk register enables: prioritization of monitoring effort (high-score risks get more attention); effective risk response planning; clear accountability for each risk; early warning through trigger event monitoring.
explanations.b: A risk description alone provides no basis for prioritization (which risks need the most attention?), response planning (what will we do if this happens?), or monitoring (who watches for this risk?). A description-only register is a risk inventory, not a risk management tool.
explanations.c: Risk registers cover ALL types of project risks: technical, schedule, cost, resource, external, organizational, quality — not just financial.
explanations.d: A risk register tracks FUTURE POTENTIAL EVENTS (risks), not historical events that have already occurred. Issues that have already occurred are tracked in the issue register.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — transition plan/knowledge transfer; handoff to operations
questions.text: Why is a TRANSITION PLAN developed during the project planning phase rather than at the end of the project?

answers.text: Developing the transition plan during planning ensures that: knowledge transfer activities are built into the project schedule; operations team requirements shape the project's deliverables from the start; runbook and documentation work are included in the project scope and WBS; and go-live support staffing and training for operations are planned before they're urgently needed
It is not developed in planning — transition plans are created after the project is complete
Transition plans are only needed for government projects
The transition plan replaces the project management plan — one document covers everything

explanations.a: TRANSITION PLAN IN PLANNING — WHY EARLY MATTERS: SCOPE INCLUSION: if transition activities (operations runbooks, knowledge transfer sessions, handover documentation) are not planned early, they won't be in the WBS → won't be budgeted → won't be scheduled → will either be skipped (creating operational failures) or rushed at the end (poor quality); OPERATIONS TEAM REQUIREMENTS SHAPE DESIGN: operations teams may require: specific monitoring configurations (must be built into the system design); alerting thresholds (must be documented during development, not after); integration with existing ITSM tools (must be planned from the start); these requirements can only be incorporated if the operations team is engaged during planning; OPERATIONS READINESS TIMING: training the operations team requires: time to learn the new system; time to practice with the system; time to develop runbooks and procedures; if planned in advance, all of this fits into the project timeline; if discovered at go-live, there is no time; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER MILESTONES: can be built into the project schedule as formal deliverables with acceptance criteria.
explanations.b: Planning the transition after the project is complete creates: undocumented systems (documentation was never in scope); unprepared operations teams (no time for proper handover training); rushed knowledge transfer that misses critical information; go-live without operations readiness — leading to post-launch failures.
