explanations.c: All projects that deliver something that must be operated long-term need transition plans — software systems, infrastructure, processes, data warehouses, etc.
explanations.d: The transition plan is one component of the broader project management plan — it doesn't replace the overall plan.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — project schedule; schedule compression; critical path and float
questions.text: A project manager builds the project schedule for a 12-month ERP implementation. After initial scheduling, the calculated project end date is Month 15 — 3 months later than the required go-live. The project has a contractual deadline for Month 12. What schedule compression options should the PM evaluate and what are the trade-offs?

answers.text: Accept the Month 15 end date — contractual deadlines can be missed if the schedule shows it's not achievable
Simply move the end date to Month 12 in the scheduling tool — changing the date compresses the schedule
Extend the team's work hours to 12-hour days — overtime always compresses schedules by the overtime ratio

Evaluate schedule compression options: fast-tracking (overlap sequential activities where soft logic allows — risks rework if early outputs change); crashing (add resources to critical path activities — increases cost); scope reduction (defer non-critical features to Phase 2 — reduces project value delivered); a hybrid approach may achieve the 3-month compression most effectively; the PM must present options with trade-offs to the sponsor before choosing

explanations.a: A contractual deadline cannot simply be accepted as missed — it has legal and financial consequences. The PM must analyze all compression options before concluding that the deadline cannot be met.
explanations.b: Moving the end date in the scheduling tool without changing the actual activities, durations, or resources is meaningless — the tool will still calculate Month 15 completion. The date change is cosmetic, not real schedule compression.
explanations.c: 12-hour days for 3 months produces: physical and mental exhaustion; declining productivity after 2-3 weeks of sustained overtime; higher error rates (tired workers make more mistakes); burnout and attrition risk; and diminishing returns. Research shows productivity gains from overtime disappear after 3-4 weeks and can produce negative net output after 2 months.
explanations.d: SCHEDULE COMPRESSION OPTIONS and trade-offs: FAST-TRACKING: overlap activities that were originally planned sequentially; example: begin configuration while requirements are still being finalized; RISK: if requirements change, configuration work may need to be redone (rework); WHEN APPROPRIATE: soft-logic dependencies where the activities can safely overlap; MAXIMUM SAVINGS: depends on how many activities can be overlapped; typically achieves 1-2 months of compression. CRASHING: add resources (people, equipment) to critical path activities; example: add 2 more developers to the configuration phase; COST INCREASE: resources are expensive; crashing typically increases cost by 15-30%; MAXIMUM SAVINGS: limited by Brooks's Law (adding people to late software projects can make them later due to communication overhead); works best for activities where more people genuinely speed up the work (like parallel data conversion); SCOPE REDUCTION (DEFERRAL): move non-MVP features to Phase 2; example: defer advanced analytics and custom reporting to Phase 2; RISK: reduced business value from Phase 1; Phase 2 may never happen; stakeholders may be disappointed; BENEFIT: allows core functionality on time without cost increase. HYBRID APPROACH: fast-track configuration with requirements (save 1 month); crash data migration with additional data engineers (save 1 month); defer advanced reporting to Phase 2 (save 1 month) = 3 months total compression with managed trade-offs. SPONSOR DECISION: present the options; the sponsor decides on cost vs. scope vs. risk trade-off.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — set meeting cadences; project governance meetings
questions.text: During planning, the project manager establishes the project's meeting cadences. For a 14-month ERP implementation with a distributed team and executive steering committee, what meeting cadences should be established and why?

answers.text: Have only one meeting type — a weekly all-hands meeting for everyone
No meetings during planning — meetings start in execution only
Only hold meetings when problems arise — proactive meetings waste time in healthy projects

Establish differentiated cadences for different meeting purposes: daily stand-ups (15 min) for the project team to synchronize; weekly status meetings (45-60 min) for work-stream leads; biweekly technical reviews (60-90 min) for architecture and design decisions; monthly steering committee (60 min) for executive governance; ad hoc decision meetings (as needed) for issues requiring immediate resolution — each type serves a different coordination purpose and has a different audience and frequency

explanations.a: An all-hands meeting every week for a large ERP implementation would: be too detailed for executives (they don't need daily stand-up content); be too high-level for the technical team (they need operational detail); waste expensive executive time on operational content; produce one meeting that serves no audience well.
explanations.b: Planning phase coordination requires meetings — team members must collaborate to develop the project plan. Meeting cadences established in planning govern execution meetings.
explanations.c: Reactive-only meetings produce: delayed problem discovery; crisis management instead of proactive oversight; no executive visibility until problems escalate; disorganized team communication. Regular proactive meetings provide the governance cadence that keeps projects on track.
explanations.d: DIFFERENTIATED MEETING CADENCES for a 14-month ERP: DAILY STAND-UP (15 min, project team): purpose: synchronize daily on progress, plan, and blockers; participants: project team + PM; why daily: blockers discovered today affect tomorrow's work; quick synchronization prevents drift; WEEKLY STATUS MEETING (45-60 min, work-stream leads): purpose: track work-stream progress; resolve cross-stream issues; review upcoming milestones; participants: PM + work-stream leads + key contributors; BIWEEKLY TECHNICAL REVIEW (60-90 min, architecture team): purpose: review technical decisions; validate integration design; address technical risks; participants: architects, tech leads, key developers; MONTHLY STEERING COMMITTEE (60 min, executives): purpose: executive governance; budget status; major risk and issue escalation; go/no-go for phase gates; participants: sponsor, key executives, PM; AD HOC DECISION MEETINGS: purpose: rapid decision-making when issues require immediate action; triggered by specific issues, not scheduled; participants: only those needed for the specific decision. SETTING IN PLANNING: all cadences established in planning so: recurring calendar invites go out before execution begins; all team members know when to expect what type of communication; meeting infrastructure is ready when execution starts.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — cost baseline; determine budget; time-phased budget
questions.text: During planning, the project manager develops the project budget and establishes the cost baseline. What distinguishes the cost baseline from the project budget, and how is the cost baseline used for performance measurement?

answers.text: The cost baseline is the time-phased budget (planned expenditure by period); the project budget adds management reserves on top of the baseline; the cost baseline is used for earned value analysis (comparing planned value to earned value to cost variance) — it shows WHEN money is expected to be spent, not just the total
The cost baseline and project budget are the same document — no distinction exists
The cost baseline includes only labor costs — hardware and software are separate
The cost baseline is the maximum the project can spend — it includes all contingency and reserves

explanations.a: COST BASELINE vs. PROJECT BUDGET HIERARCHY: WORK PACKAGE ESTIMATES: bottom-level cost estimates for each WBS work package; CONTINGENCY RESERVE: added to work package estimates to cover IDENTIFIED risks (known unknowns); the PM has authority to use contingency reserve without sponsor approval (within defined thresholds); COST BASELINE (= Work Package Estimates + Contingency): the authorized, approved budget against which project cost performance is measured; this is the EVM reference; MANAGEMENT RESERVE: added on top of the cost baseline for UNKNOWN risks (unknown unknowns); typically 5-10% of total budget; requires sponsor approval to access; PROJECT BUDGET (= Cost Baseline + Management Reserve): the total approved budget for the project. TIME-PHASED: the cost baseline is not just a total amount — it specifies how much is expected to be spent in each period (monthly, quarterly); this enables: Planned Value (PV) calculation for any point in time; comparison to actual costs (AC) and earned value (EV); EARNED VALUE ANALYSIS: at any point, compare: PV (what should have been spent per the baseline by now) vs. EV (value of work accomplished) vs. AC (what was actually spent); produces Schedule Variance (SV = EV−PV) and Cost Variance (CV = EV−AC).
explanations.b: There is a meaningful and important distinction between the cost baseline, contingency reserves, and management reserves that determines what requires change control to access.
explanations.c: The cost baseline includes ALL project costs — labor, hardware, software, travel, training, facilities, and services — everything required to execute the WBS.
explanations.d: The cost baseline does NOT include management reserves (those are above the baseline). The cost baseline = work package estimates + contingency reserve only.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — risk assessment; qualitative and quantitative analysis
questions.text: During planning, the project manager needs to prioritize 25 identified risks for a complex IT implementation. She uses a probability-impact matrix. Three risks score HIGH-HIGH: Risk A (critical API unavailable 8 weeks into project), Risk B (key developer resigns mid-project), Risk C (regulatory approval delayed by 3 months). For each, what response strategy is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: All three risks should be avoided — avoid all HIGH-HIGH risks
All three should be ignored — accepting all risks is the simplest approach
Transfer all three risks to insurance — insurance covers all HIGH-HIGH project risks

Risk A (API unavailable): mitigate + contingency (build a mock API for development; contingency: switch to alternative API vendor if unavailable past Week 6); Risk B (developer resignation): mitigate (cross-train, document knowledge, succession plan); Risk C (regulatory delay): accept with contingency (cannot control regulators; contingency: build 3-month schedule buffer, plan interim non-regulated activities during delay)

explanations.a: 'Avoid all HIGH-HIGH risks' is impractical. Risk avoidance means changing the project plan to eliminate the risk entirely — this is only possible for some risks. Developer resignation cannot be 'avoided' by changing the project scope; regulatory delays cannot be avoided by scope change.
explanations.b: Ignoring HIGH-HIGH risks is the most dangerous risk management strategy — these are the most likely and most impactful risks. Ignoring them produces unmanaged crises when they materialize.
explanations.c: Insurance (risk transfer) is primarily applicable to financial and liability risks (equipment damage, professional liability, data breach liability). Insurance cannot replace a developer or unblock an API. Insurance covers the FINANCIAL IMPACT of a risk, not the operational consequences.
explanations.d: RISK RESPONSE STRATEGIES — TAILORED BY RISK TYPE: RISK A (Critical API unavailable): NATURE: technical/external dependency risk with time constraint; MITIGATE: develop the application against a MOCK API (documented interface specification without actual production access) — this lets development proceed without waiting for the real API; when the real API is available, integration testing validates the mock API assumptions; CONTINGENCY: if the API is not available by a defined date (Week 6), trigger an alternative vendor evaluation; the risk response is executable because an alternative path exists. RISK B (Key developer resignation): NATURE: human resource/knowledge risk; MITIGATE (primary strategy): cross-training at least 1 other developer on the critical components the key developer owns; knowledge documentation (architecture decision records, code documentation, runbooks); succession plan — who could perform critical tasks if the developer leaves?; ACCEPT RESIDUAL RISK: some knowledge concentration risk remains despite mitigation; CONTINGENCY: if the developer gives notice, initiate succession plan immediately. RISK C (Regulatory approval delayed 3 months): NATURE: external regulatory risk; CANNOT MITIGATE: the organization cannot control regulatory decision timelines; ACCEPT with CONTINGENCY: acknowledge the risk; budget a 3-month schedule buffer for the regulatory-dependent milestone; plan non-regulatory work streams that can continue during the delay (non-regulated features, infrastructure, training); document the contingency plan; MONITOR: track regulatory process; escalate if delays beyond 3 months are anticipated.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — MVP; defining MVP scope; value delivery prioritization
questions.text: A product owner is defining the MVP for a new customer support portal during planning. The full product vision includes 45 features. She needs to identify which features constitute the MVP for a first release in 4 months. What criteria should guide MVP definition?

answers.text: Include all 45 features in the MVP — removing features creates an incomplete product
Include only features that take less than 1 day to build — effort is the MVP criterion

Define MVP by: (1) core value delivery (which features enable the fundamental use case — customers submitting and tracking support tickets?); (2) viability threshold (what's the minimum required to be genuinely useful, not merely functional?); (3) learning objectives (what assumptions are you testing with this release?); result: ticket submission, ticket status tracking, and email notifications are MVP; chat support, AI-powered suggestions, analytics dashboard, and bulk ticket management are post-MVP; the MVP is viable, delivers core value, and tests whether customers will self-serve instead of calling
The MVP should be defined by the development team alone based on technical feasibility

explanations.a: Including all 45 features in the 'MVP' defeats the purpose of MVP — it becomes a full product launch with the delays and risks of full-scope delivery. The MVP concept specifically addresses the 'launch small, learn, iterate' principle.
explanations.b: Building only features that take less than 1 day produces a fragmented collection of trivial capabilities — not a usable product. A ticket submission feature might take 5 days but is essential; a decorative dashboard might take 0.5 days but adds no core value. Effort alone is not a valid MVP criterion.
explanations.c: MVP DEFINITION FRAMEWORK: CORE VALUE DELIVERY: ask 'what is the fundamental job the product does?'; for a customer support portal: 'let customers submit issues and track their resolution status'; if the MVP doesn't enable this fundamental job, it's not viable; VIABILITY THRESHOLD: 'viable' means actually useful, not just technically deployable; a ticket submission form with no status tracking or notifications is technically deployable but not viable (customers can't track whether their issue is being addressed); 'viable' requires: submit ticket, track status, receive notifications; LEARNING OBJECTIVES: 'what questions are we answering with this release?'; 'will customers self-serve instead of calling support?' is the key assumption to test; the MVP tests this assumption at minimum cost; MVP SCOPE (this example): Ticket submission (required — core capability); Ticket status tracking (required — core viability); Email notifications (required — viability closes the loop); NOT MVP (post-release): Chat support (added convenience, not core); AI-powered suggestions (enhancement); Analytics dashboard (operational benefit, not user-facing value); Bulk ticket management (power user feature, not core use case); BUSINESS PLANNING: the MVP scope defines the first sprint commitment, the first release budget, and the first go-live date.
explanations.d: MVP definition requires product perspective (product owner + stakeholders), not just technical perspective. Development teams define technical feasibility; product owners define minimum BUSINESS VALUE.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — QA plan; quality standards; acceptance criteria; test strategy
questions.text: A project manager is developing the QA plan for a financial services application that must meet SOX compliance requirements. The application processes financial transactions for publicly traded company reporting. What specific elements should the QA plan include given these compliance requirements?

answers.text: Only functional testing is needed — compliance requirements are handled by the legal team, not QA
The QA plan should only include unit testing — higher-level testing is done post-deployment
SOX compliance is automatic — financial applications are always compliant by default

The QA plan must address: SOX-specific controls testing (audit trail completeness; access controls; data integrity validation); financial calculation accuracy testing (the core function — incorrect calculations = SOX violation); security testing (unauthorized access to financial data); performance testing (system must be available during period-end close without failures); test evidence retention (SOX auditors require documented evidence of testing); roles and responsibilities for quality sign-off; and independent review requirements

explanations.a: SOX compliance is a QA responsibility — it requires documented evidence that controls are operating effectively. The legal team defines compliance requirements; the QA team validates that the system meets them. Separating compliance testing from QA creates gaps.
explanations.b: Unit testing tests code functions in isolation — it cannot validate SOX compliance, which requires end-to-end system behavior testing including audit trails, access controls, and financial calculation accuracy.
explanations.c: SOX compliance requires active, documented testing and validation — systems are not compliant 'by default.' Many financial IT projects fail SOX audits because their QA plans didn't include compliance-specific testing.
explanations.d: SOX-SPECIFIC QA PLAN ELEMENTS: AUDIT TRAIL TESTING: SOX Section 302/404 requires complete audit trails; test that every financial transaction creates an immutable audit record with: user ID, timestamp, data changed, before/after values; test that audit logs cannot be deleted or modified by unauthorized users; FINANCIAL CALCULATION ACCURACY: the application's financial computations must be mathematically accurate; test all calculation algorithms against known correct results; test edge cases (zero balances, maximum values, rounding rules); CHANGE MANAGEMENT CONTROLS TESTING: SOX requires controlled change management for systems affecting financial reporting; test that unauthorized changes cannot be made to the system; test that the change log captures all modifications; ACCESS CONTROLS TESTING: test that only authorized users can access financial data; test separation of duties (person entering transactions cannot approve them); AVAILABILITY AND PERFORMANCE TESTING: period-end close (quarterly, year-end) has hard deadlines; test that the system handles peak load without failure; test disaster recovery (RPO/RTO for financial systems is very short); TEST EVIDENCE REQUIREMENTS: SOX auditors require documented test evidence; all test cases, results, and sign-offs must be retained; test evidence must be tamper-evident (cannot be modified after test); INDEPENDENT REVIEW: SOX requires independent review of control testing; internal audit or external auditor must review test evidence.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — transition plan; handover to operations; knowledge transfer
questions.text: A project is replacing a legacy billing system. The IT operations team will take over ongoing support of the new system after go-live. What should the transition plan developed during planning include?

answers.text: Only the go-live date — operations teams can figure out support after go-live
Transition planning is done by the operations team independently — the project team has no role
The transition plan only needs the vendor support contact information — vendors handle all post-go-live support

The transition plan should include: knowledge transfer sessions (technical deep dives with operations team during development); runbook development (step-by-step procedures for all common and emergency operations tasks); operations training on the new system; monitoring and alerting setup (dashboards, thresholds, escalation paths); documentation package (system architecture, integration diagrams, data dictionary, disaster recovery procedures); support model definition (Level 1/2/3 support responsibilities, SLA targets); warranty period support (project team available for 30-60 days post-go-live); acceptance criteria for handover (operations team confirms readiness)

explanations.a: Handing over a complex billing system to operations without runbooks, training, monitoring setup, or documentation creates immediate operational failures — operations staff who don't know the system will be unable to support it on day 1.
explanations.b: The project team creates the system and knows it best — they are essential for transition planning and knowledge transfer. Operations cannot independently plan a transition for a system they don't yet understand.
explanations.c: Vendor support handles vendor-specific issues — but the IT operations team must understand the full system including custom configurations, integrations, and organizational-specific procedures that the vendor doesn't know.
explanations.d: COMPREHENSIVE TRANSITION PLAN for billing system: KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER SESSIONS: ongoing during development (not just at go-live); operations team attends system design reviews; developers walk operations through each billing module as it's built; operations team builds familiarity before go-live; RUNBOOK DEVELOPMENT: procedures for: starting and stopping the system; processing batch billing jobs; handling failed transactions; running end-of-month close; backup and recovery procedures; common troubleshooting scenarios; OPERATIONS TRAINING: hands-on training in a staging environment; training 4-6 weeks before go-live; practice exercises for common operations scenarios; MONITORING AND ALERTING: configure dashboards in the monitoring tool; define alerting thresholds (billing job failure, response time degradation, disk space); define escalation paths (who gets paged at 2 AM?); DOCUMENTATION PACKAGE: system architecture diagram; integration map (all connected systems); data dictionary; network diagram; vendor support contacts; SUPPORT MODEL: Level 1: help desk (simple user questions); Level 2: operations (system-level issues); Level 3: development team/vendor (complex technical issues); SLA: define response times by severity; WARRANTY PERIOD: project team on-call support for 30-60 days post-go-live; handles issues beyond operations' capability to resolve independently; HANDOVER ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: operations team formally confirms readiness before project team releases control.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — develop sprint schedule; Agile release planning; release cadence
questions.text: During Agile planning, a product owner and project manager need to develop the sprint schedule and release plan for a 12-month product development effort. The team's velocity is expected to be approximately 30 story points per sprint. The product backlog has 360 story points of work. 2-week sprints. What should the sprint schedule and release plan define?

answers.text: Sprint 1 contains all 360 story points — everything in one sprint maximizes efficiency
Plan all 12 months in detail with every story assigned to specific sprints — detailed upfront planning prevents Agile issues
Only define Sprint 1 — Agile doesn't plan beyond the current sprint

The sprint schedule should define: total sprints (360 sp ÷ 30 sp/sprint = 12 sprints × 2 weeks = 24 weeks ≈ 6 months); the release plan should identify which sprints culminate in a release (e.g., releases at Sprints 4, 8, and 12); each sprint should have a sprint goal; the plan should account for velocity variation and include at least 2 innovation/hardening sprints; acknowledge that the backlog will evolve — the release plan is a forecast, not a commitment

explanations.a: 360 story points in one sprint is physically impossible — at 30 sp/sprint, the team can commit to 30 points per 2-week sprint. Overcommitting produces incomplete sprints and unstable teams.
explanations.b: Planning all 12 months with every story committed to specific sprints violates Agile's adaptive principle. Detailed upfront planning for Sprint 11's stories (5+ months away) produces plans that are wrong by the time they're executed because: requirements evolve; velocity varies; priorities shift. Plan in detail for the near horizon (Sprints 1-3); plan at summary level for the far horizon (Sprints 4-12).
explanations.c: 'Only define Sprint 1' is too extreme — stakeholders and the business need a forecast of when features will be delivered to plan marketing, operations, training, and other dependent activities. Release planning provides this forecast at appropriate granularity.
explanations.d: AGILE SPRINT SCHEDULE AND RELEASE PLAN: CAPACITY CALCULATION: 360 story points ÷ 30 sp/sprint = 12 sprints; 12 sprints × 2 weeks/sprint = 24 weeks ≈ 6 months; the backlog may expand (new requirements discovered) or contract (scope is de-prioritized); forecast horizon is approximately 6 months for current backlog; SPRINT GOALS: each sprint has a defined goal — a concise statement of what the sprint will accomplish; helps the team focus and enables product owner to make scope decisions within the sprint; RELEASE PLANNING: 3 planned releases at Sprint 4 (8 weeks = MVP), Sprint 8 (16 weeks = enhanced feature set), Sprint 12 (24 weeks = full feature set); each release is a potentially shippable product increment; release dates are driven by business need and sprint outcomes, not fixed dates; VELOCITY VARIATION: new teams have unstable velocity (Sprints 1-3); account for holidays, vacations, onboarding; plan for 10-15% velocity variation; INNOVATION AND HARDENING SPRINTS: reserve 1-2 sprints for: technical debt reduction; performance optimization; security hardening; documentation; these prevent 'feature factory' tunnel vision; ADAPTIVE PLANNING PRINCIPLE: the plan is a forecast — 'we expect to deliver these features by Sprint 12'; new high-value stories added to the backlog may displace lower-priority planned items; the plan updates every sprint review based on actual velocity and backlog changes.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — risk response strategies; contingency planning; risk ownership
questions.text: A project's risk register identifies: Risk 12 — 'Key vendor may deliver integration platform 6 weeks late (probability: 60%, impact: HIGH — blocks integration testing).' The project manager must develop a risk response. Which response is MOST appropriate and what should be documented?

answers.text: Accept the risk — vendor delays are out of the PM's control
Avoid the risk by replacing the vendor immediately

Implement a MITIGATION response combined with a CONTINGENCY plan: Mitigation — negotiate a contractual milestone (vendor delivers a beta version of the integration platform 8 weeks before the final deadline; provides early warning of potential delay); escalation contact established; monitor vendor progress weekly; Contingency (if vendor is >2 weeks late by a trigger date) — activate a temporary mock API environment that simulates the vendor platform; integration testing proceeds against the mock; document residual risk and risk owner (PM + vendor manager); include in status reporting
Transfer the risk by adding a clause in the vendor contract that states all delays are the vendor's financial responsibility — transfer eliminates the schedule risk

explanations.a: 60% probability HIGH-impact risk is not acceptable for passive acceptance. Simple acceptance without any contingency plan means the project team has no prepared response when the delay materializes — they improvise under pressure, producing poorer outcomes than a pre-planned response.
explanations.b: Replacing the vendor immediately (Risk Avoidance) is disproportionate for a 60% risk of a 6-week delay. Vendor replacement: takes significant procurement time (potentially longer than 6 weeks); disrupts existing contract; loses any work already done with the current vendor; creates new vendor-onboarding risks. Avoidance is appropriate only when the risk probability and impact are so high that proceeding with the current approach is not viable.
explanations.c: MITIGATION + CONTINGENCY for vendor delivery risk: MITIGATION (reduce probability/impact): CONTRACTUAL PROTECTION: negotiate a milestone delivery (beta version 8 weeks before final deadline); this gives the team early visibility into progress and a 6-week buffer; VENDOR MONITORING: weekly progress check-ins; escalation contact at vendor (PM talks to VP if weekly contacts aren't productive); EARLY WARNING TRIGGER: define trigger point — if vendor is >2 weeks behind by Week 4 milestone, activate contingency; CONTINGENCY (response if risk occurs): MOCK API ENVIRONMENT: set up an integration platform simulation (mock API) that replicates the vendor platform's interface; integration development and testing can proceed against the mock; when real platform arrives, integration testing validates mock assumptions (typically minor adjustments); SCHEDULE IMPACT: mock integration saves 4-5 of the 6-week potential delay; residual 1-2 week delay is manageable; DOCUMENTATION: risk owner (PM + vendor manager), trigger event, contingency activation criteria, mock API setup time (3-5 days), cost of mock implementation ($8K developer time). RISK TRANSFER (option D) LIMITATION: financial penalties for vendor delays (transfer) don't prevent the schedule impact — the project is still 6 weeks late even if the vendor pays financial damages. Transfer addresses financial exposure, not schedule protection.
explanations.d: Risk transfer (financial penalties) is valuable for recovering FINANCIAL costs of a delay — but it does NOT prevent the schedule delay from occurring. The project would still be 6 weeks late even if the vendor pays $100K in penalties. For a 60% probability HIGH-impact schedule risk, schedule protection (mitigation + contingency) is more valuable than financial recovery.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — performance measurement baseline; scope + schedule + cost baselines integrated
questions.text: A project has just established its three baselines: scope baseline (WBS + scope statement), schedule baseline, and cost baseline. A team lead says: 'These baselines look good independently, but how do they work together?' How should the PM explain the integration?

answers.text: The three baselines are independent documents with no connection — each is managed separately
The baselines are replaced by actual data once execution begins — they have no role in execution monitoring
Only the cost baseline matters for project performance measurement — schedule and scope are secondary

The three baselines together form the PERFORMANCE MEASUREMENT BASELINE: scope baseline defines WHAT will be delivered; schedule baseline defines WHEN it will be delivered; cost baseline defines HOW MUCH it will cost; they are interconnected — a scope change requires changing the schedule AND cost baselines; earned value management uses all three to calculate schedule variance and cost variance simultaneously; the baselines are the 'plan' against which actual execution is measured

explanations.a: The three baselines are deeply interconnected. A change to scope almost always changes both schedule and cost — treating them independently misses this interdependency and produces inaccurate planning and performance measurement.
explanations.b: Baselines are the permanent reference points AGAINST WHICH execution is measured — they are MORE important during execution than during planning. Without baselines, there is no way to determine whether the project is ahead or behind plan.
explanations.c: All three baselines are essential for project performance measurement. Cost-only measurement would miss schedule performance issues until they become cost issues (late delivery often leads to cost overruns, but the schedule problem typically appears first).
explanations.d: PERFORMANCE MEASUREMENT BASELINE INTEGRATION: SCOPE BASELINE (WHAT): defines all authorized deliverables and work packages; the WBS is the foundation — every schedule activity and cost estimate traces back to a WBS work package; SCHEDULE BASELINE (WHEN): defines when each WBS work package will be executed; produces Planned Value (PV) — the time-phased budget for each work package; COST BASELINE (HOW MUCH): defines the authorized budget for each WBS work package by period; also generates PV — the authorized budget for work scheduled to be done by a given date; EARNED VALUE INTEGRATION: at any point in execution: Planned Value (PV): from the schedule baseline — what should have been completed (and what it should have cost) by now; Earned Value (EV): from actual work completed — the budgeted value of work actually accomplished; Actual Cost (AC): from the financial system — what was actually spent; CALCULATIONS: SV = EV − PV (schedule variance — are we ahead or behind plan?); CV = EV − AC (cost variance — are we under or over budget?); INTERDEPENDENCY EXAMPLE: a scope addition to deliver an extra module: scope baseline changes (new WBS work packages added); schedule baseline changes (module requires 6 more weeks); cost baseline changes ($80K more for the module); all three must be updated through formal change control — updating scope without updating schedule and cost creates inconsistent baselines.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — risk assessment; risk register as living document; risk monitoring
questions.text: A project manager creates a comprehensive risk register during planning with 20 risks. Three months into execution, she stops updating the risk register. By Month 6, three previously unidentified risks have materialized as issues. What does this scenario demonstrate about risk management?

answers.text: The initial risk register was insufficient — a better initial register would have identified all risks
Risk registers should only be used during planning — once execution begins, risks are managed informally

Risk management is a CONTINUOUS PROCESS throughout the project lifecycle: the planning-phase risk register provides an initial assessment; execution introduces new risks as the project encounters reality; the risk register must be updated throughout execution — new risks identified, existing risks probability/impact reassessed, triggered risks transitioned to issues; three unidentified risks materializing as issues indicates inadequate ongoing risk monitoring during execution
No risk register can prevent all issues — three issues in 6 months is acceptable for any project

explanations.a: Even perfect initial risk identification cannot predict all future risks because: the project environment changes over time; new risks emerge from vendor decisions, regulatory changes, market shifts, and execution realities; risks that appeared LOW probability initially may increase as conditions change. The failure is not the initial register quality — it is the lack of ongoing monitoring.
explanations.b: Risk management is MOST active during execution — this is when risks either materialize (requiring contingency responses) or are avoided (requiring monitoring confirmation). Treating the risk register as a planning-only artifact causes exactly the scenario described.
explanations.c: CONTINUOUS RISK MANAGEMENT: PLANNING PHASE: initial risk identification and response planning; establishes the risk register and response strategies; EXECUTION PHASE — ONGOING ACTIVITIES: REGULAR RISK REVIEWS: at each status meeting, review the risk register; have any risks' probability or impact changed?; RISK TRIGGER MONITORING: watch for the trigger events defined in the risk register; if a trigger occurs, activate the contingency plan; NEW RISK IDENTIFICATION: throughout execution, team members identify new risks; these are added to the register and assessed; RISK CLOSURE: as project progresses, risks that are no longer relevant are closed; RISK-TO-ISSUE TRANSITION: when a risk occurs, it becomes an issue — the risk register entry transitions to the issue log; contingency plan is activated; WHAT SHOULD HAVE HAPPENED (in this scenario): monthly risk register review; risk owners reporting on trigger events and probability changes; new risks identified in retrospectives and status meetings; three materialized issues should have been NEW RISKS in the register before materializing — the lack of ongoing monitoring missed their emergence. PRACTICAL CADENCE: weekly: PM reviews open high-priority risks; monthly: full risk register review with risk owners; ad hoc: any risk owner can add new risks or update existing ones.
explanations.d: Three unidentified risks causing issues in 6 months indicates a risk management breakdown — not normal project behavior. While some unforeseen events are inevitable, a well-maintained risk register and ongoing monitoring significantly reduces the probability of unmanaged issues.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — transition plan; legacy system decommissioning; parallel run planning
questions.text: A project is replacing a legacy billing system with a new cloud-based solution. The transition plan must address running both systems simultaneously during a parallel run period. What should the parallel run section of the transition plan include?

answers.text: Shut down the legacy system on go-live day — running two systems simultaneously is too complex
Parallel run planning should be avoided — if the new system is tested properly, parallel run is unnecessary

The parallel run plan should define: duration (how long both systems run simultaneously — typically 1-3 billing cycles); which transactions are processed in both systems; reconciliation approach (compare outputs to validate new system accuracy); discrepancy resolution process (who decides which system's output is correct?); resource requirements (extra staff for dual processing); cutover trigger criteria (what metrics must the new system achieve before legacy is decommissioned?); and legacy decommissioning steps once cutover criteria are met
Parallel run is always 6 months — standard duration applies to all implementations

explanations.a: Shutting down the legacy system on day 1 of go-live is high-risk for a billing system. If the new system has issues: billing failures affect customers immediately; no fallback exists; revenue collection stops; a parallel run provides a safety net. The complexity of parallel run is justified by the risk reduction for financial systems.
explanations.b: Even thoroughly tested systems can encounter production issues that testing environments didn't replicate: volume differences (production may have 10× more transactions than test); data quality issues (production data has edge cases that test data didn't include); integration failures in production environment; a parallel run validates the new system against real production workload.
explanations.c: PARALLEL RUN PLAN COMPONENTS: DURATION: for billing systems — typically 1-3 full billing cycles (monthly cycles = 1-3 months); shorter: lower cost but less validation; longer: higher cost and operational burden but more validation. TRANSACTION SCOPE: all billing transactions processed in BOTH systems; or a subset (new customers in new system; existing customers in old system) — reduces parallel run burden; RECONCILIATION: compare outputs from both systems (invoices, totals, tax calculations); automate reconciliation where possible (reconciliation scripts compare output files); review all discrepancies daily; DISCREPANCY RESOLUTION: who decides which system is correct? (typically the QA lead or business SME); all discrepancies documented and traced to root cause (not just corrected); HIGH discrepancy rate → extend parallel run; LOW discrepancy rate → meet cutover criteria; RESOURCE REQUIREMENTS: additional staff for dual data entry (if not automated); reconciliation analysts; CUTOVER CRITERIA: specific, measurable thresholds: discrepancy rate <0.1%; processing time within SLA; no P1 or P2 open defects; operations team confirms readiness; LEGACY DECOMMISSIONING: once cutover criteria are met, define the steps to: disable legacy system write access; migrate any remaining data; archive legacy data per retention policy; shut down legacy infrastructure; reclaim licenses.
explanations.d: Parallel run duration depends on the system, business cycle, and risk tolerance — there is no universal 6-month standard. Billing systems typically require 1-3 billing cycles; payroll systems typically require 1-2 pay periods; ERP systems may require 3-6 months.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — determine budget; bottom-up estimating; cost aggregation
questions.text: A project manager is developing the project budget using bottom-up estimating. She has the WBS with 30 work packages and cost estimates for each. How does the bottom-up estimating process work and what produces the final project budget?

answers.text: Top-down: start with the total charter-approved budget and divide among work packages proportionally

Bottom-up: estimate the cost of each work package individually (labor, materials, equipment, overhead); aggregate work package costs by WBS level to produce deliverable costs; sum all deliverable costs to produce the project's direct cost; add contingency reserve (for identified risks); add management reserve (for unknown risks); the total = the project budget; this bottom-up aggregate is more accurate than the rough order of magnitude estimate in the business case
Use only one vendor quote as the total project budget — vendor quotes are the most accurate cost source
Budget is set by the CFO based on available funds — actual cost estimating is unnecessary

explanations.a: Top-down allocation (dividing the budget by proportional assignment) works in the opposite direction from bottom-up. Top-down uses an authorized total budget and distributes it; bottom-up builds the total from individual estimates. For accurate planning, bottom-up is more reliable because it is grounded in specific work package requirements.
explanations.b: BOTTOM-UP ESTIMATING AND BUDGET DEVELOPMENT: WORK PACKAGE LEVEL ESTIMATES: for each of the 30 work packages, estimate: LABOR: hours × rate (e.g., 200 hours × $150/hr = $30,000); MATERIALS AND EQUIPMENT: specific costs (e.g., server hardware $12,000; software licenses $8,000); OVERHEAD: allocation of indirect costs (facilities, utilities, HR support); CONTINGENCY PER WORK PACKAGE: risk-based buffer for that specific work package's risks; AGGREGATION: sum work package costs to deliverable level; sum deliverable costs to project total; TOTAL DIRECT COST: sum of all work package estimates; CONTINGENCY RESERVE: calculated from risk register; typical range 5-15% of direct cost depending on risk exposure; MANAGEMENT RESERVE: for unknown unknowns; typically 5-10% of total budget; approved by sponsor; project manager does not control management reserve; PROJECT BUDGET = Direct Cost + Contingency Reserve + Management Reserve; COMPARISON TO BUSINESS CASE: the business case used rough order of magnitude (±30-50% accuracy) for authorization; the planning-phase bottom-up estimate provides ±10-15% accuracy; if the bottom-up estimate differs significantly from the business case, the PM must flag this and potentially seek additional authorization.
explanations.c: Vendor quotes are inputs to work package estimates for outsourced work — but the project budget includes all costs: internal labor (not from vendor quotes), hardware, software, facilities, and overhead.
explanations.d: While budget constraints (from the charter) inform the planning process, actual cost estimating is essential for: knowing whether the authorized budget is sufficient; identifying where costs exceed expectations; managing the budget throughout execution.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — all planning elements: schedule, baselines, MVP, budget, QA, risk, transition integrated
questions.text: A project manager has completed most planning activities for a new financial reporting system. She reviews the planning deliverables checklist: ✅ Scope statement ✅ WBS ✅ Resource assignments ✅ Communication plan. She still needs to complete: schedule baseline, cost baseline, QA plan, risk register, and transition plan. She has 2 weeks left in the planning phase. How should she prioritize and what dependencies exist between the remaining deliverables?

answers.text: Complete all five simultaneously — no dependencies exist between planning deliverables

Priority and sequence: (1) Schedule baseline first (requires WBS and resource assignments — both complete; produces the cost basis via resource loading); (2) Cost baseline second (uses schedule for time-phasing and resource costs; then add contingency and management reserve); (3) Risk register third (meaningful risk identification requires scope, schedule, and cost context — identify risks in context of what's known); (4) QA plan fourth (can now define test strategy based on complete scope and schedule); (5) Transition plan last (defines handover after delivery — less dependent on cost/schedule; can be developed in parallel with QA); all five feasible in 2 weeks with focused effort
Only complete the schedule baseline — it is the most important planning artifact; skip the others
Extend planning for 3 more months — 5 remaining deliverables cannot be completed in 2 weeks

explanations.a: Dependencies exist between the remaining planning deliverables — a schedule baseline is an input to the cost baseline (time-phased resource costs); both are context for meaningful risk identification. Ignoring these dependencies produces inconsistent plans.
explanations.b: PLANNING COMPLETION SEQUENCE with dependencies: STEP 1 — SCHEDULE BASELINE (Days 1-5): INPUTS AVAILABLE: WBS (complete), Resource assignments (complete), Activity durations; PROCESS: define activities from WBS work packages; sequence activities (dependencies); assign durations; load resources onto schedule; calculate critical path; identify and resolve resource over-allocations; optimize and baseline; OUTPUTS: approved project schedule with activity dates; critical path identified; float analysis complete; Planned Value (PV) curve generated; DEPENDENCY: needed BEFORE cost baseline (resource loading on schedule produces labor cost by period). STEP 2 — COST BASELINE (Days 3-7, can start when schedule draft is ready): INPUTS: schedule (work packages with timing); resource assignments with rates; material and equipment estimates; PROCESS: calculate time-phased labor costs from schedule; add material/equipment costs; add contingency reserve (from initial risk list); add management reserve; OUTPUTS: project budget; cost baseline with PV by period; DEPENDENCY: meaningful only with schedule context. STEP 3 — RISK REGISTER (Days 5-9, risk workshop): INPUTS: scope (what are we building?); schedule (when, with what dependencies?); cost (what's the budget exposure?); PROCESS: risk identification workshop (team + PM); qualitative assessment (probability × impact); top risks get quantitative analysis; response strategies and owners; DEPENDENCY: better risk identification with full scope/schedule/cost context. STEP 4 — QA PLAN (Days 7-10): INPUTS: scope (what needs quality criteria?); schedule (when are testing phases?); team assignments (QA ownership); PROCESS: define quality standards; develop test strategy; write acceptance criteria; define audit schedule. STEP 5 — TRANSITION PLAN (Days 8-12, can parallelize with QA): INPUTS: scope (what is being transitioned?); schedule (when is go-live?); resource assignments (who supports?); PROCESS: knowledge transfer plan; runbook development plan; operations training schedule; cutover criteria. ALL FIVE ARE FEASIBLE in 2 weeks with: parallel workstreams; dedicated team members for each deliverable; PM coordinating dependencies.
explanations.c: Completing only the schedule baseline leaves the project with: no financial plan (cost baseline); no risk management plan; no quality standards; no transition plan. These are not optional for a financial reporting system — especially given SOX implications.
explanations.d: Five planning deliverables in 2 weeks is achievable with focused effort and parallel workstreams. Each document (schedule, cost, risk, QA, transition) takes 2-5 days of focused work — parallel progress on multiple fronts makes 2 weeks sufficient.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — sprint schedule; sprint 0; Agile release planning; team capacity
questions.text: An Agile team begins sprint planning. The project manager suggests starting with 'Sprint 0' before the first development sprint. A developer asks: 'What happens in Sprint 0, and why isn't it just Sprint 1?' How should the PM explain?

answers.text: Sprint 0 is just a delay — start Sprint 1 immediately to deliver value faster

Sprint 0 is a setup sprint that prepares the team to develop effectively: setting up development environments, CI/CD pipelines, testing frameworks, architecture proof-of-concept, backlog refinement, team working agreements, and technical infrastructure — work that isn't a user-facing feature but is required before the team can deliver Sprint 1 value effectively; it produces no shippable product increment but produces the CONDITIONS for increments to follow
Sprint 0 delivers the entire MVP — all MVP features in one sprint
Sprint 0 is when stakeholders are identified — sprint planning doesn't begin until all stakeholders are known

explanations.a: Starting Sprint 1 without proper infrastructure setup produces: developers unable to write testable code (no test framework); no automated build process (integration testing is manual and slow); architecture unclear (developers make inconsistent decisions in their code); a team that wastes Sprint 1 capacity on setup tasks that should have been done in Sprint 0.
explanations.b: SPRINT 0 PURPOSE AND ACTIVITIES: DEVELOPMENT ENVIRONMENT SETUP: all developers have working environments with required tools, plugins, and configurations; version control, branching strategy, and code review process established; DEVOPS AND CI/CD PIPELINE: automated build and test pipeline configured; deployment to development environment automated; code quality gates (linting, test coverage) established; without CI/CD, Sprint 1 integration is manual and error-prone; ARCHITECTURE AND TECHNICAL FOUNDATION: key architectural decisions made (what frameworks? what patterns?); proof-of-concept for the highest-risk technical components (is the proposed API integration feasible?); shared data models and interface contracts agreed; BACKLOG PREPARATION: product backlog refined with acceptance criteria for Sprint 1 stories; Sprint 1 stories are in 'ready' state (defined, estimated, accepted criteria clear); TEAM AGREEMENTS: working agreements established (code review standards, Definition of Done, branch naming conventions, communication norms); DISTINCTION FROM SPRINT 1: Sprint 0: produces setup infrastructure and team foundations; NOT a shippable product increment; duration typically 1-2 weeks; Sprint 1: produces a shippable product increment; team uses the infrastructure built in Sprint 0 to deliver efficiently.
explanations.c: The entire MVP in one sprint is physically impossible for a meaningful product. Sprints are typically 1-4 weeks; MVPs typically require multiple sprints. Sprint 0 is a setup sprint, not a feature delivery sprint.
explanations.d: Stakeholder identification is an initiation phase activity — Sprint 0 focuses on technical setup and Agile infrastructure preparation. Delaying sprints until 'all stakeholders are known' would indefinitely postpone development.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — QA plan; acceptance criteria; quality metrics; definition of done
questions.text: A QA plan for an e-commerce platform needs acceptance criteria for three deliverables: the checkout flow, the inventory management system, and the payment processing integration. Write effective acceptance criteria for each.

answers.text: Acceptance criteria for all three: 'Works correctly' — if it works, it meets acceptance criteria
Checkout flow: functional (can complete purchases); Inventory: accurate; Payment: processes payments — high-level descriptions are sufficient for acceptance criteria

Checkout flow: checkout process completes successfully for 99% of test cases; page load <3 seconds at 500 concurrent users; zero P1 defects; supports 5 payment types. Inventory management: inventory adjustments reflect within 30 seconds; zero inventory count discrepancies in a 1,000-item stress test; reorder threshold alerts trigger at configured levels. Payment processing: 99.9% of test transactions processed correctly; all transactions logged with audit trail; PCI-DSS compliance validation passed; encryption verified for all financial data in transit
Acceptance criteria should not be written until post-deployment — testing in production identifies the real acceptance criteria

explanations.a: 'Works correctly' is not an acceptance criterion — it cannot be objectively tested. What does 'correctly' mean? Who decides? This creates disputes at project close when the team says 'it works' and the client says 'it doesn't work correctly.'
explanations.b: 'Functional,' 'accurate,' and 'processes payments' are directional descriptions, not measurable acceptance criteria. They cannot be tested objectively — the client can always dispute whether the system is 'accurate enough' or 'functional enough.'
explanations.c: EFFECTIVE ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA must be SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound): CHECKOUT FLOW: '99% of test cases complete successfully' — specific, measurable, objectively testable; '<3 seconds at 500 concurrent users' — specific performance standard; 'zero P1 defects' — severity-specific quality bar; '5 payment types' — specific capability list; INVENTORY MANAGEMENT: '30-second reflection window' — measurable time constraint; '1,000-item stress test with zero discrepancies' — measurable accuracy at scale; 'reorder alerts trigger at configured levels' — functional behavior specified; PAYMENT PROCESSING: '99.9% of test transactions correct' — specific accuracy rate; 'all transactions logged with audit trail' — completeness requirement; 'PCI-DSS compliance validation passed' — compliance standard; 'encryption verified for all financial data in transit' — security requirement; WHY SPECIFIC ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA MATTER: OBJECTIVE COMPLETION: both parties agree on what 'done' looks like; prevents 'that's not what I meant' disputes; TESTABLE: acceptance criteria can be directly translated into test cases; CONTRACTUAL CLARITY: for vendor-delivered systems, acceptance criteria are the contractual standard for payment authorization; LEGAL PROTECTION: if a vendor claims delivery, specific acceptance criteria determine whether the delivery is acceptable.
explanations.d: Acceptance criteria written after deployment are useless for guiding development and testing. Retroactive acceptance criteria are a governance failure — the project must know what 'done' means BEFORE building starts.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — transition plan; SaaS vendor relationship; support model transition
questions.text: A project is transitioning from a self-hosted CRM to a cloud SaaS CRM. The internal IT team currently manages the on-premises CRM. Post-transition, the SaaS vendor manages the infrastructure. The transition plan must address the change in support responsibilities. What specific aspects should the transition plan address?

answers.text: No transition plan needed — the SaaS vendor handles all support automatically

The transition plan should address: redefining the support boundary (vendor manages infrastructure; internal IT manages user administration, integrations, and configuration); vendor SLA terms and escalation paths; internal IT skill retooling (from server administration to SaaS administration); data migration from on-premises to SaaS; user provisioning strategy; integration reconfiguration; license management; and vendor relationship governance
Simply cancel the IT team's roles — SaaS replaces all internal IT functions
The transition plan only addresses the cutover weekend — everything else is the vendor's responsibility

explanations.a: Even SaaS products require significant internal IT involvement: user provisioning and deprovisioning; integration with other internal systems; configuration management; data governance; vendor relationship management. 'The vendor handles everything' is incorrect — the vendor handles infrastructure; IT handles everything above the infrastructure layer.
explanations.b: SAAS TRANSITION PLAN COMPONENTS: SUPPORT BOUNDARY REDEFINITION: VENDOR manages: infrastructure, uptime, platform patches, hardware; INTERNAL IT manages: user accounts and permissions; SSO and directory integration; API integrations with other internal systems; CRM configuration and customization; data governance (what data is in the CRM?); internal user support (help desk); VENDOR SLA REVIEW AND INTERNALIZATION: ensure internal IT understands the vendor's SLA terms; establish internal escalation path to vendor (who calls the vendor?); define what IT can resolve internally vs. what requires vendor escalation; INTERNAL IT SKILL RETOOLING: server administrators → SaaS administrators (completely different skill set); training needed: CRM administration certification; integration platform skills (if using iPaaS for integrations); vendor-specific support tools; DATA MIGRATION PLAN: migrate data from on-premises to SaaS; validate data integrity post-migration; archive on-premises data per retention policy; USER PROVISIONING STRATEGY: bulk import of existing users; SSO configuration (SAML or OIDC integration with Active Directory); role and permission mapping; LICENSE MANAGEMENT: track license utilization; manage additions and removals; periodic reconciliation; VENDOR GOVERNANCE: designated vendor relationship owner; regular business reviews; contract renewal management.
explanations.c: The internal IT team's role CHANGES — it does not disappear. SaaS moves operational responsibility from infrastructure management to vendor relationship management, user administration, and integration management. These are different skills but equally important roles.
explanations.d: The transition extends well beyond the cutover weekend: user training (weeks before cutover); data migration validation (weeks in parallel run); support model establishment (months of process change); skill development (ongoing). Limiting the transition plan to the cutover weekend creates a support vacuum on day 2 of operation.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — budget; contingency reserve; management reserve; reserve analysis
questions.text: A project manager calculates the direct project cost at $1,800,000. She needs to add contingency reserve and management reserve to produce the total project budget. The risk register shows HIGH risks worth approximately $150,000 in potential impact. The organization's policy is to hold 5% of project cost as management reserve. What is the complete budget breakdown?

answers.text: Total budget = $1,800,000 — no reserves are needed if the estimate is accurate

Direct cost: $1,800,000; Contingency reserve: $150,000 (based on risk register HIGH-risk impacts); Cost baseline: $1,950,000; Management reserve: $97,500 (5% × $1,950,000); Total project budget: $2,047,500
Total budget = $1,800,000 + 20% = $2,160,000 — add 20% to all projects regardless of risk
Management reserve = contingency reserve; the terms are interchangeable

explanations.a: No reserves on a $1.8M project is imprudent. The risk register identifies $150K in HIGH-risk impacts — these are KNOWN potential costs. Without contingency, any risk that materializes immediately causes a cost overrun.
explanations.b: BUDGET LAYERS CALCULATION: DIRECT COST (work package estimates): $1,800,000; includes all planned labor, materials, equipment, and overhead; CONTINGENCY RESERVE (for KNOWN risks): $150,000 (from risk register high-impact risks); purpose: funds the execution of contingency plans when identified risks materialize; PM AUTHORITY: the PM can authorize use of contingency reserve for responses to identified risks without sponsor re-approval (within defined thresholds); COST BASELINE (= Direct Cost + Contingency): $1,800,000 + $150,000 = $1,950,000; this is the PERFORMANCE MEASUREMENT BASELINE; earned value analysis is performed against this baseline; MANAGEMENT RESERVE (for UNKNOWN risks): 5% × $1,950,000 = $97,500; purpose: funds responses to unforeseen events (unknown unknowns); SPONSOR AUTHORITY: use of management reserve requires sponsor approval; it is above the PM's autonomous spending authority; TOTAL PROJECT BUDGET (= Cost Baseline + Management Reserve): $1,950,000 + $97,500 = $2,047,500; this is the total approved budget request presented to the finance team; PRACTICAL COMMUNICATION: 'The project direct cost is $1.8M; with contingency for identified risks ($150K) and management reserve for unforeseens ($97.5K), the total budget request is $2.05M'; the sponsor and finance team understand the breakdown and the PM's authority boundaries.
explanations.c: A flat 20% addition regardless of risk is arbitrary — it may be insufficient for high-risk projects or excessive for low-risk projects. Reserve analysis should be based on the actual risk profile.
explanations.d: Contingency and management reserves are NOT interchangeable: CONTINGENCY RESERVE: for identified risks (known unknowns); PM controls; MANAGEMENT RESERVE: for unidentified risks (unknown unknowns); sponsor controls; conflating them misrepresents who has authority to spend each reserve.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — MVP; MVP scope definition conflict; stakeholder alignment
questions.text: A product team is in planning for a new healthcare portal. The product owner proposes an MVP of: patient appointment scheduling and basic medical record viewing. The clinical director says: 'Any portal without secure messaging to physicians, prescription refill requests, and lab result access is not viable — patients won't use it without those features.' How should this MVP scope conflict be resolved?

answers.text: The product owner's decision is final — the product owner defines MVP unilaterally
Include all features requested by the clinical director — stakeholder requirements always trump MVP thinking

Conduct an MVP scope negotiation: validate the clinical director's claim with user research (do patients actually require all three features for basic viability?); assess the effort impact of adding secure messaging, prescription refills, and lab results; negotiate a 'minimum' that both agree is viable; potentially phase the delivery (MVP = appointments + records + lab results; Phase 2 = secure messaging + prescription refills if data shows lower immediate need); document the agreed MVP scope
Conduct A/B testing in production to determine which MVP is better — deploy both simultaneously

explanations.a: The product owner defines MVP with stakeholder input — not unilaterally. A healthcare product that patients won't use because it lacks critical features is not 'viable.' The clinical director's perspective represents user reality that the product owner must incorporate.
explanations.b: Including all features from every stakeholder request without prioritization defeats MVP thinking — the team would build a full-featured product from day one without learning from user feedback. The clinical director's input should be considered, not automatically accepted in full.
explanations.c: MVP SCOPE NEGOTIATION PROCESS: VALIDATE THE CLAIM: user research is the most credible arbiter — conduct a brief survey or focus group with 20-30 patients: 'Would you use a portal with only appointment scheduling and basic medical records? What would make you choose phone over portal?'; if 80% say they need lab results for basic adoption → lab results are MVP; if only 30% need secure messaging immediately → it's Phase 2; EFFORT IMPACT ASSESSMENT: calculate the additional development time for each contested feature: lab results (3 additional sprints?); secure messaging (4 sprints?); prescription refills (2 sprints?); understanding the cost of including each feature informs the trade-off conversation; NEGOTIATED MVP: find the minimum set that BOTH parties believe is genuinely viable based on evidence: appointment scheduling + record viewing + lab results = MVP (patient critical need confirmed by research); secure messaging + prescription refills = Phase 2 (high value but not essential for initial adoption); DOCUMENT AND COMMIT: agreed MVP scope documented in the product charter/backlog; both product owner and clinical director formally acknowledge; BENEFIT: avoids both the extremes (trivially small MVP that fails; kitchen-sink MVP that takes 18 months).
explanations.d: A/B testing competing MVP definitions in production exposes real patients to a potentially inadequate healthcare product. For healthcare portals, patient safety and regulatory considerations preclude uncontrolled A/B testing of core feature sets.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — completing planning; criteria for transitioning to execution
questions.text: A project manager is determining whether the planning phase is complete enough to begin execution. Which criteria BEST indicate planning is ready for execution authorization?

answers.text: Planning is never complete — begin execution immediately after the charter is signed

Planning is complete when: the project management plan is developed (all subsidiary plans); all three baselines (scope, schedule, cost) are approved; the risk register is established; the team is assigned and oriented; communication channels are operational; and the sponsor provides formal execution authorization
Planning is complete when the schedule is ready — all other plans can be developed during execution
Planning is complete when 100% of risks are identified and mitigated — execution cannot begin while any risk exists

explanations.a: Beginning execution immediately after the charter (skipping planning) produces: undefined scope (team doesn't know what to build); no schedule (no coordination of work); no budget (spending is uncontrolled); unidentified risks (crises happen without warning); no quality standards (deliverables have no acceptance criteria). This is the definition of project chaos.
explanations.b: PLANNING COMPLETION CRITERIA: ALL SUBSIDIARY PLANS DEVELOPED: scope management plan; schedule management plan; cost management plan; quality management plan; resource management plan; communication management plan; risk management plan; procurement management plan; SCOPE BASELINE APPROVED: scope statement, WBS, WBS dictionary — approved by sponsor; SCHEDULE BASELINE APPROVED: project schedule with all activities, dependencies, resources, and milestones — approved by sponsor; COST BASELINE APPROVED: time-phased budget with contingency — approved by sponsor; RISK REGISTER ESTABLISHED: top risks identified, assessed, and responses planned; TEAM ASSIGNED AND ORIENTED: all required team members committed; onboarding complete; access provisioned; kickoff meeting conducted; COMMUNICATION INFRASTRUCTURE OPERATIONAL: all team members can access project tools; communication channels tested; FORMAL EXECUTION AUTHORIZATION: sponsor explicitly approves the project management plan and authorizes execution; this is the planning-phase gate that triggers the transition to execution; WHY FORMAL AUTHORIZATION: the sponsor's approval of the plan signifies: they accept the proposed scope, schedule, and cost baseline; they agree the project is ready to execute; they authorize resource consumption; the PM has explicit authority to proceed.
explanations.c: The schedule alone is insufficient — execution without scope baseline produces uncontrolled scope; execution without a budget produces uncontrolled spending; execution without a risk register produces unmanaged crises. The schedule is necessary but not sufficient.
explanations.d: 100% risk identification is impossible — all projects have unknown unknowns. The standard for execution readiness is: all HIGH and MEDIUM risks identified and responded to; contingency reserves established for residual risk; not zero remaining risk. Projects that wait for zero risk never begin execution.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — reviewing all planning deliverables for consistency; integrated plan review
questions.text: Before authorizing execution, the PMO director reviews the planning deliverables for a $4M data platform project. She identifies three inconsistencies: (1) The schedule shows 12 months but the cost baseline is planned over 15 months; (2) The risk register has no risks for data migration (a known complexity area); (3) The QA plan doesn't mention UAT but the scope statement has a 'UAT delivery' deliverable. Diagnose each inconsistency and prescribe corrections.

answers.text: None are significant — minor inconsistencies are acceptable in planning documents

(1) Schedule vs. cost baseline mismatch: the cost baseline must be time-phased to match the schedule; if the project takes 12 months, the cost baseline must reflect 12 months of spending — not 15; correct by re-aligning cost time-phasing to the 12-month schedule. (2) No data migration risks: data migration is high-risk (data quality, volume, transformation complexity, mapping accuracy, rollback planning); correct by conducting a specific data migration risk assessment and adding 3-5 data migration risks to the register. (3) UAT not in QA plan: if UAT is a scope deliverable, the QA plan must describe how UAT will be conducted (who, when, criteria, duration, acceptance threshold); correct by adding a UAT section to the QA plan
Only fix inconsistency (1) — the cost/schedule alignment is the only material issue
Approve execution anyway — these inconsistencies will resolve themselves during execution

explanations.a: All three inconsistencies are material and would cause project governance failures if not corrected before execution.
explanations.b: INCONSISTENCY DIAGNOSIS AND CORRECTION: (1) SCHEDULE/COST TIMELINE MISMATCH: DIAGNOSIS: the cost baseline represents a 15-month spending plan but the schedule shows a 12-month delivery; this creates: incorrect Planned Value (PV) calculations for earned value analysis (PV would be wrong in the early months if costs are time-phased differently from schedule); budget availability mismatch (the team needs to spend for 12 months of work but the finance team has planned 15 months of expenditure — monthly budget allocations would be misaligned); CORRECTION: re-run the time-phased cost model to match the 12-month schedule; the SAME total budget but phased over 12 months instead of 15; the cost baseline is approved after reconciliation with the schedule. (2) DATA MIGRATION RISKS MISSING: DIAGNOSIS: data migration is one of the highest-risk activities in any system replacement project; common risks: data quality failures (30% of records have missing fields, duplicate records, incorrect formatting); volume underestimation (actual data volume is 3× the estimate); transformation complexity (business rules for converting old data structures to new ones are unclear or conflict); no risks for this area = blind spot in risk management; CORRECTION: conduct a dedicated data migration risk workshop; add 3-5 specific data migration risks: 'Data quality assessment reveals migration-blocking issues' (HIGH probability, HIGH impact); 'Historical data volume exceeds estimates' (MEDIUM probability, HIGH impact); 'Business rule conflicts during transformation' (MEDIUM probability, HIGH impact); assign risk owners; develop mitigation and contingency responses. (3) UAT NOT IN QA PLAN: DIAGNOSIS: the scope baseline includes UAT as a deliverable; the QA plan must describe how that deliverable will be tested; without a UAT section in the QA plan: who conducts UAT is unclear (business users? QA team?); UAT duration is unplanned (not in schedule?); acceptance criteria for UAT are undefined; CORRECTION: add a UAT section to the QA plan including: who participates (business users, product owner); UAT entry criteria (all dev testing complete, zero P1 defects); test scenario development approach; UAT duration (typically 2-4 weeks for major systems); acceptance threshold (e.g., 95% of test scenarios passed, zero P1 open defects); UAT exit criteria and sign-off authority.
explanations.c: All three inconsistencies are material: the cost/schedule mismatch affects EVM accuracy; missing data migration risks leave the team blind to a high-probability failure area; UAT absent from QA plan means a major quality gate has no plan. Fixing only one of three misses critical governance gaps.
explanations.d: 'These inconsistencies will resolve themselves' is never true — inconsistent documents produce inconsistent execution. The schedule/cost mismatch will produce EVM reporting errors; the data migration risk gap will produce unplanned crises; the UAT gap will produce undefined acceptance criteria at go-live.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Planning phase — entire planning phase orchestration; all deliverables; quality and readiness
questions.text: A project manager reflects on a failed $3M ERP implementation post-mortem. The post-mortem identifies these planning failures: no MVP was defined (the project tried to deliver all 200 features at once); the risk register was complete at planning but never updated; no transition plan existed (IT operations was blindsided at go-live); the QA plan had no acceptance criteria; and the communication plan didn't cover the 400 end users who needed training information. Map each failure to its planning phase activity and explain the downstream consequence each caused.

answers.text: Planning failures are minor — project execution always compensates for planning gaps
All five failures trace to the same cause: insufficient time in planning — allocate more planning time to prevent all failures

Five distinct failures with distinct consequences: (1) No MVP definition → all 200 features required for go-live → 18-month delays trying to achieve 100% scope before release → lost business value; (2) Risk register not updated → 3 unmanaged risks became critical issues → unplanned $400K cost overrun; (3) No transition plan → IT operations unprepared at go-live → 3-week production outage as operations scrambled to support an unknown system; (4) No acceptance criteria in QA plan → go-live debate ('is it done?') required 4 extra weeks of rework → schedule overrun; (5) No end-user communication plan → 400 employees unaware of changes → mass confusion at go-live → adoption failure and productivity loss for 3 months
Only the transition plan failure matters — the other four are normal project outcomes

explanations.a: Planning failures do not 'compensate' themselves — they compound. An execution team working without acceptance criteria, a risk register, or an end-user communication plan is managing chaos without guardrails.
explanations.b: All five failures have different root causes: no MVP definition = scoping philosophy failure; risk register not updated = governance compliance failure; no transition plan = omission of a required planning activity; no acceptance criteria = QA plan quality failure; no end-user comms = stakeholder identification gap. More planning time doesn't fix a scoping philosophy or stakeholder identification gap if the PM doesn't know to address them.
explanations.c: FIVE PLANNING FAILURES → DOWNSTREAM CONSEQUENCES: (1) NO MVP DEFINED: PLANNING ACTIVITY MISSED: MVP definition during planning; CONSEQUENCE: all 200 features are 'required' for launch; no partial delivery pathway; when Sprint 15 of 20 has delivery-blocking defects, the entire go-live is blocked; business waits 18 months instead of receiving value incrementally; lost revenue opportunity during the delay; LESSON: MVP definition enables phased value delivery and reduces launch risk. (2) RISK REGISTER NOT MAINTAINED: PLANNING ACTIVITY MISSED: risk monitoring plan and ongoing risk reviews; CONSEQUENCE: 3 new risks emerged during execution (vendor API change, key architect departure, data quality issues) — none were in the risk register; no contingency plans existed for these risks; when they materialized, the team improvised poorly, costing $400K; LESSON: risk management is continuous — the planning-phase register is a starting point, not a final product. (3) NO TRANSITION PLAN: PLANNING ACTIVITY MISSED: transition plan / knowledge transfer planning; CONSEQUENCE: IT operations team received an ERP system they'd never seen; no runbooks, no training, no monitoring setup; the go-live weekend turned into a 3-week incident as operations stumbled through supporting an unknown system; LESSON: operations readiness must be planned as part of the project, not after. (4) NO ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: PLANNING ACTIVITY MISSED: QA plan acceptance criteria development; CONSEQUENCE: at go-live readiness review, executives debated 'is it good enough?' for 4 weeks; each stakeholder had different standards; the team spent 4 weeks in rework based on opinions rather than pre-agreed criteria; LESSON: acceptance criteria provide objective go-live gates.
