(5) END USERS NOT IN COMMUNICATION PLAN: PLANNING ACTIVITY MISSED: stakeholder identification completeness (400 users not included); CONSEQUENCE: 400 employees showed up Monday morning to a completely new ERP with no training, no communication about what changed, and no support resources; productivity collapsed 60% for 3 months; help desk flooded; adoption crisis; LESSON: end-user communication is as important as executive communication in any user-facing system implementation.
explanations.d: All five failures produced measurable, significant project damage. Dismissing four of five as 'normal outcomes' prevents learning and future prevention.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — purpose; performing work according to the project plan
questions.text: What is the PRIMARY purpose of the project execution phase?

answers.text: To perform the work defined in the project management plan, produce project deliverables, and manage all the people and processes needed to build the product — while monitoring performance against the established baselines
To develop the project management plan and establish baselines
To close out the project and release project resources
To conduct the project kickoff meeting and authorize the project

explanations.a: EXECUTION PHASE PURPOSE: the execution phase is where the project plan is converted into actual deliverables. KEY ACTIVITIES: TASK EXECUTION: performing the work defined in the WBS and schedule; TEAM MANAGEMENT: directing, motivating, and supporting the project team; VENDOR MANAGEMENT: managing external vendor relationships and deliverables; QUALITY ASSURANCE: conducting quality activities (reviews, testing, audits) to ensure deliverables meet standards; CHANGE MANAGEMENT: managing organizational change management (OCM) to enable adoption; STAKEHOLDER COMMUNICATION: keeping stakeholders informed and engaged; PERFORMANCE MONITORING: tracking actual progress against baselines (scope, schedule, cost) and taking corrective actions; ISSUE AND RISK MANAGEMENT: actively managing issues and monitoring risks; CHANGE CONTROL: evaluating and implementing approved changes to the plan. NOTE: execution and monitoring/controlling typically happen simultaneously — the PM executes and monitors in parallel; the 'monitoring and controlling' activities are embedded within the execution phase throughout the project.
explanations.b: Developing the project management plan and establishing baselines are PLANNING phase activities. Execution begins after planning is complete and baselines are approved.
explanations.c: Project closure activities (lessons learned, archiving, releasing resources) are the CLOSING phase activities.
explanations.d: Project kickoff and authorization are INITIATION phase activities that precede planning and execution.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — vendor management; contract administration; performance monitoring
questions.text: During execution, the project manager is managing a vendor who is responsible for delivering a custom integration layer. The vendor has delivered the first milestone but the output doesn't match the agreed acceptance criteria. What should the project manager do?

answers.text: Formally reject the deliverable in writing (citing specific acceptance criteria not met); request a revised delivery within the contract's specified correction period; document the rejection in the contract file; escalate if the vendor does not correct within the specified timeframe
Accept the delivery anyway — demanding quality from vendors creates conflict
Pay the vendor and note the deficiencies for the next milestone — catching up is the vendor's problem
Cancel the contract immediately — any quality miss triggers termination

explanations.a: VENDOR DELIVERABLE REJECTION PROCESS: FORMAL WRITTEN REJECTION: document specifically which acceptance criteria are not met; written rejection creates a contractual record; the rejection letter specifies the deficiencies clearly; CORRECTION PERIOD: most contracts specify a correction period (e.g., 10-14 business days) for the vendor to address deficiencies and resubmit; REQUEST REVISED DELIVERY: specify a clear resubmission deadline; CONTRACT FILE DOCUMENTATION: maintain records of all rejection notices, deficiency documentation, and vendor responses; this is essential for: payment dispute prevention (vendor cannot claim they weren't notified); contract enforcement; lessons learned; ESCALATION PATH: if vendor fails to correct within the specified timeframe: escalate to the vendor's management; contact the contract's escalation point; potentially invoke SLA penalty clauses; most contracts have formal dispute resolution procedures. VENDOR MANAGEMENT PRINCIPLE: clear, documented communication about deliverable quality issues is the most effective way to maintain vendor performance — it creates accountability without unnecessary conflict.
explanations.b: Accepting a deliverable that doesn't meet acceptance criteria without documentation sets a dangerous precedent: it implies the deficient work is acceptable; it establishes that acceptance criteria are not enforced; the vendor has no incentive to improve; the project accumulates technical debt.
explanations.c: Paying for unaccepted deliverables creates the impression that substandard work is acceptable. The contract's payment terms should be tied to accepted deliverables — not delivered (but substandard) deliverables.
explanations.d: Immediate contract termination for a first-milestone quality issue is disproportionate. Most quality issues can be corrected through the formal rejection and correction process. Contract termination is appropriate only after repeated failure to correct after reasonable opportunity.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — OCM: assess organizational readiness; change capacity analysis
questions.text: In organizational change management (OCM), 'assessing organizational readiness' means:

answers.text: Evaluating how prepared the organization is to absorb and adopt the change — including: current change capacity (how many changes are happening simultaneously?), cultural factors affecting adoption, leadership commitment, stakeholder resistance levels, and organizational history with similar changes
Assessing whether the organization's financial accounts are ready for the project's costs
Assessing whether the project team is technically ready to begin development
Reviewing whether the project charter has been formally signed

explanations.a: ORGANIZATIONAL READINESS ASSESSMENT in OCM: PURPOSE: determine whether the organization has the capacity and capability to successfully adopt the change being implemented; KEY DIMENSIONS ASSESSED: CHANGE CAPACITY: how many other changes are happening simultaneously? If the organization is already overwhelmed with changes, adding another may fail due to 'change fatigue'; CULTURAL FACTORS: is the organization's culture generally open to change or change-resistant? Past change history matters; LEADERSHIP COMMITMENT: are senior leaders actively championing the change? Passive support is insufficient — leaders must model the desired behaviors; STAKEHOLDER AWARENESS AND DESIRE: how aware are affected employees of the change? How much do they want it (or resist it)?; CAPABILITY: do employees have the skills needed to adopt the change? Is training available?; READINESS ASSESSMENT METHODS: surveys and questionnaires to measure awareness, desire, knowledge, and ability; interviews with department heads and team leads; historical data on adoption rates from prior changes; USE OF ASSESSMENT: readiness assessment results drive: change management plan priorities; communication emphasis; training focus areas; timing and pace of change rollout; A LOW READINESS SCORE does not mean canceling the change — it means: more robust change management support is needed; timeline may need adjustment; leadership engagement must be strengthened first.
explanations.b: Financial readiness is addressed through budget management — not organizational change readiness assessment. OCM readiness is about PEOPLE and CULTURE, not finances.
explanations.c: Technical team readiness is project resource management — not OCM organizational readiness assessment.
explanations.d: Charter signature is a governance activity in the initiation phase — not an OCM assessment.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — OCM: identify and engage change champions; champion network
questions.text: In organizational change management, CHANGE CHAMPIONS are:

answers.text: Influential individuals within the affected organization who genuinely believe in the change, are trusted by their peers, and actively promote adoption through their networks — they bridge the gap between the project team and the broader organization
External consultants who are paid to support the change — change champions are vendors
Project team members who write the technical documentation for the new system
The project sponsor who authorized the project budget

explanations.a: CHANGE CHAMPIONS in OCM: DEFINITION: influential individuals WITHIN the affected organization who: BELIEVE in the change: genuinely support it (not just compliant or indifferent); PEER TRUST: are respected and trusted by their colleagues — when they say 'this is a good change,' people believe them; ACTIVE PROMOTION: actively share positive messages, answer colleagues' questions, demonstrate the new system/process in their daily work; NETWORK INFLUENCE: their organic influence reaches people the project team cannot directly engage. WHY CHAMPIONS ARE ESSENTIAL: employees trust colleagues more than executives and project teams; a message from a respected peer carries more weight than the same message from HR or IT; champions can surface and address resistance that employees would never express to the project team; CHAMPION CHARACTERISTICS: respected in their area; early adopters or at least open-minded about change; sufficient time commitment (change champion role requires 10-20% of their time); not a formal manager (peer trust, not hierarchical authority); CHAMPION NETWORK: identify 1 champion per department/business unit; the combined network reaches the entire organization; CHAMPION ACTIVITIES: attend training early; demonstrate the new system to peers; answer questions; provide feedback on adoption issues to the project team; IDENTIFYING CHAMPIONS: look for informal leaders, go-to people for questions, team members who volunteer early for new initiatives.
explanations.b: Change champions are INTERNAL organizational members — their credibility comes from being trusted peers within the organization, not from being paid external consultants.
explanations.c: Technical documentation writers are project team members — not change champions. Change champions are business-side organizational members, not necessarily technical contributors.
explanations.d: The project sponsor may advocate for the change at the executive level — but 'change champion' in OCM specifically refers to trusted peer-level advocates within the business, not the executive sponsor.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — tracking and reporting; status reporting; performance data collection
questions.text: During project execution, effective tracking and reporting serves what PRIMARY purpose?

answers.text: To demonstrate to stakeholders that the project manager is busy — reports prove effort

To provide accurate, timely visibility into project performance (schedule, budget, scope, quality, risks) so that the PM and stakeholders can identify variances early and take corrective action before problems escalate
To create legal documentation for contract disputes — status reports are primarily legal instruments
To justify additional budget requests — reports are used to ask for more money

explanations.a: Reports that demonstrate PM busyness without informing decisions are bureaucratic overhead. The value of tracking and reporting is decision support, not activity documentation.
explanations.b: TRACKING AND REPORTING PURPOSE: effective status reporting in execution: EARLY VARIANCE DETECTION: schedule variance identified at Week 4 can be corrected; the same variance discovered at Week 12 may be unrecoverable; PERFORMANCE VISIBILITY: all stakeholders see the same accurate picture of project health; DECISION SUPPORT: data-driven decision making — corrective actions are based on actual performance, not intuition; ACCOUNTABLE GOVERNANCE: stakeholders can fulfill their governance responsibilities only with accurate information; TRACKING ACTIVITIES: collecting actual start/finish dates; measuring percentage complete on activities; recording actual costs incurred; capturing defect counts and test results; monitoring risk trigger events; REPORTING OUTPUTS: schedule status (activities ahead/behind/on plan); cost status (budget vs. actual, CPI, SV, CV); scope status (approved changes, pending changes); risk status (open risks, recently closed, newly identified); quality status (defect rates, test completion); issue log (open issues and resolution status); REPORTING CADENCE: aligns with communication plan; executive dashboards monthly; team status weekly; financial reporting per accounting cycles.
explanations.c: Status reports may become relevant in contract disputes — but this is a secondary function, not their primary purpose. Primary purpose is project management visibility and decision support.
explanations.d: Budget requests are submitted through the change control process when scope changes require additional funding — status reports track and report existing budget performance, not generate new funding requests.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — task execution; managing work according to the project plan; PM oversight
questions.text: A project is in execution. Two developers are working on a critical integration module. At the weekly status meeting, Developer A says the module will be done 'sometime next week.' Developer B hasn't provided an update in 10 days. The module is on the critical path with a deadline in 8 days. How should the project manager manage this situation?

answers.text: Proactively manage the situation: request a specific completion date from Developer A ('What day specifically, and what's remaining?'); contact Developer B immediately to determine current status (the 10-day silence is a red flag on a critical path activity); assess whether the 8-day deadline is achievable; if at risk, immediately identify options (overtime, temporary contractor support, scope reduction) and present to the sponsor with a recommendation
Escalate immediately to the sponsor — any uncertainty requires executive intervention
Wait for the developers to report completion — developers know their work best
Reassign both developers — vague status updates indicate performance problems

explanations.a: PROACTIVE TASK EXECUTION MANAGEMENT: DEVELOPER A — SPECIFIC STATUS REQUEST: 'Sometime next week' is not an acceptable status for a critical path activity with an 8-day deadline; PM asks: 'What specific tasks remain? How many hours to complete each? What day will it be done? Are there any blockers?'; this produces an actionable, specific status; DEVELOPER B — IMMEDIATE OUTREACH: 10 days without update on a critical path module is a serious red flag; PM contacts Developer B directly today: 'I haven't received a status update in 10 days. What's the current state? How many days remain?'; SITUATION ASSESSMENT: after getting updated status from both developers, the PM can determine: is the 8-day deadline achievable?; what is the specific risk (1 day late? 3 days?)?; CORRECTIVE ACTION OPTIONS IF AT RISK: authorize limited overtime for the critical path module (cost vs. schedule trade-off); engage a temporary contractor to assist (if the work can be divided); reprioritize — can any other work be deferred to focus resources on this module?; ESCALATION TO SPONSOR: if corrective actions require additional resources (cost impact) or if the deadline will be missed despite all actions → escalate with: current situation, options evaluated, PM recommendation; only escalate when the PM's authority is insufficient or the impact exceeds defined thresholds.
explanations.b: Every uncertainty does not require immediate sponsor escalation — that would overwhelm the sponsor with operational details they shouldn't need to manage. The PM should first assess the situation themselves before escalating.
explanations.c: 'Wait and see' on a critical path activity 8 days from the deadline is the worst possible choice. By the time completion is clear, it may be too late to take corrective action.
explanations.d: Vague status updates indicate a PM communication standard issue — not necessarily individual performance problems. The appropriate response is to establish clearer status reporting expectations, not immediately reassign team members.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — vendor management; SLA monitoring; vendor performance management
questions.text: A project uses a cloud infrastructure vendor with a 99.9% uptime SLA. During testing, the vendor experiences three outages totaling 11 hours of downtime in a 30-day period. The SLA allows only 43 minutes of downtime per month (99.9% = 0.1% × 720 hours = 0.72 hours). The project's testing phase has been disrupted. What vendor management actions should the project manager take?

answers.text: Accept the outages — cloud vendors always have some downtime

Document the SLA breach with precise downtime data; formally notify the vendor in writing of the SLA violation; invoke the SLA's penalty or service credit clauses; quantify the project impact (testing days lost, schedule impact, team cost); escalate to the vendor's account manager and the PM's sponsor; assess whether the vendor's reliability is acceptable for production deployment
Switch to a different vendor immediately — any SLA breach requires vendor replacement
Wait until the contract ends to address SLA performance — penalties only apply at contract renewal

explanations.a: 11 hours vs. 43 minutes allowed is not 'some downtime' — it is 15× the contracted allowance. Passively accepting this as normal would: set a precedent that SLAs are not enforced; allow the vendor to continue without accountability; expose the production system to the same reliability risk; damage the project's testing schedule.
explanations.b: SLA BREACH MANAGEMENT: DOCUMENTATION: precise records of each outage (start time, end time, duration, service affected, confirmed root cause); total downtime (11 hours) vs. allowed (43 minutes); testing activities disrupted and their business impact; FORMAL WRITTEN NOTIFICATION: notify the vendor in writing, citing the contract section and specific SLA: 'Per Section 4.2 of the contract, the monthly uptime SLA is 99.9% (maximum 43 minutes downtime). During the period [dates], three outages totaling 11 hours represent an SLA violation of [specific magnitude]. We are formally invoking the SLA remedy provisions.'; INVOKE PENALTY/CREDIT CLAUSES: most cloud SLAs include service credits for breaches; calculate and formally request the applicable credits; this creates financial accountability; PROJECT IMPACT DOCUMENTATION: quantify the cost of disruption: testing team days lost × daily rate; schedule extension required; potential downstream delivery impact; ESCALATION TO VENDOR MANAGEMENT: if the vendor's support team doesn't respond adequately, escalate to the account manager and the vendor's VP of Customer Success; RISK ASSESSMENT: should production deployment proceed with a vendor demonstrating 15× the allowed downtime? Present this assessment to the sponsor — they may choose to: delay production deployment pending vendor performance improvement; evaluate backup vendors; implement redundancy to mitigate vendor reliability risk.
explanations.c: Immediate vendor replacement for first-occurrence SLA breaches is disproportionate: vendor replacement takes months; new vendor has onboarding risk; the current vendor may improve after being formally held accountable. Replacement should be considered only if the vendor fails to improve after being formally notified.
explanations.d: SLA penalties are typically contractual remedies triggered by breach notification — not deferred to renewal. Most contracts have defined timeframes within which penalties must be claimed (often 30-60 days after the breach).

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — OCM: develop change management plan; ADKAR model; change approach
questions.text: A change manager is developing an organizational change management plan for a new procurement system implementation affecting 300 purchasing employees. The readiness assessment showed 40% awareness, 25% desire, and significant resistance from department heads who fear loss of control. Using the ADKAR model, what should the change management plan address?

answers.text: Focus only on training — if employees know how to use the system, they will adopt it

The ADKAR-based change plan should address: Awareness (40% is low — intensive communications campaign explaining WHY the change is happening, what it means for each role); Desire (25% is critically low — address resistance by involving department heads in system design; demonstrate benefits specific to their teams; address fear of losing control by clarifying the new governance model); Knowledge (training program for all 300 users); Ability (supervised practice and support during go-live); Reinforcement (post-go-live recognition and performance measurement that rewards adoption)
ADKAR is only for large organizational transformations — this procurement system is too small
Address Awareness only — once employees know about the change, adoption follows naturally

explanations.a: Training addresses Knowledge and partially Ability — but with only 25% Desire, 300 employees who don't want the change will resist even if they know how to use the system. Training alone fails when motivation to change is absent.
explanations.b: ADKAR MODEL APPLICATION for procurement system: AWARENESS (currently 40%, needs 90%+): employees who don't know why the change is happening cannot commit to it; ACTIONS: multi-channel communication campaign (email series, team meetings, intranet, posters); clear messaging: why is the current procurement system inadequate? what business problem does this solve? what are the go-live dates?; DESIRE (currently 25%, critically low — the most urgent gap): desire requires addressing the SPECIFIC motivators and concerns of each stakeholder group; DEPARTMENT HEADS (fear loss of control): hold dedicated sessions with each department head; clarify what they will gain (better visibility, faster approvals, real-time reporting) vs. what changes (approval workflows are now system-controlled); involve them in configuring the approval thresholds — give them meaningful control within the new system; PURCHASING STAFF: show time savings (how much manual work is eliminated?); demonstrate ease of use in live demos; share peer success stories; KNOWLEDGE (training — to be developed): role-based training for purchasing staff vs. approvers vs. requestors; ABILITY (supported go-live): help desk support with rapid response; floor walkers during first 2 weeks; training sandbox for practice; REINFORCEMENT (post go-live): recognize departments that achieve target adoption rates; track and communicate adoption metrics; remove rewards tied to old-system behaviors.
explanations.c: ADKAR is applicable to any change affecting people — a 300-person system implementation with 40% awareness and significant resistance is exactly the scenario ADKAR was designed to address. Size is not a threshold for change management applicability.
explanations.d: Awareness alone rarely produces adoption. The readiness data already shows: 40% awareness and 25% desire. Even among those who are aware (40%), most still have low desire. Knowledge, ability, and reinforcement are all needed.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — OCM: execute change management activities; managing resistance
questions.text: During the execution of a new HR system implementation, the change manager identifies that three department managers are actively discouraging their teams from engaging with the new system ('Just keep using spreadsheets — the new system will probably be replaced in a year anyway'). This resistance is undermining change efforts across all three departments. What change management intervention is MOST effective?

answers.text: Address resistance directly with the managers: one-on-one meetings to understand their specific concerns (fear of losing control? previous failed implementations? belief the system is wrong choice?); address each concern factually and specifically; engage them in the change as part of the solution (involve them in testing, get their input on training); escalate to their department head or sponsor if one-on-one engagement fails; the change plan should have a specific resistance management protocol
Replace the resistant managers — leadership resistance cannot be tolerated
Ignore the resistant managers — employees will eventually adopt the system regardless
Go around the resistant managers and communicate directly with their teams only — exclude the managers from change communications

explanations.a: RESISTANCE MANAGEMENT for actively resistant managers: ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION (one-on-one meetings): 'I've heard you have concerns about the new system. Can we talk through what's on your mind?'; listen carefully — specific concerns require specific responses: 'I've seen 3 new systems fail in 2 years. Why will this one be different?' → address with evidence (executive commitment, ROI data, governance plan, success at comparable organizations); 'I'll lose visibility into my team's work' → demonstrate the system's reporting capabilities (show them actual dashboards); 'My team doesn't have time for training right now' → negotiate a training schedule that works for their team's workload; INVOLVEMENT AS SOLUTION: people who help design solutions adopt them more readily; offer the resistant managers a role: input into their department's configuration; advisory role in testing their department's workflows; first look at the new system's features relevant to their work; ESCALATION (if engagement fails): if one-on-one engagement doesn't shift behavior, escalate to the sponsor: 'Three department managers are actively discouraging adoption. This is at risk of undermining the project. I need your help engaging them at the executive level.'; executive-level conversation from the sponsor carries different weight than PM engagement; GOING AROUND MANAGERS (option D): bypassing managers to communicate directly with their teams creates: further manager resistance (they feel disrespected); dysfunctional communication dynamics; teams caught between conflicting messages from the PM and their manager.
explanations.b: Replacing resistant managers is an extreme escalation that: is the sponsor's or HR's decision, not the PM's; damages organizational relationships; may not address the underlying concerns (new manager may have the same concerns); should be considered only after all engagement attempts have failed.
explanations.c: Three managers actively telling their teams 'just use spreadsheets' will create adoption failure in their departments regardless of technical implementation quality. Passive resistance leads to: teams not attending training; system used minimally as workaround; adoption metrics showing failure in those departments; potential project failure if the departments are critical users.
explanations.d: Going around managers to communicate only with their teams: creates confusion (managers are still discouraging while the project team encourages); managers will feel disrespected and may escalate their resistance; teams will look to their manager for guidance and may follow the manager's lead.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — budget updates; Estimate at Completion (EAC); cost performance
questions.text: A project is 40% complete. The cost baseline is $1,000,000. Actual Cost (AC) to date = $450,000. Earned Value (EV) = $350,000. The project manager calculates CPI = 0.78. The sponsor asks: 'What is the forecasted final cost of this project?' How should the PM respond?

answers.text: 'Based on current performance, the Estimate at Completion (EAC) = BAC/CPI = $1,000,000/0.78 = $1,282,051. This means if current cost efficiency continues, the project will cost approximately $1.28M — $282K over the original budget. We should investigate why costs are running 28% over earned value and identify corrective actions.'
'The project will finish at $450,000 — we've already spent that much'
'The project will finish at $1,000,000 — we're on budget'
'We cannot forecast costs until the project is 90% complete — too much uncertainty exists'

explanations.a: EAC CALCULATION AND INTERPRETATION: CPI = EV / AC = $350,000 / $450,000 = 0.778; EAC (performance-based) = BAC / CPI = $1,000,000 / 0.778 = $1,285,347 (≈$1.28M); INTERPRETATION: if the project continues at its current cost efficiency (CPI = 0.78), the final cost will be approximately $1.28M; the project is currently running 28% over earned value — for every $1 of completed work, the team is spending $1.28; ESTIMATE TO COMPLETE (ETC) = EAC − AC = $1,285,000 − $450,000 = $835,000 remaining to spend; VARIANCE AT COMPLETION (VAC) = BAC − EAC = $1,000,000 − $1,285,000 = −$285,000 (projected overrun); PM ACTIONS: investigate root cause of CPI < 1.0: Is it scope additions (unauthorized work consuming budget)? Incorrect original estimates? Inefficient execution? Vendor overruns? corrective actions depend on root cause; brief the sponsor on the EAC and the corrective plan; if corrective actions cannot recover the budget, the sponsor needs to authorize additional funding through change control. ALTERNATIVE EAC FORMULAS exist depending on assumptions (remaining work performed at budget rate, or at modified rate) — the performance-based formula (BAC/CPI) is often the most realistic for projects that have been consistently over-budget.
explanations.b: $450,000 is the Actual Cost to date — not the final cost. The project is only 40% complete; significant spending remains.
explanations.c: CPI of 0.78 (< 1.0) means the project is OVER BUDGET — spending $1.28 for every $1.00 of work accomplished. Reporting 'on budget' is inaccurate.
explanations.d: EAC forecasting is most valuable when the project still has enough time to take corrective action (30-50% complete is ideal for intervention). Waiting until 90% complete means insufficient runway for correction.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — timeline updates; schedule variance analysis; recovery options
questions.text: At the 5-month mark of a 10-month project, the Schedule Performance Index (SPI) = 0.82. The project is behind schedule. The sponsor asks for an honest assessment and a recovery plan. What should the PM present?

answers.text: 'The project is slightly behind but will catch up naturally — no action needed'
'We need to rebaseline the schedule to show SPI = 1.0 — adjusting the baseline will fix the metric'

SPI = 0.82 means the project is accomplishing only 82% of planned work per period; at this rate, the 10-month project will take approximately 10/0.82 = 12.2 months. Present: current status (SPI, specific activities behind, root cause); forecast (12.2-month completion without corrective action); recovery options (fast-tracking, crashing, scope deferral); PM recommendation; if full recovery is not achievable, present an honest revised timeline with the sponsor's approval
'SPI is a lagging indicator — it doesn't accurately reflect current schedule status'

explanations.a: SPI of 0.82 sustained over 5 months is a significant schedule performance problem. 'Catch up naturally' is not a credible plan — schedule delays rarely recover without active intervention. Presenting this to the sponsor without a plan is not professional project management.
explanations.b: Adjusting the baseline to match actual performance eliminates the measurement reference point that allows performance assessment. Rebaselining masks the problem rather than solving it — the project would still finish late; it just wouldn't show as late against the revised baseline.
explanations.c: SCHEDULE VARIANCE ANALYSIS AND RECOVERY PLAN: CURRENT STATUS: SPI = 0.82 (18% behind schedule pace); specific activities that are behind and why (root cause): resource constraints? scope additions? estimation errors? vendor delays?; FORECAST: without corrective action: projected completion = 10 months ÷ 0.82 = 12.2 months (2.2 months late); RECOVERY OPTIONS: FAST-TRACKING: identify 2-3 critical path activities that can be overlapped (if soft logic); savings potential: 1-2 months; risk: rework if early outputs change; CRASHING: add resources to critical path activities; savings potential: 1-2 months; cost: additional budget required; SCOPE DEFERRAL: identify features that can be moved to Phase 2; savings potential: 1-2 months; trade-off: reduced Phase 1 value; PRODUCTIVITY IMPROVEMENT: address root cause of 82% efficiency (remove blockers, improve processes); savings potential: 0.5-1 month; COMBINED APPROACH: hybrid of 2-3 options may achieve full recovery; PM RECOMMENDATION: 'I recommend fast-tracking two critical path activities (saves ~1 month) and deferring 3 lower-priority features to Phase 2 (saves ~1.5 months). This achieves a 10.7-month completion — 0.7 months late but within acceptable range.'; SPONSOR DECISION: present the options and recommendation; sponsor decides on trade-offs.
explanations.d: SPI is a valuable leading indicator — at Month 5 of 10, a persistent SPI of 0.82 is a reliable signal that the project will finish late without corrective action. Dismissing it as a 'lagging indicator' ignores actionable performance data.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — OCM: evaluate change effectiveness; adoption metrics; measuring OCM success
questions.text: Three months after go-live of a new inventory management system, the change manager needs to evaluate whether the organizational change management was effective. What metrics and methods should she use?

answers.text: Only ask the project team whether the change was successful — they implemented it
Only check whether the system is technically functioning — technology adoption equals change success

Evaluate across multiple dimensions: system adoption rate (% of users actively using the system vs. workarounds); proficiency metrics (time to complete tasks in the new system vs. old system); error rates (data entry errors, system errors); user satisfaction survey (ease of use, support quality, training adequacy); business outcome metrics (inventory accuracy improvement, cycle time reduction); change fatigue indicators (user morale, overtime, complaints); compare all metrics to baseline and target values set in the change management plan
Change effectiveness evaluation is not needed — go-live completion means the change was successful

explanations.a: The project team has subjective interest in reporting success — they implemented the change. Change effectiveness must be measured from the user/business perspective, not the implementation team's perspective.
explanations.b: Technical functionality (the system runs) is a necessary but insufficient indicator of change success. A system that functions technically but is used in only 20% of cases (with 80% using workarounds) has NOT achieved effective change.
explanations.c: CHANGE EFFECTIVENESS EVALUATION FRAMEWORK: ADOPTION METRICS: system login rates (are users actually using it?); transaction volume in the new system vs. legacy system or manual processes; % of users who have completed all required tasks in the new system; PROFICIENCY METRICS: time to complete a standard transaction (should approach or beat legacy system within 3-6 months of go-live); error rate in new system (should decline as proficiency increases); supervisor ratings of team performance in the new process; USER SATISFACTION: brief survey (Net Promoter Score for the new system; ease of use rating; training rating; support quality rating); open-ended feedback on what would help more; BUSINESS OUTCOMES: primary goal achievement (was the inventory management goal achieved?): inventory accuracy improvement (x% to y%); cycle time reduction; stockout reduction; RESISTANCE INDICATORS: usage of workarounds (still using spreadsheets?); complaints to management or HR; turnover rates in affected departments; COMPARISON TO BASELINES: compare current metrics to: pre-go-live baselines (the as-is state); targets set in the change management plan; POST-EVALUATION ACTIONS: if adoption is below target → additional training, coaching, or change intervention; if business outcomes are not met → investigate whether it's a change issue or a technical issue; document lessons learned for future change initiatives.
explanations.d: Go-live is when the change STARTS — not when it's complete. Adoption, proficiency, and business outcomes develop over 3-12 months after go-live. Declaring success at go-live without measuring actual adoption frequently masks low adoption that the organization later struggles to recover.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — OCM: transition to normalized operations; embedding change in culture
questions.text: A new supply chain system has been live for 4 months. The project team is still heavily involved in daily support. Users still frequently ask the project team (rather than IT helpdesk) for help. The project team's PM wants to officially hand over to operations. What does 'transitioning to normalized operations' require and what indicators signal readiness?

answers.text: Simply announce the handover date and stop supporting users — operations will figure it out
Transition is ready when users forget the old system — time passage normalizes operations automatically

Transition to normalized operations requires: IT helpdesk trained and capable of handling 90%+ of user issues independently; users routing support to helpdesk (not project team); adoption metrics showing stable, high utilization; runbooks and documentation complete and validated; operations team managing system health monitoring; change management plan activities complete. Readiness indicators: helpdesk ticket volume from project team to operations team showing consistent shift; user escalation calls to project team declining; adoption metrics stable at target levels; operations team performing routine maintenance tasks independently
Normalized operations require re-implementing the system — the initial implementation is considered temporary

explanations.a: Abruptly ending support without validating operations readiness creates a support vacuum: users unable to get help from IT helpdesk (not trained); escalations go to project team anyway; productivity drops as unresolved issues accumulate; operations team scrambles without runbooks or training.
explanations.b: Time passage doesn't normalize operations if the underlying support capability is missing. Users will still ask the project team after 4 months if the IT helpdesk can't answer their questions.
explanations.c: TRANSITION TO NORMALIZED OPERATIONS REQUIREMENTS: HELPDESK CAPABILITY READINESS: IT helpdesk can resolve 90%+ of user issues without project team escalation; helpdesk staff have completed system training; call scripts and troubleshooting guides are in place; knowledge base is populated; USER SUPPORT ROUTING: users know the helpdesk is the correct support channel; the project team should redirect all direct support requests to helpdesk during the transition period ('Please submit a ticket to the IT helpdesk for system issues — they're fully trained to help you'); ADOPTION STABILITY: adoption metrics (system usage, error rates, proficiency) are stable and at or near targets; the system is not experiencing major usability crises; DOCUMENTATION COMPLETENESS: runbooks for all routine operations tasks; incident response procedures; DR procedures validated; OPERATIONS INDEPENDENCE: operations team monitoring system health without project team prompting; routine maintenance (patching, backup, performance tuning) performed independently; READINESS INDICATORS: weekly helpdesk ticket volume shows: increasing helpdesk handles (operations handles ↑); decreasing project team direct contacts ↓; operations team managing monitoring alerts independently; user satisfaction survey showing stable/improving scores. FORMAL HANDOVER: a formal transition meeting or handover document signed by: IT operations lead accepting responsibility; project PM releasing responsibility; transition includes a HYATUS PERIOD (30-60 days of project team on-call availability) where operations leads but project team is available for escalation.
explanations.d: Normalized operations means the system becomes part of routine operations — not re-implementation. The goal is embedding the change into organizational processes so it feels like 'the way we work,' not 'the new system.'

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — OCM: follow-up; reinforcement of change; sustaining adoption
questions.text: Six months after a new ERP go-live, adoption has stabilized at 75% (target was 90%). The change management team has disbanded. A post-implementation survey reveals that many users still prefer workarounds because 'the old system was faster for routine tasks.' How should the change manager address this delayed adoption challenge?

answers.text: Accept 75% adoption — exceeding 75% is not worth additional effort
Re-implement the system — low adoption indicates the system failed
Let the 25% of holdouts continue using workarounds — coexisting systems is an acceptable long-term state

Conduct targeted follow-up: investigate specifically which tasks feel faster in the old system (user perception vs. reality?); determine if the 'faster' perception is a training gap (users haven't learned efficient shortcuts), a genuine system limitation (some workflows are actually less efficient), or a change resistance issue (users haven't mentally committed to the new system); address root cause: training gaps → advanced user training; genuine limitations → report to vendor or submit enhancement requests; resistance → re-engage change champions for peer coaching; implement reinforcement (recognize departments achieving 90%+ adoption; leadership visibility); establish 90% adoption as a formal performance expectation

explanations.a: 25% gap below target (75% vs. 90%) in an ERP is significant — especially if those 25% are using workarounds (spreadsheets, old system), creating: data integrity issues (data not in the ERP is invisible to management); inefficiency (dual processing); compliance risks; ongoing support burden. The project was measured against 90% adoption as a success criterion.
explanations.b: 75% adoption after 6 months doesn't indicate system failure — it indicates incomplete change adoption. Re-implementation would be an extreme and costly overreaction.
explanations.c: Accepting coexisting systems long-term creates: permanent data integrity issues; ongoing support burden for two systems; undermined ROI on the ERP investment; inconsistent processes across the organization. The 90% adoption target exists for good business reasons.
explanations.d: SUSTAINED ADOPTION FOLLOW-UP: ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION: 'faster for routine tasks' has multiple explanations that require different responses: USER PERCEPTION VS. REALITY: users who learned the old system for years feel slower in the new system simply due to muscle memory; timed comparison test may show new system is actually faster but users haven't reached proficiency; TRAINING GAP: power users of the new ERP can complete routine tasks in 30% less time than new users; users never received advanced training on shortcuts and keyboard combinations; action: advanced 'power user' training workshops; GENUINE SYSTEM LIMITATIONS: some task workflows may genuinely be less efficient in the new ERP (more clicks, more screens); action: document and submit enhancement requests; work with vendor on configuration improvements; CHANGE RESISTANCE: some users haven't mentally committed to the new system (still in 'resistance' or 'compliance' stage of ADKAR vs. 'internalization'); REINFORCEMENT MECHANISMS: create friendly competition between departments for highest adoption rates; leadership visibility — managers check that team members are using the ERP for all required tasks; remove the option to use workarounds (disable old system access if possible); recognize and celebrate 90%+ adoption departments.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — vendor management; formal vendor performance review; relationship governance
questions.text: A project has been in execution for 4 months with a major implementation vendor. The project manager conducts the quarterly vendor performance review. What should this review cover and what outcomes should it produce?

answers.text: Only review the vendor's invoice accuracy — financial compliance is the only relevant vendor metric

The quarterly review should cover: deliverable quality vs. acceptance criteria (% of deliverables meeting standards on first submission); schedule adherence (on-time delivery rate); resource performance (assigned staff quality, turnover on the project); issue resolution timeliness (how quickly do vendor issues get resolved?); communication quality (responsiveness, proactiveness); upcoming milestone readiness; contractual compliance; the review should produce: documented performance scorecard; improvement actions for any metrics below threshold; formal communication to vendor; updated relationship management notes
Quarterly reviews are unnecessary — monthly invoices provide sufficient performance visibility
Only ask the vendor to self-assess — vendors know their own performance best

explanations.a: Invoice accuracy is one element — but a vendor who bills correctly while delivering late, low-quality work is still failing the project. Performance review must cover all dimensions of vendor contribution.
explanations.b: QUARTERLY VENDOR PERFORMANCE REVIEW CONTENT: DELIVERABLE QUALITY: % of deliverables accepted on first submission; number of rejection cycles per deliverable; severity of deficiencies in rejected deliverables; trend (improving or declining?); SCHEDULE ADHERENCE: planned vs. actual milestone dates; days late per deliverable; forecast for upcoming milestones; RESOURCE PERFORMANCE: are the vendor's assigned staff the people committed in the SOW?; any unexplained staff changes on the project?; performance quality of vendor staff; ISSUE RESOLUTION: average days to resolve reported issues; % of issues resolved within SLA; open issues older than 30 days; COMMUNICATION: responsiveness to PM requests; proactive communication about risks and issues; quality of written communications and reports; CONTRACTUAL COMPLIANCE: NDA compliance; data handling compliance; reporting obligations met; SCORECARD OUTCOMES: overall performance rating (Green/Yellow/Red); specific improvements required with timelines for Yellow/Red areas; formal documentation sent to vendor; if RED: formal notice per contract; escalation plan; UPCOMING MILESTONE READINESS: vendor's confidence assessment for next quarter's deliverables; resource plans for critical milestones. REVIEW PROCESS: PM + vendor PM; use pre-defined scoring criteria (not subjective); both parties sign off on the agreed improvement actions.
explanations.c: Monthly invoices show financial transactions — they provide no visibility into deliverable quality, schedule adherence, or resource performance. Quarterly performance reviews serve a different and critical governance function.
explanations.d: Vendor self-assessment is one INPUT to the review — but the PM must provide the objective perspective and customer experience data. A balanced review incorporates both PM assessment and vendor self-assessment.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — tracking and reporting; status report design; RAG status; executive communication
questions.text: A project manager sends the same 12-page detailed status report to all stakeholders weekly. Executives report they don't read it; team members say it has too much executive-level content. What should the PM do to improve the status reporting approach?

answers.text: Stop sending status reports — if no one reads them, they have no value
Make the report 20 pages — more detail serves all audiences better
Send all information verbally — written reports are ineffective

Design tiered status reports for different audiences: executive summary (1-2 pages — RAG status, key milestones, budget vs. actual, top 3 risks, decisions needed); team status update (4-6 pages — detailed task status, blockers, action items, technical decisions); this ensures each audience receives relevant information at the appropriate level of detail

explanations.a: If no one reads the reports, the reporting function is failing — but the solution is better reports, not no reports. Status reports serve essential governance and accountability functions.
explanations.b: Making reports longer universally increases the information overload problem. The issue is inappropriate format for the audience, not insufficient detail.
explanations.c: Verbal-only reporting provides no written record, no audit trail, and no consistent information distribution. Written reports are essential for governance, documentation, and communication consistency.
explanations.d: TIERED STATUS REPORTING: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY (1-2 pages, for sponsor and steering committee): RAG STATUS: Red/Amber/Green for schedule, budget, scope, quality; KEY MILESTONES: what was accomplished last period, what's planned next period, forecast end date vs. baseline; BUDGET STATUS: spend-to-date vs. plan; EAC vs. BAC; key cost drivers; TOP 3 RISKS: highest priority risks, current status, PM action; DECISIONS NEEDED: specific decisions the executives must make this period; executives DON'T need: task-level status; technical architecture discussions; vendor communication logs. TEAM STATUS (4-6 pages, for PM + team leads): TASK-LEVEL STATUS: each active WBS work package or sprint story; BLOCKERS AND DEPENDENCIES: what is preventing progress and what is needed; ACTION ITEMS: all open action items with owner and due date; TECHNICAL DECISIONS: architectural or technical decisions made this period; RISK REGISTER UPDATES: new risks identified, existing risks updated; FORMAT: PM creates the executive summary from the team status; the team status is the source of detail; the executive summary is the distilled view. COMMUNICATION PLAN UPDATE: update the communication plan to reflect tiered reporting; distribute the appropriate report to each stakeholder group; eliminate the 12-page one-size-fits-all report.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — change control in execution; integrated change control; tracking changes
questions.text: During execution, the product owner requests adding a new feature not in the current scope baseline. The developer says 'it's just 3 days of work.' What should the project manager do and why does the 3-day estimate not determine whether the change goes through change control?

answers.text: Approve the change — 3 days is small enough to skip change control
Ask the product owner to wait until a future project — new features cannot be added during execution
Add the feature in the next sprint — Agile projects don't need change control for backlog additions

Process the change through formal change control regardless of effort estimate: document the change request; conduct impact analysis (scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk); present to appropriate decision authority (PM if within authority threshold, CCB or sponsor if above); if approved, update all three baselines; the 3-day effort estimate doesn't determine change control applicability because: (1) a scope addition is a scope addition regardless of size; (2) the 3-day estimate may be wrong — 'small' changes frequently expand; (3) if approved outside change control, it sets a precedent that any 'small' change can bypass governance

explanations.a: A 3-day scope addition processed without change control: doesn't update the scope baseline; doesn't update the schedule (3 days taken from elsewhere without explicit approval); doesn't update the cost baseline; sets a precedent — when the next 3-day change arrives, the developer will cite this precedent. Twenty '3-day' unauthorized additions = 60 days = 3 months of unplanned project scope creep.
explanations.b: Scope changes during execution are managed through change control — not permanently deferred. The change control process allows legitimate changes to be approved and incorporated while maintaining governance.
explanations.c: In Agile, the product owner can add items to the backlog — but items that affect committed sprint scope, release timeline, or budget require change control. 'Backlog addition' is only change-control-free if it doesn't affect existing commitments.
explanations.d: CHANGE CONTROL IN EXECUTION — WHY SIZE DOESN'T DETERMINE APPLICABILITY: SCOPE ADDITION IS A SCOPE ADDITION: any work not in the current scope baseline represents unauthorized scope if performed without approval; scope baseline integrity applies to ALL additions regardless of size; ESTIMATE UNCERTAINTY: a developer's '3-day' estimate is subject to the same uncertainties as any estimate: undiscovered complexity; integration issues; testing overhead; 'small' changes that consume a week are common; PRECEDENT CONCERN: one approved informal change creates precedent for all future 'small' changes; teams learn that small changes bypass governance → scope creep accumulates; INTEGRATED CHANGE CONTROL: ALL changes must go through the same process (simplified for small changes, more rigorous for large ones); the change control process for small changes takes hours, not weeks; APPROVAL AUTHORITY TIERING: small changes (under $5K, under 3 days, no scope milestone impact) → PM approves alone; medium changes → CCB review; large changes → sponsor approval. FOR AGILE: even in Agile, scope changes affecting the project charter's committed scope or budget should go through change control; a new backlog item within the existing release scope and budget may simply be added by the product owner — but changes that affect the release timeline or budget require formal review.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — OCM all 7 elements integrated; complete OCM lifecycle
questions.text: A project manager is implementing a new financial reporting system affecting 200 finance employees. Map the 7 OCM elements to specific activities for this project.

answers.text: OCM has only 3 elements: communication, training, and support
The 7 OCM elements apply only to large-scale organizational transformations — a 200-person system implementation is too small
OCM is the same as user training — train users and change management is complete

All 7 OCM elements mapped: (1) Assess organizational readiness: survey finance employees; measure current awareness, desire, change capacity; identify resistance hot spots; (2) Identify change champions: recruit respected finance analysts as system ambassadors; (3) Develop change management plan: ADKAR-based interventions targeting the readiness gaps; (4) Execute change management activities: communications campaign; training rollout; department head engagement; resistance management; (5) Evaluate change effectiveness: adoption surveys at 30/60/90 days post-go-live; proficiency metrics; (6) Transition to normalized operations: handover from project support to IT helpdesk when adoption is stable; (7) Follow-up: address remaining adoption gaps; reinforcement activities for 90% adoption target

explanations.a: Communication, training, and support are three activities within the broader OCM framework — they address the Knowledge and Ability components of ADKAR but miss Awareness, Desire, and Reinforcement. A 3-element OCM approach produces incomplete adoption.
explanations.b: All projects that affect how people work require OCM — regardless of scale. 200 finance employees implementing a new financial reporting system is a significant change for those individuals. OCM scale adjusts to the size of the change.
explanations.c: Training addresses KNOWLEDGE and begins building ABILITY — but without Awareness (do employees know why?), Desire (do they want to?), and Reinforcement (will the change stick?), training alone produces low adoption.
explanations.d: ALL 7 OCM ELEMENTS MAPPED TO FINANCIAL REPORTING SYSTEM: (1) ASSESS ORGANIZATIONAL READINESS: survey 200 finance employees on: awareness of the upcoming change; desire/openness to the new system; perception of current system limitations; interview finance managers about change capacity and concerns; assess organizational history (how did the last finance system change go?); OUTPUT: readiness score by department; priority areas for intervention. (2) IDENTIFY CHANGE CHAMPIONS: identify 5-7 respected senior financial analysts (one per department) who are early adopters; briefed on the system early; trained first; become peer advisors. (3) DEVELOP CHANGE MANAGEMENT PLAN: tailor interventions to readiness gaps; if awareness is low → communication campaign; if desire is low → manager engagement; if knowledge gap → role-specific training; set adoption targets (90% active users by Month 3 post-go-live). (4) EXECUTE CHANGE MANAGEMENT ACTIVITIES: communications: monthly newsletter; leadership messages; system preview sessions; training: role-based training for each finance role; resistance: one-on-one with resistant managers; champions: champion training and deployment; (5) EVALUATE CHANGE EFFECTIVENESS: 30-day post-go-live survey; system usage metrics (login frequency, transaction volumes); proficiency assessment; (6) TRANSITION TO NORMALIZED OPERATIONS: when adoption > 85% and helpdesk handles 90%+ of user issues; formal handover from project to IT; (7) FOLLOW-UP: address persistent adoption gaps; advanced training for power users; remove access to old system to prevent regression.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — tracking and reporting; comparing actual vs. baseline; earned value monitoring
questions.text: A project manager is conducting a monthly performance review at Month 4 of 12. She collects: Planned Value (PV) = $400,000; Earned Value (EV) = $380,000; Actual Cost (AC) = $410,000. Calculate the key performance metrics and interpret the project health.

answers.text: SV = +$20,000 (ahead of schedule); CV = +$30,000 (under budget) — the project is performing well

SV = EV − PV = $380,000 − $400,000 = −$20,000 (behind schedule); CV = EV − AC = $380,000 − $410,000 = −$30,000 (over budget); SPI = 0.95 (95% of planned work accomplished); CPI = 0.927 (getting $0.93 of value per $1 spent); the project is both behind schedule AND over budget — dual negative requiring investigation and corrective action
SV = PV − EV = $400,000 − $380,000 = $20,000 (positive); CV = AC − EV = $410,000 − $380,000 = $30,000 (positive) — both are favorable
Only the CPI matters — schedule variance is irrelevant for project performance

explanations.a: This answer uses inverted formulas. SV = EV − PV = $380K − $400K = −$20K (negative = behind schedule). CV = EV − AC = $380K − $410K = −$30K (negative = over budget). Both are unfavorable.
explanations.b: EARNED VALUE CALCULATIONS: SCHEDULE VARIANCE: SV = EV − PV = $380,000 − $400,000 = −$20,000; INTERPRETATION: SV negative → BEHIND SCHEDULE; the project accomplished $20,000 less planned work than planned by Month 4; SPI = EV / PV = $380,000 / $400,000 = 0.95; INTERPRETATION: SPI < 1.0 → BEHIND SCHEDULE; only 95% of planned work has been accomplished; COST VARIANCE: CV = EV − AC = $380,000 − $410,000 = −$30,000; INTERPRETATION: CV negative → OVER BUDGET; the project spent $30,000 more than the value of work accomplished; CPI = EV / AC = $380,000 / $410,000 = 0.927; INTERPRETATION: CPI < 1.0 → OVER BUDGET; getting $0.927 of value per $1.00 spent; COMBINED INTERPRETATION: the project is in the WORST QUADRANT: both behind schedule AND over budget; PM ACTIONS: immediate root cause investigation: why is EV less than PV? (activities not completing on schedule?); why is AC greater than EV? (spending more than estimated for accomplished work?); corrective action options depend on root causes; present to sponsor with recovery plan; EAC FORECAST: BAC / CPI = [BAC] / 0.927 → project will cost approximately 7.8% more than budget if current efficiency continues.
explanations.c: SV = EV − PV (EV first, then PV); CV = EV − AC (EV first, then AC). This answer inverts both formulas, producing incorrect signs and wrong interpretations.
explanations.d: Both SPI and CPI are essential for understanding project performance. Schedule variance indicates whether the project is on track to meet the deadline; cost variance indicates whether the project is within budget. Monitoring only CPI would miss schedule problems that often become cost problems later.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — vendor management; vendor governance structure; escalation management
questions.text: A project uses a major system integrator for a $2M implementation. Four months in, technical decisions are being made by junior vendor staff without PM visibility, the vendor's PM is frequently unavailable, and project status updates are inconsistent. What governance structures should the project manager establish or reinforce?

answers.text: Accept the governance gaps — large vendors know how to manage their own work
Replace the vendor immediately — governance failures require vendor termination
Monitor the situation for 2 more months before taking any action — governance issues resolve over time

Establish a formal governance framework: weekly joint status meetings (PM + vendor PM required attendance); formal decision log (all project decisions documented, reviewed by PM before implementation); escalation protocol (2-level escalation: PM → PM + vendor PM; then vendor account executive); clear RACI for vendor decisions (which decisions can vendor make autonomously, which require PM approval?); weekly written status report requirement; and escalate the PM availability issue directly to the vendor's account executive

explanations.a: 'Large vendors know how to manage their work' is a passive acceptance of significant governance risks: unauthorized technical decisions may create rework (vendor staff implementing their preferred approach, not the agreed approach); PM unavailability creates communication bottlenecks; inconsistent status updates leave the PM unable to accurately report project health. This is not acceptable governance on a $2M engagement.
explanations.b: Governance failures that are addressed proactively through structure establishment rarely require vendor termination. Termination is a last resort after documented escalation and failure to improve.
explanations.c: Governance gaps compound over time — unauthorized technical decisions accumulate into an unmanageable technical debt; 2 months of PM unavailability means 2 months of uncaptured decisions and unresolved issues. Waiting to take action allows governance failures to become project failures.
explanations.d: VENDOR GOVERNANCE FRAMEWORK ESTABLISHMENT: WEEKLY JOINT STATUS MEETINGS: venue for PM + vendor PM to review status, resolve issues, align on next steps; MANDATORY ATTENDANCE of vendor PM (not junior staff as substitutes); create accountability for the vendor PM's engagement; FORMAL DECISION LOG: record all decisions made on the project: date, description, who made the decision, whether PM-approved; junior staff making unauthorized decisions creates inconsistency; RACI DEFINES DECISION AUTHORITY: technical decisions within documented architecture → vendor autonomy; architectural changes → PM review and approval; scope interpretations → PM decision; design decisions affecting other systems → multi-party review; ESCALATION PROTOCOL: Level 1: PM + vendor PM jointly resolve; Level 2: PM + vendor account executive + sponsor; 48-hour response requirement for Level 1; WRITTEN STATUS REQUIREMENTS: weekly written status report format defined in SOW; failure to deliver on time triggers escalation; VENDOR PM AVAILABILITY ISSUE: escalate directly to the vendor's account executive: 'The project is experiencing governance issues due to vendor PM availability. I need this resolved within the week. If the current PM is reassigned without adequate coverage, we will need to escalate this to our executive sponsor.'

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — OCM: execute change management activities; communication campaign
questions.text: A change manager is executing communications for a new cloud HR system rollout. The communications plan includes emails, town halls, and an intranet page. Three months before go-live, adoption of communications is low (30% email open rate, poor town hall attendance). What should the change manager do?

answers.text: Continue with the planned communications — low engagement is expected and will improve closer to go-live
Cancel the town halls — if employees aren't attending, they're not useful
Increase email frequency to 3× per week — more emails improve engagement

Diagnose why engagement is low and adapt communications: survey or interview a sample of employees to understand the communication channel preferences and barriers; adapt channels (short videos instead of long emails?; manager cascade instead of company-wide town halls?; team meetings where the manager delivers the message?); increase message relevance (are employees unclear on what the change means for THEM specifically — role-specific messaging?); engage managers as communication amplifiers (managers delivering messages in team meetings gets higher engagement than company-wide emails); and re-assess whether the right channels are being used

explanations.a: Assuming engagement will improve closer to go-live without investigating the root cause is risky: if employees are not engaged with communications 3 months before go-live, awareness and desire will be low at go-live, producing adoption failure.
explanations.b: Town halls may be the wrong format (too large, too formal, too one-directional) — but canceling without replacing them with a more effective alternative leaves a communication gap.
explanations.c: Increasing email frequency with the same format that already has 30% open rate will produce: email fatigue; potentially lower open rates; employee resentment about information overload. More of an ineffective channel doesn't improve communication effectiveness.
explanations.d: LOW COMMUNICATION ENGAGEMENT DIAGNOSIS AND ADAPTATION: DIAGNOSE ROOT CAUSE: short survey or 5-10 employee interviews: 'Did you receive the HR system communications? Did you read/attend them? What would make communications more useful or accessible?'; POSSIBLE ROOT CAUSES AND ADAPTATIONS: CHANNEL MISMATCH: employees prefer short videos to long emails → produce 2-minute video updates instead of 3-paragraph emails; employees don't attend company-wide town halls → replace with 15-minute team meeting presentations where direct managers deliver the message; MESSAGE RELEVANCE: 'What does this mean for me?' is the most powerful communication motivator; generic company-wide messages have low relevance for any individual; create role-specific messaging ('What changes for a payroll processor'; 'What changes for an HR business partner'); MANAGER CASCADE: messages delivered by direct managers in team meetings have significantly higher engagement than company-wide emails: employees trust their direct manager more than company announcements; managers can answer specific questions; team meetings create conversation, not one-way broadcasting; TIMING: communications 3 months before go-live may feel abstract and distant to employees → increase practical 'what will you need to do' messaging as go-live approaches; MEASURE IMPROVEMENT: track open rates, meeting attendance, and survey scores after adapting channels.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — all execution elements integrated; managing complexity in execution
questions.text: A project is in Month 6 of 12 execution. The PM's weekly review reveals: SPI = 0.88 (behind schedule), CPI = 1.05 (under budget); a key vendor is 3 weeks late on a critical deliverable; the OCM change manager reports only 35% employee awareness (target was 60% at this stage); and one developer is performing below expectations (delivering features with frequent defects). What is the MOST IMPORTANT finding and in what order should these issues be addressed?

answers.text: All four issues are equally important — address them simultaneously
Developer performance is the most important — individual performance issues are the root cause of all other problems
CPI = 1.05 (under budget) means the project is performing well — no action needed on any dimension

Priority order: (1) Vendor 3-week delay (if on critical path, this directly extends the project end date — most urgent, most irreversible); (2) Schedule variance SPI=0.88 (behind schedule and the vendor delay compounds this — needs recovery plan); (3) OCM awareness gap (35% vs. 60% target — if uncorrected, adoption will fail at go-live, which is increasingly close); (4) Developer performance (ongoing management issue — important but doesn't have the same urgency as the critical path vendor delay)

explanations.a: The four issues have different urgency and different impact levels. Treating them as equal would misallocate the PM's management attention — the vendor critical path delay needs immediate action today, not next week.
explanations.b: The developer's performance is a concern — but a single developer's defects can be managed through code review and testing. The vendor critical path delay has system-level impact that cannot be managed through individual coaching.
explanations.c: CPI=1.05 is one positive indicator in a report with three concerning signals. A single positive metric in the context of schedule delays, vendor non-performance, and OCM gaps does not mean 'no action needed.'
explanations.d: PRIORITY ANALYSIS: (1) VENDOR 3-WEEK DELAY (CRITICAL PATH — MOST URGENT): if the vendor's deliverable is on the critical path, 3 weeks late = project 3 weeks late; every week of inaction compounds the delay; IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: contact vendor PM today — get a firm revised delivery date; escalate to vendor account executive if PM is evasive; invoke contract provisions for late delivery; assess impact on the critical path — can any subsequent activities begin earlier with partial deliverable?; brief sponsor on the delay and recovery options. (2) SCHEDULE VARIANCE SPI=0.88 (HIGH PRIORITY): with the vendor delay compounding a pre-existing SPI=0.88, the schedule risk is significant; ACTIONS: identify which activities are behind and why (separate from vendor delay?); develop a recovery plan (fast-tracking, crashing, scope deferral); present to sponsor with timeline implications. (3) OCM AWARENESS GAP (HIGH PRIORITY with time-sensitive trend): 35% vs. 60% target at Month 6 means go-live (Month 12) is 6 months away; at current trajectory, awareness may not reach the target before go-live; ACTIONS: root cause investigation (wrong channels? messages not resonating?); adapt communication plan and increase manager cascade messaging; this must be addressed before it becomes a go-live adoption crisis. (4) DEVELOPER PERFORMANCE (IMPORTANT, NOT URGENT TODAY): defect-producing developer affects quality but not schedule (if testing catches defects); ACTIONS: provide specific feedback; pair with senior developer for code review; if performance doesn't improve after 2-4 weeks, escalate to HR. INSIGHT: CPI=1.05 is FAVORABLE — the project is under budget despite schedule challenges; this budget surplus may enable crashing (adding resources to recover schedule).

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — tracking and reporting; RAG status; executive dashboard reporting
questions.text: A project manager needs to determine the correct RAG (Red/Amber/Green) status for the project schedule. The project is 2 days behind on a non-critical activity with 10 days of float; 1 week behind on a near-critical path activity with 5 days of float; and the critical path itself is on schedule. What RAG status should be reported for schedule and why?

answers.text: Green — the critical path is on schedule so the overall schedule is Green
Red — any delay in any activity makes the schedule Red

Amber/Yellow — the critical path is currently on schedule (no Red signal) but the near-critical path activity is 1 week behind with only 5 days of float; 5 days of remaining float against a 7-day delay means this activity has effectively become critical; if it experiences any further delay, it will affect the project end date; this warrants Amber status with a note about the near-critical path risk
Green — float absorbs all delays; any delay covered by float is automatically Green

explanations.a: A purely critical-path-focused RAG would miss near-critical path risks. An activity that is 7 days behind with 5 days of float has EXCEEDED its float — it is now effectively on the critical path. Reporting Green while a critical-path-threatening delay exists misrepresents project health.
explanations.b: A 2-day delay on an activity with 10 days of float poses no schedule risk (8 days of float remaining). Reporting Red for this situation would be an overreaction that creates alarm where none is warranted.
explanations.c: RAG STATUS DETERMINATION — SCHEDULE: ACTIVITY 1 (2 days behind, 10 days float): remaining float = 10 − 2 = 8 days; still has significant buffer; no schedule risk; GREEN for this activity. ACTIVITY 2 (7 days behind, 5 days float): remaining float = 5 − 7 = −2 days; the delay HAS EXCEEDED the available float; this activity is NOW effectively on the critical path (has no remaining buffer); any further delay WILL extend the project end date; this is an AMBER indicator. CRITICAL PATH: currently on schedule; GREEN for the critical path. OVERALL SCHEDULE RAG: AMBER — because while the formal critical path is on schedule, a near-critical activity has exceeded its float and is functionally impacting the critical path; AMBER DEFINITION: 'The schedule is at risk but the end date is not yet threatened. A near-critical path activity has exceeded its float — if not corrected this week, it will extend the project end date.'; ESCALATION: the PM should have a corrective action plan ready when reporting Amber; executives receiving Amber expect a mitigation plan; STATUS REPORT NARRATIVE: 'Schedule Amber: Critical path on schedule. Activity [X] on the near-critical path is 7 days behind with 5 days of float consumed. Mitigation: [specific actions to recover the 2-day overrun in Activity X].'
explanations.d: Float is a resource that can be consumed. When a delay exceeds available float, the delay becomes critical. 'Float absorbs all delays' is only true when the delay is LESS THAN the available float — here it exceeds float by 2 days.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — phase gate review; go/no-go decision; milestone-triggered evaluation
questions.text: A project is completing Phase 1 (requirements and design) before proceeding to Phase 2 (development). The project manager prepares for the Phase 1 gate review. What should the gate review assess and what are the possible outcomes?

answers.text: The gate review only checks whether the schedule was met — if Phase 1 completed on time, proceed to Phase 2

The gate review assesses: all Phase 1 deliverables completed and approved (requirements document, architecture design, data model); quality metrics met (acceptance criteria); risk status (are Phase 2 risks manageable with the current plan?); team readiness for Phase 2; stakeholder alignment on the Phase 2 approach; and produces a decision: Go (proceed to Phase 2), No-Go (Phase 1 deliverables incomplete — cannot proceed), or Conditional Go (proceed with specific conditions that must be met within a defined timeframe)
Phase gate reviews are only for government projects — commercial projects don't use phase gates
The gate review is performed by the development team alone — they know whether the design is ready

explanations.a: Schedule compliance is one element of a phase gate review — but it is insufficient alone. A phase that completed on time but produced poor-quality deliverables should result in a No-Go. Quality and completeness matter more than timing.
explanations.b: PHASE GATE REVIEW CONTENT AND OUTCOMES: DELIVERABLE COMPLETENESS: is everything that was planned for Phase 1 complete? Requirements document (all functional and non-functional requirements documented); Architecture design (all components, integrations, and technology choices defined); Data model (entity-relationship diagram, data dictionary); Any other Phase 1 WBS deliverables; QUALITY STANDARDS MET: did each deliverable meet its acceptance criteria?; Were defects/gaps corrected?; RISK STATUS REVIEW: are there new Phase 2 risks identified during Phase 1 work that require plan updates?; Are Phase 2 contingency plans adequate given what was learned in Phase 1?; PHASE 2 READINESS: is the team ready for Phase 2? Are required developers, architects, and infrastructure in place?; STAKEHOLDER ALIGNMENT: do business and IT stakeholders agree the requirements are complete and the design is sound?; GATE DECISION OPTIONS: GO: all criteria met → Phase 2 authorized; NO-GO: criteria not met → Phase 1 must be extended to address deficiencies; examples: key requirements still missing; design has unresolved integration conflicts; CONDITIONAL GO: proceed to Phase 2 with specific conditions: 'Three outstanding requirements must be resolved by [date] before the first development sprint begins'; 'Security review approval must be obtained within 2 weeks'; GATE REVIEW AUTHORITY: the sponsor or steering committee chairs the gate review; the PM presents the evidence; the sponsor makes the go/no-go decision.
explanations.c: Phase gate reviews are a best practice for all project types: government, commercial, IT, construction, pharmaceutical. The formality varies, but the concept (evaluate before proceeding to the next phase) applies universally.
explanations.d: The gate review must include stakeholders, the sponsor, and business representatives — not just the development team. Business alignment and quality review require broader participation than the technical team alone.
