questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — quality management in execution; defect management; quality audits
questions.text: During execution, the QA team observes that code reviews are consistently being skipped ('no time — sprint deadline is tomorrow'). Defect density has risen to 5 defects per 1,000 LOC (target is <2). Testing cycles are consuming an increasing percentage of the sprint. How should the project manager address this quality management breakdown?

answers.text: Accept the quality degradation — sprint deadlines must be met at any cost
Remove all code reviews from the process — if they're being skipped anyway, remove them formally

Intervene on the process: require mandatory code reviews (update Definition of Done to require peer review before any PR is merged — this makes skipping a violation of DoD, not just a preference); address the root cause of 'no time' (are sprint commitments too large? are reviews taking too long?); if sprints are over-committed, reduce sprint capacity by 20% to accommodate quality activities; provide data to the team: the 5x defect increase and growing testing overhead IS the cost of skipping reviews — making this visible may change behavior
Hire more QA engineers to test more — quality is QA's responsibility, not developers'

explanations.a: Sprint deadlines met with 5 defects/1,000 LOC (2.5× target) is a false success: each defect discovered later in testing costs 5-10× more to fix than if caught in code review; defects escaping to UAT or production cost 100× more; the 'on-time sprint' is achieving volume at the expense of quality — and testing cycles are growing as a direct consequence; this trajectory leads to a testing crisis before go-live.
explanations.b: Formally removing code reviews because they're being skipped normalizes a process failure. Code reviews exist because: they catch defects before testing; they maintain code quality standards; they spread knowledge across the team; they prevent security vulnerabilities. Removing them to reflect current behavior makes the quality problem permanent.
explanations.c: QUALITY MANAGEMENT INTERVENTION: MANDATORY CODE REVIEW in DEFINITION OF DONE: update the DoD to require: peer code review completed; reviewer approval recorded in the version control system; no PR merges without review; this makes skipping a DoD violation — incomplete without review → story not Done → cannot be counted as sprint velocity; SPRINT CAPACITY ADJUSTMENT: if the team says 'no time,' investigate whether: sprint commitments are too large (overcommitting leads to quality shortcuts); review process itself is inefficient (the average review takes 3 hours — could be 45 minutes with better tooling?); if sprints are genuinely over-committed: reduce sprint commitment by 15-20% to create capacity for quality activities; the reduced velocity with proper quality produces more net value than higher velocity with defect debt; DATA TRANSPARENCY: show the team the data: 'When we skip code reviews, our defect density increases 2.5× (2 → 5/1,000 LOC). Each defect found in testing costs 3× what review would have caught. Your growing testing cycle IS the cost of skipping reviews — we're spending more time in testing than we're saving by skipping reviews.'; PM MONITORING: track defect density weekly; set 30-day target to return to <3/1,000 LOC; code review compliance rate tracked in sprint reports.
explanations.d: Hiring more QA engineers to test more defects addresses the symptom (more testers can find more defects) not the cause (defects being introduced because of skipped code reviews). QA's role is to validate quality, not to compensate for quality not being built in.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — vendor management; change order management; scope creep prevention
questions.text: During execution, the vendor submits 5 change orders in 2 months for 'additional scope not included in the original SOW.' The PM believes some are legitimate (genuinely new requirements) but others appear to be re-characterizing work that WAS in the original SOW. How should the PM manage this vendor change order situation?

answers.text: Approve all 5 change orders — vendor relationships are damaged by rejecting change requests
Reject all 5 change orders — vendors frequently over-claim scope additions

Evaluate each change order individually against the original SOW: compare each CO against the SOW's explicit scope statements; for claimed additions that appear to be in the SOW, document the specific SOW section and formally dispute the change order in writing; for genuinely new requirements, evaluate cost and schedule impact, assess whether the work is needed, and process through the project's change control process; escalate to legal/procurement if vendor disputes the SOW interpretation
Escalate immediately to the sponsor — vendor change orders are above the PM's authority

explanations.a: Approving all change orders without evaluation exposes the project to: significant cost overruns (potentially $100Ks of additional spend); scope creep funded by the change order budget; setting a precedent that all change orders are approved → vendor submits more; the PM's fiduciary responsibility requires evaluation of each change order against the contract.
explanations.b: Blanket rejection without evaluation ignores legitimate scope additions. New requirements discovered during execution are real and must be addressed — either within existing scope (if the SOW covers them) or through approved change orders (if they are genuinely new).
explanations.c: CHANGE ORDER EVALUATION PROCESS: FOR EACH OF THE 5 CHANGE ORDERS: STEP 1 — MAP TO SOW: read the SOW carefully; can the claimed work be traced to an existing SOW statement?; example: 'CO-3 claims the integration testing of the billing module is out of scope. SOW Section 4.2 explicitly states 'Integration testing for all implemented modules.' CO-3 is not a valid change order.'; STEP 2 — DOCUMENTED DISPUTE OR APPROVAL: IF IN SOW: document the specific SOW reference; provide formal written notification to the vendor: 'Change Order 3 is not approved. The requested work is covered by SOW Section 4.2. Please review and confirm.'; IF GENUINELY NEW: assess: Is this work actually needed for project success?; What is the cost and schedule impact?; Process through internal change control (PM authority if within threshold; CCB/sponsor if above); Negotiate the change order price (vendor's first number is rarely the final number); ESCALATION TRIGGERS: if the vendor disputes the SOW interpretation on 3+ items → involve procurement/legal to clarify contract interpretation; if the vendor continues submitting questionable change orders after dispute → address the pattern in the quarterly performance review; DOCUMENTATION: maintain a change order log with: CO number, description, SOW reference (if disputed), resolution, date; PATTERN RECOGNITION: 5 change orders in 2 months is a pattern; investigate whether: the SOW had gaps that the vendor is legitimately filling; the vendor is opportunistically expanding scope; the project's requirements are genuinely evolving (in which case the internal change control process needs strengthening).
explanations.d: Individual change order evaluation is within the PM's authority and responsibility. The sponsor should be informed of the pattern (5 COs in 2 months) but the PM leads the evaluation. Only escalate when: COs exceed the PM's financial authority; vendor disputes cannot be resolved at PM level.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — all execution elements: task management, vendor, OCM, tracking integrated
questions.text: A project is at Month 8 of a 12-month ERP implementation. Status review reveals: SPI = 0.91, CPI = 0.96; integration testing is 3 weeks behind (the vendor is partly responsible); OCM awareness is at 70% (target 80%); 150 of 500 end users have completed training; the vendor submitted 3 change orders this week; and the operations transition plan is still in draft. Identify the top three priorities and the PM's immediate actions for each.

answers.text: Focus only on OCM — adoption failure is the most visible post-go-live consequence
All issues require equal attention — allocate equal time to all six issues

Top 3 priorities: (1) Integration testing delay (3 weeks behind, on critical path to UAT → directly threatens go-live in 4 months — immediate vendor meeting to diagnose root cause, recovery plan, formal notice if vendor-caused); (2) Transition plan in draft (4 months to go-live; operations preparation takes months — must be finalized and execution begun immediately); (3) Vendor change orders (3 COs in 1 week suggests either scope drift or SOW gaps — evaluate each against SOW before any approvals); Lower priority (still important): OCM awareness at 70% (10% below target — address this month but not today); training 150/500 (4 months remaining is sufficient for the remaining 350 — schedule more sessions); SPI/CPI near 1.0 (concerning but not critical at these levels)
No action needed — an SPI of 0.91 is close enough to 1.0 to indicate healthy project performance

explanations.a: OCM is important — but integration testing being 3 weeks behind with 4 months to go-live is a more urgent operational issue. OCM has more time to be addressed; integration testing delay compounds directly into UAT, then go-live.
explanations.b: Equal attention allocation ignores the different urgency levels. The integration testing delay needs attention TODAY (every day of delay costs another day of schedule). The transition plan draft needs attention this week. SPI=0.91 warrants monitoring but not emergency action today.
explanations.c: PRIORITIZED EXECUTION MANAGEMENT: PRIORITY 1 — INTEGRATION TESTING 3 WEEKS BEHIND (CRITICAL PATH IMPACT): with 4 months to go-live, UAT and final deployment still ahead, a 3-week integration delay is serious; if UAT is planned for Month 10 (in 2 months), and testing is 3 weeks late, UAT is at risk of being compressed; IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: joint meeting with vendor today/tomorrow: root cause analysis (what specifically is blocking testing?); if vendor-caused: formal written notice per contract; agree on a recovery plan with specific dates; escalate to vendor account executive if PM is unresponsive; consider options: fast-track remaining integration testing (parallel testing tracks); bring in additional testing resources; PRIORITY 2 — TRANSITION PLAN IN DRAFT WITH 4 MONTHS TO GO-LIVE: knowledge transfer takes months; operations training takes weeks; runbook development takes weeks; if the plan isn't finalized today, execution of the transition plan won't begin until Month 10 or later — leaving only 2 months for activities that need 3-4 months; IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: schedule transition plan finalization workshop this week; operations team must be engaged immediately; submit plan for sponsor approval; begin operations team briefings as soon as possible; PRIORITY 3 — VENDOR CHANGE ORDERS (3 IN 1 WEEK): 3 change orders in one week is unusual and suggests scope drift; IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: review each CO against the SOW before any approval; dispute any COs that appear to be within original scope; if genuinely new requirements, escalate immediately to scope change management; notify sponsor of the pattern. LOWER PRIORITIES (address this month): OCM at 70% vs. 80% target → add manager cascade communications this month; training 150/500 → schedule additional training sessions; SPI=0.91, CPI=0.96 → monitor, prepare corrective options if trends worsen.
explanations.d: SPI=0.91 combined with integration testing 3 weeks behind with 4 months to go-live is a project that needs active management. Calling this 'healthy' ignores compounding risk factors.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — transition to closing; go-live readiness; execution phase completion criteria
questions.text: A project has completed development, integration testing, and UAT. The PM is preparing for go-live and then project closure. What criteria should confirm the project is ready to transition from execution to go-live (and subsequently to closing)?

answers.text: The project is ready for go-live when the PM feels confident — intuition is the best go-live indicator

Go-live readiness criteria: all UAT scenarios passed with zero P1 and fewer than 3 P2 open defects; performance testing validates SLA compliance (response time, concurrency); security review completed and approved; operations team trained and ready (runbook complete); user training completion >90% of target users; data migration validated (reconciliation complete); rollback plan tested and documented; infrastructure provisioned and validated; stakeholder sign-off obtained from sponsor and key business owners; cutover plan finalized and communicated
Go-live readiness is confirmed when all 500 features are deployed — partial feature sets are never acceptable
Go-live readiness is confirmed when the project team declares they're done — no external criteria are needed

explanations.a: Go-live decisions based on PM intuition (without objective criteria) produce: subjective debates between project team ('we're ready') and business ('we're not ready'); go-live events with significant post-launch issues because no standardized readiness bar was set; inconsistent decisions across different project managers.
explanations.b: GO-LIVE READINESS CRITERIA (objective, pre-agreed checklist): UAT COMPLETION: all UAT scenarios executed with documented results; specific quality thresholds met (zero P1 defects, fewer than X P2 defects with remediation plan for each); UAT formally signed off by the product owner or business representative; PERFORMANCE VALIDATION: system meets SLA response time and concurrency requirements under load testing; critical business transactions tested at peak volume; SECURITY: security review completed; all HIGH vulnerabilities remediated; penetration testing passed (if required); OPERATIONS READINESS: IT operations team trained; runbooks complete and validated (dry run performed); monitoring and alerting configured; helpdesk briefed and ready; USER TRAINING: minimum 90% of target users trained; training assessment scores above threshold; support resources available (job aids, FAQ, help desk); DATA MIGRATION: data migration from legacy system complete; reconciliation confirms data integrity (counts match, key fields accurate); fallback data available if rollback is needed; ROLLBACK PLAN: rollback procedure documented and tested; rollback decision criteria defined (if X happens in the first 4 hours, we roll back); INFRASTRUCTURE: production environment provisioned; load balancing configured; DR environment ready; backup verified; STAKEHOLDER SIGN-OFF: sponsor and key business owners formally confirm readiness through a pre-defined go/no-go review process; CUTOVER PLAN: step-by-step cutover procedures communicated to all parties; timing and responsibilities clear; AFTER GO-LIVE: project enters a warranty period before formal closing.
explanations.c: Go-live with an MVP or phased feature set is common and appropriate — waiting for all 500 features before going live defeats the MVP principle and extends time-to-value unnecessarily.
explanations.d: Project team self-declaration of readiness is insufficient governance. External validation (business sign-off, security approval, operations readiness confirmation) is required for responsible go-live authorization.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — conflict resolution: 5 modes overview
questions.text: Project managers encounter conflict regularly during execution. Which of the following correctly lists the five conflict resolution modes?

answers.text: Confronting/Problem-Solving, Compromising, Smoothing/Accommodating, Forcing, and Avoiding/Withdrawing — the five modes used in project management
Avoiding, Competing, Collaborating, Accommodating, Compromising — from the Thomas-Kilmann model
Escalating, Negotiating, Mediating, Arbitrating, and Litigating — formal dispute resolution methods
Ignoring, Discussing, Delegating, Deciding, and Implementing — the conflict management lifecycle

explanations.a: THE FIVE PROJECT MANAGEMENT CONFLICT RESOLUTION MODES: (1) CONFRONTING / PROBLEM-SOLVING: both parties work together to find a solution that fully satisfies everyone; win-win; takes time and requires mutual trust; best for: important issues where both parties' interests genuinely matter; (2) COMPROMISING: each party gives up something to reach middle ground; partial win for both; best for: moderately important issues; when full resolution is not feasible; (3) SMOOTHING / ACCOMMODATING: emphasize areas of agreement; downplay differences; one party gives way to the other; short-term peace but issue may resurface; best for: preserving relationships; when the issue is minor; (4) FORCING: one party imposes their position on the other; win-lose; damages relationships; best for: emergencies requiring immediate decision; non-negotiable standards (safety, legal requirements); (5) AVOIDING / WITHDRAWING: postpone or withdraw from the conflict; neither resolves nor wins; best for: when the issue is trivial; buying time to gather information or cool down.
explanations.b: The Thomas-Kilmann model (Avoiding, Competing, Collaborating, Accommodating, Compromising) is a closely related model. The Project+ exam uses a specific set of five modes that overlap significantly but uses different terminology — specifically: Confronting/Problem-Solving (= Collaborating), Forcing (= Competing), Smoothing/Accommodating (= Accommodating). Both models cover the same conceptual space.
explanations.c: These are formal legal/dispute mechanisms — not the standard project management conflict resolution modes. They represent external escalation options far beyond normal PM conflict handling.
explanations.d: This describes a generic decision process, not conflict resolution modes.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — conflict resolution: confronting/problem-solving mode; win-win
questions.text: A project manager uses the CONFRONTING/PROBLEM-SOLVING conflict resolution mode. What characterizes this approach?

answers.text: Both parties openly address the disagreement together, treating it as a problem to be solved collaboratively — aiming for a solution that genuinely satisfies both parties' underlying needs; this is the PREFERRED approach for most project conflicts because it produces durable resolutions and preserves relationships
The conflict is avoided until it naturally resolves — confronting means waiting for the right moment
The PM uses their authority to impose a decision — problem-solving means making a unilateral decision
One party agrees to the other's position to restore harmony — confronting means politely disagreeing once then accepting

explanations.a: CONFRONTING / PROBLEM-SOLVING: ALSO CALLED: Collaborating (Thomas-Kilmann); CORE APPROACH: treat the conflict as a PROBLEM to be SOLVED together; both parties openly discuss their underlying interests (not just their positions); seek a solution that meets both parties' genuine needs; CHARACTERISTICS: requires mutual trust and willingness to engage honestly; most time-intensive mode; produces the most durable resolution (both parties feel heard and satisfied); WHEN TO USE: important, ongoing relationships where relationship quality matters; when both parties' interests are legitimate and important; when a creative solution may exist that serves both needs; when understanding the other party's perspective is valuable; EXAMPLE: a developer and business analyst disagree on requirements scope; confronting mode → joint session to understand each other's actual concerns ('you want simple implementation, I want complete functionality') → find a phased approach that delivers core functionality simply in Phase 1, with complexity additions in Phase 2; BEST FOR LONG-TERM RESOLUTION: of the five modes, confronting/problem-solving produces the most durable outcomes because both parties own the solution.
explanations.b: Waiting for conflict to naturally resolve is the AVOIDING/WITHDRAWING mode. Confronting means directly addressing the conflict — the opposite of waiting.
explanations.c: Unilateral decision-making using authority is the FORCING mode, not confronting/problem-solving. Confronting/problem-solving requires collaborative engagement from both parties.
explanations.d: Agreeing to the other's position to restore harmony is the SMOOTHING/ACCOMMODATING mode, not confronting/problem-solving.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — conflict resolution: avoiding/withdrawing; when to use; limitations
questions.text: When is AVOIDING/WITHDRAWING an APPROPRIATE conflict resolution mode for a project manager?

answers.text: When the conflict is trivial and not worth the time to resolve; when both parties need time to cool down before a productive conversation is possible; or when gathering more information before engaging is prudent — the issue will be addressed later, just not right now
When a team member and the PM have a serious disagreement about go-live timing — this is a situation to avoid
When the conflict involves an important project decision that must be resolved before work can proceed
Avoiding is always the best approach — it prevents all conflict from escalating

explanations.a: AVOIDING / WITHDRAWING — APPROPRIATE USES: TRIVIAL ISSUES: not every conflict deserves energy expenditure; if the disagreement is about something that won't meaningfully affect project outcomes, avoiding is efficient — the time and relationship capital spent resolving a trivial issue exceeds the benefit; COOLING-DOWN PERIOD: when emotions are running high, immediate confrontation often produces poor outcomes; withdrawing temporarily to allow both parties to regain composure before a constructive conversation is strategic, not cowardly; the conflict is re-engaged after the cooling-down period; INFORMATION GATHERING: when more information is needed before a productive conversation is possible ('I need to review the contract before we can meaningfully discuss this scope issue'); LIMITATIONS: avoiding is NOT appropriate when: the issue must be resolved for work to proceed; the conflict will escalate if not addressed; important relationships are at stake; the issue is recurring and avoidance has failed previously; KEY INSIGHT: avoiding is a TEMPORARY tactic — it postpones, not permanently resolves. It is appropriate when the timing is wrong, not when the issue is wrong.
explanations.b: A serious disagreement about go-live timing directly affects the project's critical path — this requires resolution, not avoidance. Go-live timing conflicts are high-stakes decisions that cannot be postponed indefinitely.
explanations.c: If the conflict involves an important decision that must be resolved before work proceeds, avoiding is inappropriate — the work is blocked until the conflict is resolved. Avoiding creates a dependency delay.
explanations.d: Avoiding all conflict would mean: unresolved scope disagreements; unaddressed resource conflicts; unresolved technical debates — all of which compound into project failures. Avoiding some conflicts strategically is appropriate; avoiding all conflicts is negligent.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — conflict resolution: forcing; when appropriate; relationship cost
questions.text: A project manager uses the FORCING conflict resolution mode. In which situation is this MOST appropriate?

answers.text: When a new safety regulation requires immediate implementation regardless of the team's preference — the matter is non-negotiable and time-critical
When two team members disagree about the best technical architecture — forcing produces the best technical decisions
Forcing is never appropriate — it always damages relationships beyond repair
When the PM wants to demonstrate authority to the team — power demonstration is the best use of forcing

explanations.a: FORCING — APPROPRIATE USE: when a decision is NON-NEGOTIABLE (regulatory requirement, safety standard, legal obligation) and URGENT; the PM has legitimate authority and the stakes require immediate action without extended deliberation. EXAMPLE: a new data privacy regulation takes effect next week; the team debates whether to comply; the PM must force compliance immediately — 'This is not a discussion. The regulation is mandatory. Here is what we are implementing.'; CHARACTERISTICS: win-lose outcome (PM wins; the other party loses); fastest resolution; does not require buy-in from the other party; RELATIONSHIP COST: the losing party may feel overruled and become less engaged; if overused, forcing erodes team trust and psychological safety; WHEN APPROPRIATE: emergencies requiring immediate decisions (system outage during project); non-negotiable standards (safety, legal, regulatory compliance); when the PM has unambiguous legitimate authority; WHEN INAPPROPRIATE: technical decisions where team expertise exceeds the PM's; decisions where team buy-in is required for successful execution; interpersonal conflicts (forcing will escalate, not resolve).
explanations.b: Technical architecture decisions benefit from collaborative input from the team (confronting/problem-solving produces better technical decisions through discussion). Forcing a technical decision without understanding the team's reasoning bypasses potentially superior technical insights.
explanations.c: Forcing is appropriate in specific, limited circumstances — primarily emergency and non-negotiable situations. 'Never appropriate' is incorrect.
explanations.d: Using forcing to demonstrate authority (without substantive justification) is a misuse of the mode that will damage team morale and trust. Forcing is a tool for specific situations, not a leadership style.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — conflict resolution: compromising; partial satisfaction; appropriate contexts
questions.text: Two developers on the project team disagree about sprint velocity commitment. Developer A wants to commit 40 points (ambitious but risks incomplete delivery). Developer B wants 28 points (conservative but not maximizing capacity). The sprint planning deadline is in 2 hours. Using COMPROMISING, how does the PM facilitate resolution and what is the trade-off?

answers.text: Compromising mode: facilitate agreement on a middle-ground commitment (approximately 34 points, between 28 and 40); acknowledge that neither party fully gets what they want; the trade-off is that compromising may not be the OPTIMAL solution (perhaps 38 points is genuinely achievable, or perhaps 30 is truly the sustainable rate); it resolves the immediate conflict quickly when time is limited, but may miss the optimal answer that deeper analysis would find
Side with Developer B — conservative commitments prevent incomplete delivery
Side with Developer A — higher velocity is always better
Compromising mode means splitting the difference mathematically: (40+28)/2 = 34 points exactly — always use the precise midpoint

explanations.a: COMPROMISING in velocity commitment conflict: PROCESS: PM facilitates a structured discussion; both parties articulate their reasoning; Developer A: 'We have 5 stories ready and the team had 38-point velocity last sprint'; Developer B: 'Two team members are on partial sprint due to other commitments — effective capacity is 75%'; COMPROMISE OUTCOME: 34 points (between 28 and 40); both parties concede something: Developer A (willing to commit 40) accepts 34; Developer B (wants only 28) accepts 34; CHARACTERISTICS: both parties are partially satisfied; resolution is faster than confronting/problem-solving; TRADE-OFFS OF COMPROMISING: ADVANTAGE: efficient resolution when time is constrained (2-hour deadline); DISADVANTAGE: may not find the OPTIMAL answer — if the team actually has capacity for 37 points based on a careful analysis, 34 is unnecessarily conservative; the 'split the difference' approach doesn't necessarily reflect what the data shows; WHEN COMPROMISING IS APPROPRIATE: time pressure (sprint planning deadline approaching); both parties have legitimate concerns; a middle ground exists that is acceptable to both; perfect resolution is not critical (the velocity can be adjusted next sprint based on actual performance); PRECISION NOTE: compromising doesn't always mean the exact mathematical midpoint — it means a negotiated middle ground both can accept.
explanations.b: Siding with Developer B is also FORCING. Accommodating would be Developer A giving in to Developer B's preference.
explanations.c: Siding with Developer A is the FORCING mode (one party wins, one loses). Compromising requires both parties to give up something.
explanations.d: Compromising doesn't require mechanical midpoint calculation — it requires a negotiated middle ground. Sometimes the midpoint is appropriate; other times the acceptable middle is closer to one party's position based on evidence and context.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — conflict resolution: smoothing/accommodating; relationship preservation; limitations
questions.text: The project manager uses SMOOTHING/ACCOMMODATING when a key stakeholder pushes for a feature addition outside the scope. The PM agrees to include it to avoid conflict. Three weeks later, the same stakeholder pushes for another addition. What does this pattern reveal about the PM's use of smoothing and what is the appropriate response?

answers.text: The pattern is positive — a PM who always accommodates stakeholders is relationship-focused
Smoothing resolved both conflicts — accommodation is the right approach for stakeholder requests

Repeated accommodation has established a precedent that scope requests will be granted without change control; the stakeholder learned that pushing produces results; the PM should have used confronting/problem-solving the first time to understand the stakeholder's need and explain the change control process; now the PM must reinforce scope management: acknowledge the stakeholder's interest, explain the change control process, and apply it consistently going forward — accommodating repeatedly undermines project governance
The pattern is a vendor management issue — scope requests are not stakeholder concerns

explanations.a: A PM who always accommodates stakeholders is producing scope creep, not relationship success. Accommodation that bypasses change control eventually produces: budget overruns; schedule delays; team burnout from unauthorized additions; stakeholder disappointment when the project delivers 'everything requested' but months late and over budget.
explanations.b: Accommodation the first time 'resolved' the immediate conflict but created a new problem: a precedent that scope additions are easy to obtain. The second request is a direct consequence of the first accommodation.
explanations.c: REPEATED SMOOTHING — SCOPE CREEP ENABLEMENT: WHAT HAPPENED: First conflict (Week 1): stakeholder requests out-of-scope feature; PM accommodates → feature added without change control; STAKEHOLDER LEARNING: 'Direct requests to the PM produce results'; Second conflict (Week 4): stakeholder makes another request, confident the pattern will repeat; WHAT SHOULD HAVE HAPPENED (First conflict): use CONFRONTING/PROBLEM-SOLVING: 'I understand you see value in this feature. Let me explain how we handle additions to the project scope. If this feature is important to the project's objectives, let's document it as a formal change request, assess the impact on budget and schedule, and get it approved through the change control process. I want to make sure this gets proper consideration.'; This approach: acknowledges the stakeholder's request respectfully; explains the process; positions the PM as following good governance (not blocking the request); CURRENT SITUATION (after two accommodations): PM must reinforce the boundary now: 'I realize I handled the previous request informally. Going forward, all scope additions must go through our change control process. This protects the project's timeline and budget for everyone. I'd like to help you submit a formal change request for both this request and the previous one.'; smoothing is APPROPRIATE for minor issues where the relationship matters more than the issue — but scope additions are not minor issues.
explanations.d: Scope creep originating from stakeholder requests is absolutely a stakeholder management issue. Vendor management is a separate concern. The pattern reveals a stakeholder management failure through repeated accommodation.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — conflict resolution: selecting the appropriate mode by situation
questions.text: Match each conflict scenario to the MOST appropriate resolution mode: (1) Two developers have been arguing for 3 days about database architecture — the project is being delayed; (2) A team member is upset about meeting scheduling during a conflict with their child's school event — it's a one-time meeting; (3) A new security regulation requires immediate implementation of access controls, but developers object to the complexity; (4) A business analyst and tester disagree on whether a feature meets acceptance criteria.

answers.text: All four should use compromising — it's the safest approach in all conflict situations
(1) Compromising; (2) Avoiding; (3) Smoothing; (4) Forcing

(1) Confronting/Problem-Solving — the issue directly blocks project work and requires a genuine collaborative resolution on a technical matter where both parties have expertise; (2) Smoothing/Accommodating — a minor scheduling inconvenience for a one-time event; relationship preservation outweighs the insignificant scheduling issue; (3) Forcing — the regulation is non-negotiable; developer objection to compliance is not a legitimate conflict to 'resolve'; (4) Confronting/Problem-Solving — unclear acceptance criteria require open analysis of the requirements together, not win-lose
(1) Avoiding; (2) Forcing; (3) Confronting; (4) Compromising

explanations.a: Compromising in all situations is an inflexible approach: a security regulation is not something to compromise on (forcing is appropriate); a trivial scheduling matter doesn't need the full compromising effort (smoothing is more appropriate); a 3-day blocking architecture debate needs collaborative resolution, not just a midpoint.
explanations.b: This matching is largely incorrect: (1) A 3-day blocking debate needs confronting, not just compromising; (2) A one-time scheduling inconvenience warrants smoothing, not avoiding; (3) A regulatory requirement warrants forcing, not smoothing; (4) An acceptance criteria dispute needs confronting, not forcing.
explanations.c: CONFLICT MODE MATCHING: (1) DATABASE ARCHITECTURE DEBATE (3 DAYS, BLOCKING PROJECT) → CONFRONTING/PROBLEM-SOLVING: the issue is technical and important — both parties have relevant expertise; a compromised technical decision may be technically inferior; confronting mode: bring both developers together with the PM; have each party explain their technical reasoning; identify what they agree on; find a technically sound solution that addresses both concerns (perhaps a hybrid architecture, or a technical proof-of-concept to test both approaches); the 3-day delay makes resolution urgent; (2) MEETING SCHEDULING / SCHOOL EVENT → SMOOTHING/ACCOMMODATING: the PM accommodates by scheduling the meeting differently or recording it for the team member; the relationship value of accommodating a minor personal need far exceeds the cost of rescheduling; the issue is not important enough for confronting/problem-solving; (3) SECURITY REGULATION / DEVELOPER OBJECTION → FORCING: the regulation is legally mandatory — developer comfort is not a legitimate override; 'forcing': 'This is required by law. I understand it adds complexity. We will implement these access controls. I'm available to discuss how to minimize the implementation burden, but the compliance itself is not negotiable.'; (4) ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA DISPUTE → CONFRONTING/PROBLEM-SOLVING: unclear acceptance criteria are a genuine ambiguity issue; both the BA and tester have valid perspectives; reviewing the requirement together, comparing to the original user story and acceptance criteria, and reaching a shared interpretation produces a better outcome than having one party win.
explanations.d: This matching is largely incorrect across all four scenarios.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — phase gate review; entry and exit criteria; go/no-go governance
questions.text: A project using a phased delivery model has four phases: Discovery, Design, Build, and Deploy. The steering committee asks the PM to define ENTRY and EXIT criteria for each phase gate. What purpose do entry and exit criteria serve?

answers.text: Entry criteria define what must be TRUE before a phase can BEGIN (ensuring the team has the inputs and approvals needed); exit criteria define what must be ACHIEVED before a phase can END and the next phase can begin (ensuring quality and completeness); together they create a disciplined progression through phases that prevents starting work before prerequisites are met and prevents premature advancement to the next phase
Entry and exit criteria are administrative checklists with no governance value
Only exit criteria matter — entry criteria are unnecessary because phases start automatically
Entry criteria are the budget approval; exit criteria are the final budget report — phase gates are primarily financial checkpoints

explanations.a: ENTRY AND EXIT CRITERIA PURPOSE: ENTRY CRITERIA — prerequisites to BEGIN a phase: ensure the team has everything they need before starting the next phase's work; examples for BUILD phase entry criteria: design phase exit criteria met; technical architecture approved; development environment provisioned; development team fully onboarded; all development tool licenses procured; security review of the design complete; WHY ENTRY CRITERIA MATTER: starting development without approved architecture produces rework (developers build against unvalidated assumptions); starting deployment before UAT is complete produces production defects. EXIT CRITERIA — requirements to COMPLETE a phase and AUTHORIZE the next: ensure the phase achieved its objectives before the project moves on; examples for BUILD phase exit criteria: all planned features developed and unit tested; integration testing complete with zero P1 defects; code review standards met (100% of PRs reviewed); UAT environment ready; test data loaded; performance testing complete; documentation updated. WHY EXIT CRITERIA MATTER: prevent 'done when we're tired of it' phase completion — objective criteria determine when the phase is truly complete; ensure quality gates are met before the next phase exposes stakeholders to the output (deploying untested code to UAT wastes stakeholder time). GOVERNANCE VALUE: the steering committee can evaluate phase gate progress objectively; the PM can make a data-driven go/no-go recommendation; disagreements about phase completion are resolved by the criteria, not by subjective opinion.
explanations.b: Entry and exit criteria are the substance of phase gates — without them, a phase gate is a meeting that produces a 'yes' without rigorous evaluation. Entry/exit criteria transform phase gates from ceremonies into governance mechanisms.
explanations.c: Entry criteria are essential — they prevent the team from starting a phase without the prerequisites needed for success. Starting development without approved architecture, provisioned environments, or licensed tools produces immediate blockers.
explanations.d: Phase gates include financial checkpoints, but they are primarily quality and readiness assessments. Budget is one element, not the sole purpose of phase gate criteria.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — phase gate review; go/no-go/conditional decisions; gate outcomes
questions.text: At a phase gate review between Design and Development, the steering committee finds: 3 of 15 critical requirements are still under discussion; the architecture is approved; team is ready; the first development sprint can begin on non-disputed requirements immediately. What gate decision is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: Full GO — start development on all requirements including the 3 disputed ones
Full NO-GO — no development can begin until all 15 requirements are fully resolved

CONDITIONAL GO: authorize development to begin on the 12 fully approved requirements immediately; set a specific deadline for the 3 disputed requirements (within 2 weeks); gate condition: the 3 requirements must be resolved before any development work on the affected features begins; the conditional approval balances progress (don't block 12 ready features) with governance (don't design and build requirements that are still changing)
NO decision — defer the gate review for 2 weeks until all requirements are resolved before the meeting

explanations.a: Starting development on the 3 disputed requirements when they're still under discussion produces: development work that will likely need to be redone when requirements are finalized; waste of developer time on features that may change significantly; technical debt from building on uncertain foundations.
explanations.b: A full NO-GO blocks 12 ready features from entering development — creating an unnecessary schedule delay of 2 weeks or more for work that is clearly ready to begin. This is overly conservative governance.
explanations.c: CONDITIONAL GO DECISION — OPTIMAL GOVERNANCE: the conditional GO balances two competing concerns: 1. PROGRESS: 12 of 15 requirements are approved and development-ready; blocking development on these delays the project unnecessarily; 2. QUALITY: 3 requirements are disputed and not ready for development; building on disputed requirements produces rework; CONDITIONAL GO STRUCTURE: 'The steering committee approves progression to Development Phase with the following conditions: (a) Development begins immediately on the 12 approved requirements; (b) Development on the 3 disputed requirements (Feature 8, 11, 14) is held until requirements are finalized; (c) The business analyst and product owner must resolve the 3 disputed requirements by [date 2 weeks from today]; (d) The PM will confirm resolution before development begins on those features; (e) If requirements are not resolved by [date], a new gate review is triggered.'; CONDITIONAL GO BENEFITS: project makes progress (12 features enter development); governance is maintained (disputed features are held); the responsible parties have a deadline to resolve the dispute; the PM has clear authority to proceed with parts of the work without another steering committee session for the resolved items.
explanations.d: Waiting 2 weeks for all requirements before even holding the review meeting is a 2-week delay across all 15 features — including the 12 that are completely ready. This sacrifices progress unnecessarily.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — tracking and reporting; earned value management; EVM interpretation
questions.text: A PM receives these EVM figures at Month 3 of a 9-month project: BAC = $900,000; PV = $300,000; EV = $270,000; AC = $285,000. Calculate SV, CV, SPI, and CPI, and interpret the overall project health.

answers.text: SV = EV−PV = $270K−$300K = −$30K (behind schedule); CV = EV−AC = $270K−$285K = −$15K (over budget); SPI = 0.90 (behind schedule); CPI = 0.947 (over budget per unit of work); EAC = $900K/0.947 = $950K; the project is behind schedule AND over budget — dual negative but margins are modest at this stage; investigation and corrective action warranted
SV = +$30,000 (ahead); CV = −$15,000 (slightly over budget); project is ahead of schedule but slightly over budget
SV = PV−EV = $30K (positive); CV = AC−EV = $15K (positive) — project is on track
EVM calculations are only valid at project completion — mid-project EVM is inaccurate

explanations.a: EVM CALCULATIONS: SCHEDULE VARIANCE (SV): SV = EV − PV = $270,000 − $300,000 = −$30,000; negative SV = behind schedule; the project has accomplished $30,000 less work than was planned by Month 3; SCHEDULE PERFORMANCE INDEX (SPI): SPI = EV / PV = $270,000 / $300,000 = 0.90; SPI < 1.0 = behind schedule; only 90% of planned work has been completed; COST VARIANCE (CV): CV = EV − AC = $270,000 − $285,000 = −$15,000; negative CV = over budget; the project spent $15,000 more than the value of work accomplished; COST PERFORMANCE INDEX (CPI): CPI = EV / AC = $270,000 / $285,000 = 0.947; CPI < 1.0 = over budget; getting $0.947 of value for every $1.00 spent; ESTIMATE AT COMPLETION (EAC): EAC = BAC / CPI = $900,000 / 0.947 = $950,368; projected cost overrun: ~$50K (5.6% over BAC); OVERALL INTERPRETATION: the project is in the BEHIND SCHEDULE AND OVER BUDGET quadrant; HOWEVER: the margins are modest (SPI 0.90, CPI 0.947) and it is only Month 3 of 9 — there is time for correction; PM ACTIONS: investigate root cause (are specific activities causing the delays and overruns?); develop a recovery plan; brief the sponsor; monitor for trend (if SPI/CPI continue declining, escalation is needed).
explanations.b: SV = EV − PV = $270K − $300K = −$30K (NEGATIVE = behind schedule). A negative SV means behind schedule, not ahead. CV = EV − AC = $270K − $285K = −$15K (NEGATIVE = over budget). Option A inverts both signs.
explanations.c: This answer uses inverted formulas: SV should be EV−PV (not PV−EV); CV should be EV−AC (not AC−EV). The signs are wrong.
explanations.d: EVM is specifically designed for mid-project monitoring — it is MOST valuable during execution when there is still time to take corrective action. 'Only valid at completion' is incorrect.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — tracking scope; scope creep detection; baseline integrity
questions.text: During execution, the project manager notices that the team has been implementing several features that aren't in the WBS. When asked, developers say: 'These were requested directly by the business stakeholders — they seemed reasonable.' The PM calculates that unauthorized additions have consumed approximately 15% of the project budget. What governance failure occurred and how should the PM respond?

answers.text: No governance failure — responsive teams add value by accommodating stakeholder requests
The team's work is acceptable because stakeholders requested it — stakeholder requests always authorize scope
The developers acted correctly — business stakeholders have full authority to authorize scope additions

A scope baseline integrity failure occurred: unauthorized scope additions were implemented without change control, consuming 15% of the budget (approximately $X) without sponsor authorization; PM response: (1) document all unauthorized additions; (2) submit retrospective change requests to formally assess and authorize the work already done; (3) brief the sponsor on the uncontrolled spending; (4) re-establish change control discipline with the team ('all scope requests go through the change request process regardless of who requests them'); (5) implement stronger monitoring to catch future unauthorized additions early

explanations.a: 'Responsive' behavior that bypasses change control produces: unauthorized budget consumption ($X in unplanned spending); schedule impacts (work done instead of planned work = planned work delayed); quality risks (unauthorized features lack acceptance criteria; how do we know they're done correctly?); precedent (stakeholders learn to bypass the PM for scope additions).
explanations.b: Business stakeholders do NOT have authority to add scope directly — they have authority to REQUEST scope additions through the formal change control process. The PM and sponsor authorize scope changes; stakeholders submit requests for consideration.
explanations.c: Business stakeholders do not have authority to authorize scope changes — that authority belongs to the sponsor/CCB. Developers who implement based on stakeholder requests alone are not following project governance.
explanations.d: SCOPE BASELINE INTEGRITY FAILURE: WHAT HAPPENED: business stakeholders bypassed change control by directly requesting features from developers; developers, wanting to be helpful, implemented without PM approval; 15% of budget (~$X) was spent on unauthorized work; GOVERNANCE FAILURES: developers did not enforce change control; stakeholders were not informed of the change request process (or chose to bypass it); PM monitoring did not detect the additions early enough; PM RESPONSE: DOCUMENT ALL ADDITIONS: list every feature added outside the WBS; estimate the cost consumed for each; RETROSPECTIVE CHANGE REQUESTS: create formal CRs for each addition: assess their business value; determine if they should be formally incorporated into the scope baseline; if no business value → they shouldn't have been built; BRIEF SPONSOR: 'I've identified unauthorized scope additions that have consumed approximately $X (15% of our budget). I'm submitting retrospective CRs for each. Here is my recommendation for which to retain and which to remove.' → the sponsor may need to authorize additional budget or reduce future scope to compensate; RE-ESTABLISH DISCIPLINE: team meeting to re-emphasize: all scope requests from ANY source go through the change request process; developers are not authorized to implement features without PM approval; provide stakeholders with the change request process; MONITORING: compare WBS work packages to actual work being done weekly; any work not in the WBS requires a CR.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — tracking and reporting; issue log; risk vs. issue distinction
questions.text: During execution, the PM receives a report: 'The integration API is returning errors on 15% of transactions.' Is this a risk or an issue, and how should it be managed?

answers.text: This is a risk — unexpected API errors are potential future problems

This is an ISSUE (not a risk): a risk is a potential future problem that has not yet occurred; an issue is a problem that is CURRENTLY OCCURRING and requires active management; the API errors are happening NOW, affecting 15% of current transactions; management: log in the issue log with severity, owner, impact, and target resolution date; assign a resolution owner; investigate root cause immediately; develop and execute a remediation plan; escalate if resolution is blocked or exceeds defined severity thresholds
This is neither a risk nor an issue — it is a quality defect only tracked by QA
All problems during execution are risks — the risk register covers all project concerns

explanations.a: A risk has NOT YET OCCURRED — it is a potential future problem with a probability assessment. 'The API MAY have errors during integration testing' is a risk. 'The API IS returning errors on 15% of transactions' is an issue because it is actively happening.
explanations.b: RISK vs. ISSUE DISTINCTION: RISK: a potential future event that, if it occurs, would affect project objectives; managed in the RISK REGISTER; has a probability (hasn't occurred yet); example: 'There is a 30% probability that the integration API will have performance issues under high load'; ISSUE: a problem that is CURRENTLY OCCURRING that requires active resolution; managed in the ISSUE LOG; probability is no longer relevant — the event has occurred; example: 'The integration API is returning errors on 15% of transactions RIGHT NOW'; WHEN A RISK BECOMES AN ISSUE: when the risk event occurs, it transitions from the risk register to the issue log; the contingency plan (pre-planned response) is activated; ISSUE LOG FIELDS: Issue ID; Description (API errors on 15% of transactions); Severity (P1 — production-blocking); Impact (15% of transactions failing, affecting downstream processes); Owner (integration lead); Root cause analysis: in progress; Resolution plan: vendor engagement + failover routing; Target resolution date; Status; ESCALATION: is this issue a P1 that requires immediate sponsor notification? (15% failure rate during testing = likely yes; 15% in production = definitely yes).
explanations.c: A 15% transaction error rate is both a quality issue AND a project management issue requiring active management through the issue log. Quality defects of this magnitude affect schedule and scope — they are not just QA-only concerns.
explanations.d: Not everything is a risk — issues (actively occurring problems), defects (quality failures discovered), decisions (documented choices), and actions (assigned tasks) are all tracked in separate management artifacts. Conflating all concerns into the risk register produces an unmanageable mega-document.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — budget/timeline updates; updating the cost baseline; change control
questions.text: During execution, a risk the team identified in planning materializes: a key vendor raises their rates by 25%, adding $80,000 to the project cost. The PM has contingency reserves of $60,000. How should the PM update the budget and what governance steps are required?

answers.text: Absorb the entire $80,000 from contingency — contingency covers all vendor cost increases
Ignore the increase — budget problems resolve themselves later in the project
Reduce scope to offset the $80,000 cost increase — scope reduction is always the first response to cost overruns

Use $60,000 from contingency (covers the identified risk impact); for the remaining $20,000 over contingency, submit a formal change request to the sponsor requesting access to management reserve or additional budget authorization; update the cost baseline to reflect the contingency consumption; document the change in the risk register (risk materialized) and issue log (active cost issue)

explanations.a: Contingency reserves cover cost of planned risk responses — they are not unlimited. The contingency was $60,000; the vendor increase is $80,000. Using $60,000 from contingency is appropriate (within the PM's authority for identified risk responses). However, the remaining $20,000 exceeds the available contingency and requires sponsor authorization.
explanations.b: An $80,000 unplanned cost increase on a project cannot be ignored. It will eventually produce a significant budget overrun and require explanation to the sponsor — much better to address it proactively.
explanations.c: Scope reduction is one option when cost overruns cannot be funded — but it should be evaluated along with other options (using reserves, requesting additional authorization) and presented to the sponsor with trade-offs. Automatic scope reduction without sponsor discussion is not appropriate.
explanations.d: BUDGET UPDATE WITH RISK MATERIALIZATION: STEP 1 — USE CONTINGENCY (PM AUTHORITY): the vendor rate increase was an identified risk; using contingency for identified risk responses is within the PM's authority (up to defined thresholds); apply $60,000 of contingency to cover the first $60,000 of the vendor increase; STEP 2 — CHANGE REQUEST FOR REMAINING $20,000: the remaining $20,000 exceeds available contingency; this requires: a formal change request submitted to the sponsor; request access to management reserve ($20,000 from the unknown-unknowns buffer) OR request additional budget authorization; the sponsor must approve spending above the cost baseline; STEP 3 — UPDATE COST BASELINE: the approved change request authorizes a $20,000 increase to the cost baseline; update the cost baseline document to reflect: contingency used: $60,000 (from $60,000 contingency balance → $0 remaining); cost baseline increase: $20,000 (from management reserve or new authorization); STEP 4 — DOCUMENTATION: risk register: update the risk entry (risk materialized; response activated; contingency consumed); issue log: add an issue for the $20,000 shortfall pending sponsor decision; COMMUNICATION: brief the sponsor on the risk materialization and the budget impact BEFORE submitting the formal change request; no executive likes surprises in formal change requests.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — conflict resolution: escalation; when PM escalates vs. resolves independently
questions.text: A PM has tried confronting/problem-solving three times with two team leads who have a persistent disagreement about technical approach. After three sessions, the disagreement remains unresolved and is delaying a critical path activity. The PM has run out of tools to resolve the conflict independently. What should happen?

answers.text: Let the conflict continue until it resolves naturally — some conflicts are never resolved
Force a decision using the PM's authority — forcing should have been used in the first session
Remove one team lead from the project — persistent disagreement indicates one party is being unreasonable

Escalate the conflict to the appropriate authority (the project sponsor or functional manager) with a clear briefing: nature of the technical disagreement; why it remains unresolved after three sessions; the specific schedule impact (critical path delay); the PM's recommendation for resolution (if one exists); escalation is appropriate when the PM has genuinely exhausted their own conflict resolution tools and the conflict has material project impact

explanations.a: A conflict blocking a critical path activity cannot be left to natural resolution. If the conflict is unresolved, the critical path activity remains blocked, the project falls further behind schedule, and the problem compounds over time.
explanations.b: Using forcing AFTER three failed collaborative sessions may be appropriate in some cases — but first, the question is whether a decision-maker with more authority (sponsor or functional manager) should make the call. Forcing by the PM may be perceived as overriding legitimate technical expertise. Escalation first is typically more appropriate.
explanations.c: Removing a team lead from the project for a technical disagreement is an extreme HR action that requires functional manager and HR involvement. Persistent disagreement often reflects legitimate technical complexity — not unreasonableness. This action would also risk losing critical technical expertise.
explanations.d: CONFLICT ESCALATION CRITERIA AND PROCESS: WHEN TO ESCALATE: the PM has genuinely tried multiple resolution approaches (three sessions is documented evidence); the conflict is blocking a critical path activity (material project impact); the conflict may involve organizational dynamics that exceed the PM's authority (e.g., a technical disagreement that requires a senior technical decision-maker); ESCALATION CONTENT: description of the disagreement (technical approach A vs. technical approach B — what are the specific differences?); attempted resolution methods (three confronting/problem-solving sessions with outcomes summarized); current impact (critical path activity X is blocked; current delay = 5 days); PM recommendation (if available): 'Based on my analysis, Approach A better aligns with our architecture standards because...' OR 'I cannot determine a technical preference — I need a senior technical decision'; ESCALATION PROCESS: brief the sponsor verbally first; then submit formal escalation documentation; AFTER ESCALATION: the sponsor or senior technical authority makes the decision; both team leads accept the decision (they escalated, they accept the outcome); the PM documents the resolution in the decision log; OPTION B CONSIDERATION: if the sponsor decides that the PM should force a decision based on the PM's own judgment, THEN forcing is appropriate — but the escalation step first is more professional than forcing unilaterally after three failed sessions.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — monitoring and controlling; proactive vs. reactive management
questions.text: A project manager takes a 'management by exception' approach — only reviewing status when problems are reported to them. Three months into execution, a critical integration module is 4 weeks behind (missed by the passive approach). What should the PM have done differently and what does proactive monitoring look like?

answers.text: Management by exception is the best approach — the team should manage themselves without PM oversight

Proactive monitoring means: weekly progress reviews comparing actual vs. planned on all critical path activities; weekly EVM calculations to detect cost and schedule variances early; regularly asking critical path owners 'What's your current status? Are there any blockers?' rather than waiting for reports; reviewing the schedule weekly to identify activities that are slipping before they become critical; running regular risk trigger monitoring sessions
Daily reports from all team members — comprehensive monitoring means collecting information every day
The PM should have caught this during the monthly steering committee meeting — monthly reviews are sufficient for critical path monitoring

explanations.a: 'Management by exception' (waiting for problems to be reported) is appropriate as a management STYLE for experienced, empowered teams on NON-CRITICAL PATH activities. It is inappropriate for critical path monitoring — by the time a team member reports a critical path problem, the delay is often already 2-4 weeks.
explanations.b: PROACTIVE MONITORING FRAMEWORK: WEEKLY CRITICAL PATH REVIEW: identify the current critical path activities; compare actual vs. planned progress for each; any activity that is behind schedule on the critical path requires immediate attention; WEEKLY EVM: calculate PV, EV, AC for key activities; SPI trend over 3-4 weeks is more revealing than a single week's data; declining SPI trend means 'we're falling further behind each week'; PROACTIVE STAKEHOLDER CHECK-INS: 'I notice Activity X is due on Friday — are you on track? What help do you need?'; this is not micromanagement — it is active PM engagement with critical path owners; RISK TRIGGER MONITORING: review the risk register weekly; are any risk triggers occurring?; SCHEDULE TRACKING IN THE PM TOOL: update actual start/finish dates as work completes; the schedule tool automatically recalculates float and critical path; issues become visible before they're reported; WHAT PROACTIVE MONITORING ACHIEVES: a 4-week behind integration module would have been detected at 1-week behind if critical path activities were reviewed weekly; a 1-week delay is recoverable; a 4-week delay may not be; BALANCE: proactive monitoring doesn't mean daily reports from all team members — it means regular, structured, critical-path-focused reviews that give the PM early warning.
explanations.c: Daily reports from all team members is micromanagement that: reduces team autonomy; creates administrative burden; consumes team productive time; produces more data than the PM can process. Targeted proactive monitoring (weekly critical path reviews, weekly EVM) is effective without being burdensome.
explanations.d: Monthly steering committee meetings are governance forums — they are insufficient for operational project monitoring. A critical path activity that slips 4 weeks will not surface in a monthly meeting until it's already past critical. Weekly operational monitoring is needed for critical path activities.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — tracking and reporting; reporting cadence; reporting to different audiences
questions.text: A project manager is calibrating the reporting frequency for different stakeholders. The executive sponsor reviews project reports; the project team leads review operational reports; and the Finance Controller tracks budget reports. What reporting frequencies are MOST appropriate for each and why?

answers.text: All stakeholders receive daily reports — consistent reporting frequency ensures no one is left out

Executive sponsor: monthly (or at key milestones — executives need strategic-level visibility on exceptions, not operational detail); project team leads: weekly (operational detail needed to manage work-stream progress); Finance Controller: aligned with accounting cycles — typically monthly with ad hoc escalation if budget variances exceed thresholds
All stakeholders receive weekly reports — weekly is the standard for all project reporting
Only the project team receives reports — stakeholders don't need regular updates

explanations.a: Daily reporting for executive sponsors creates: information overload; attention fatigue (executives stop reading reports); false urgency on operational fluctuations that don't require executive action; wasted time preparing reports with insufficient value to justify the frequency.
explanations.b: AUDIENCE-CALIBRATED REPORTING FREQUENCIES: EXECUTIVE SPONSOR (monthly + milestone-triggered): what executives need: Is the project on track to deliver on time and budget? What decisions do I need to make? Are there risks requiring my attention?; monthly report provides this without overloading; ADDITIONAL TRIGGERS: any significant variance (Red status on any dimension); approaching phase gate (brief before the meeting); scope change requiring approval; CONTENT: 1-2 page dashboard: RAG status, milestone summary, top risks, decisions needed; PROJECT TEAM LEADS (weekly): what team leads need: which tasks are complete, in progress, or blocked in their work-stream?; what are the dependencies? what actions are needed this week?; weekly cadence matches the project's operational rhythm (sprint-length or week-length work cycles); CONTENT: work-stream task status, blockers, action items, decisions, risks; FINANCE CONTROLLER (monthly + exception-triggered): what finance needs: actual spend vs. budget by cost center; forecast (EAC); variance explanation for any material differences; monthly aligns with accounting close cycles; exception triggers: any variance >5% or >$20K warrants an ad hoc report; CONTENT: budget vs. actuals table, EAC, variance analysis, projected spend for the next period. WHY DIFFERENTIATED FREQUENCY: the same information delivered to all audiences at all frequencies produces: waste (producing more reports than needed); frustration (wrong level of detail for the audience); disengagement (stakeholders stop reading irrelevant reports).
explanations.c: Weekly reporting is appropriate for operational stakeholders — but executives don't need weekly operational updates, and Finance Controllers typically need budget reports aligned with accounting cycles.
explanations.d: Stakeholders have governance responsibilities that require regular, accurate project information. The sponsor authorizes resources and must stay informed to make informed decisions.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — conflict resolution: choosing modes based on relationship and importance
questions.text: A project manager observes three simultaneous conflicts: (A) Two developers argue about which testing framework to use — the decision doesn't affect the schedule or integration points, but emotions are high; (B) The vendor PM and the project PM disagree on whether a change order is legitimate — $75,000 and 3-week schedule impact at stake; (C) A senior developer insists on implementing a specific security approach that the PM believes is technically inferior but the developer has much deeper security expertise. Recommend the appropriate conflict mode for each and justify the selection.

answers.text: All three should use forcing — the PM has authority and must make decisions efficiently
All three should use confronting/problem-solving — collaborative resolution is always best
(A) Compromising; (B) Forcing; (C) Avoiding

(A) Smoothing — the framework choice is technically minor and relationship preservation outweighs the debate; let the team decide or flip a coin; (B) Confronting/Problem-Solving is needed — $75K and 3 weeks requires careful collaborative analysis of the SOW scope; if unresolved, escalate to legal/procurement; (C) Defer to the developer's expertise — the PM should express their concern once but yield to the domain expert; this is effectively Smoothing/Accommodating with recognition that the developer has legitimate technical authority in their domain

explanations.a: All three forcing is inappropriate: (A) technical team decisions benefit from team input, not PM imposition; (B) a $75K contract dispute requires careful analysis, not forcing; (C) forcing an inferior technical approach over a domain expert's recommendation is unwise.
explanations.b: All three confronting/problem-solving ignores: (A) the low stakes of framework choice relative to time spent; (C) the PM's lack of domain expertise (confronting assumes both parties have equally valid positions — a PM confronting a security expert is not an equal conversation).
explanations.c: (A) Compromising when the stakes are low wastes collaborative effort; (B) Forcing a $75K contract dispute bypasses legitimate SOW analysis; (C) Avoiding a security decision is irresponsible — security issues don't resolve themselves.
explanations.d: TAILORED CONFLICT MODE SELECTION: (A) DEVELOPER FRAMEWORK DEBATE (Low stakes, high emotion) → SMOOTHING: the testing framework choice has no schedule or integration impact; the technical quality difference between the two frameworks is marginal in this context; the COST of prolonged conflict (emotional team dynamics, time in meetings) FAR EXCEEDS the benefit of picking the 'right' framework; SMOOTHING APPROACH: 'Both frameworks are valid choices. Since this doesn't affect our integration points, I'll let the team make the call. Can you two agree on criteria for deciding?'; or: 'You both make good points. Let's use [Framework X] for now — we can revisit if there are problems'; relationship preservation > marginal technical optimization. (B) VENDOR CHANGE ORDER ($75K, 3 WEEKS) → CONFRONTING/PROBLEM-SOLVING: the stakes are materially significant (5% of a $1.5M contract; 3-week schedule impact); both parties may have legitimate interpretations of the SOW; the PM cannot simply force or compromise away $75K — it must be analyzed against the contract; CONFRONTING APPROACH: 'Let's review the SOW together and map each item in the change order to specific SOW sections. For items clearly outside the SOW, we agree they're in scope for the CO. For items that appear in the SOW, we discuss the interpretation.'; if confronting fails: escalate to procurement/legal for contract interpretation; (C) SECURITY APPROACH DISAGREEMENT (PM vs. domain expert) → SMOOTHING/ACCOMMODATING WITH EXPRESSED CONCERN: the developer has deep security expertise the PM lacks; the PM should NOT force or compromise on security decisions they don't fully understand; APPROPRIATE APPROACH: express the concern once: 'I have a concern about the security approach — can you help me understand why [alternative approach] was ruled out?'; genuinely listen to the answer; if the developer's explanation is sound: accommodate (they have legitimate domain authority); document the PM's concern and the developer's rationale in the decision log; if security concern escalates: involve an independent security reviewer.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — quality tracking; defect density monitoring; quality metrics reporting
questions.text: A project manager includes quality metrics in the monthly status report. What quality metrics BEST indicate execution health for a software development project?

answers.text: Only the number of features deployed — feature count is the only quality indicator
Only lines of code written — developer productivity is the primary quality metric
Customer satisfaction surveys only — end-user satisfaction is the only quality indicator that matters

Defect density (defects per 1,000 lines of code — trend vs. target); defect discovery rate by phase (are defects being found in code review before testing, or escaping to UAT?); test coverage percentage (what % of code has automated tests?); open defect aging (P1 defects older than 24 hours; P2 older than 72 hours); code review compliance rate; test execution completion rate vs. plan; post-deployment defect rate

explanations.a: Feature count (velocity) measures productivity, not quality. A team delivering 30 features per sprint, each with 10 defects, is high-velocity but low-quality. Features must be delivered with defined quality standards.
explanations.b: Lines of code is a notoriously poor quality metric — more code can mean more complexity (negative quality indicator). Code quality is better measured by defect density, test coverage, and code review compliance.
explanations.c: Customer satisfaction surveys measure perceived quality after delivery — they are lagging indicators that arrive too late to correct problems during execution. Leading indicators (defect density during development, test coverage) enable proactive quality management.
explanations.d: SOFTWARE QUALITY METRICS for execution status reporting: DEFECT DENSITY: defects per 1,000 lines of code or per story point; target: <2 defects/1,000 LOC; trend analysis is more valuable than the snapshot (is the rate improving or worsening?); DEFECT DISCOVERY PHASE: WHERE defects are found indicates quality process effectiveness: found in code review (best — cheapest to fix); found in unit testing (good); found in integration testing (fair — higher cost to fix); found in UAT (poor — expensive); found in production (worst — most expensive, damages reputation); ideally, defects should be shifting LEFT (caught earlier in the development cycle); TEST COVERAGE: automated test coverage %; target: typically ≥80% for business-critical code; declining coverage means new code is being added without corresponding tests; OPEN DEFECT AGING: P1 (critical) open defects should be resolved within 24 hours; P2 open >72 hours needs escalation; P3 open >2 weeks needs review; accumulating defect backlogs signal team capacity or priority issues; CODE REVIEW COMPLIANCE: % of PRs that received review before merge; target: 100%; declining compliance signals quality shortcuts; POST-DEPLOYMENT DEFECT RATE: defects found in production after release; the most visible quality failure to end users; CUSTOMER SATISFACTION (option D): is a LAGGING indicator that measures perception of quality after delivery — valuable but insufficient alone for execution monitoring.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — tracking risk; risk response execution; risk trigger monitoring
questions.text: A risk register entry states: 'Risk: Key data migration vendor may miss the Month 7 delivery date (probability: 40%, impact: HIGH). Trigger: If vendor falls >2 weeks behind at the Month 5 checkpoint, activate contingency.' At Month 5, the vendor reports they are 3 weeks behind schedule. What should happen?

answers.text: Wait until Month 7 to assess impact — triggers are only indicators, not action points

The trigger event has occurred (3 weeks behind at Month 5 checkpoint > the 2-week trigger threshold); the PM must immediately activate the pre-planned contingency response: engage the backup vendor or internal team for parallel data migration work; formally document the trigger activation; brief the sponsor on the risk materialization; continue monitoring the primary vendor to determine if they can still deliver
Lower the risk's probability assessment since the vendor is now working on the migration
Close the risk — it materialized and is now an issue only; no contingency needed

explanations.a: Triggers exist precisely to enable EARLY ACTION — waiting until Month 7 to assess impact defeats the entire purpose of defining a trigger. At Month 7, the PM would discover the vendor can't deliver with no time for contingency. At Month 5, with the trigger activated, there are still 2 months to execute the contingency plan.
explanations.b: TRIGGER ACTIVATION AND CONTINGENCY EXECUTION: TRIGGER CONDITION MET: the risk register defined '3 weeks behind at Month 5 checkpoint' as the trigger; the vendor is exactly 3 weeks behind at Month 5 → trigger ACTIVATED; IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: ACTIVATE CONTINGENCY: begin engaging the backup vendor or allocating internal data migration resources; contingency plans are most valuable when activated early — 2 months before the delivery date allows the backup plan to succeed; FORMAL DOCUMENTATION: update the risk register: 'Risk triggered at Month 5; contingency activated on [date]; primary vendor still engaged but backup engaged for parallel track'; transition the risk to the issue log (it has now become an active problem); SPONSOR BRIEFING: inform the sponsor: 'The data migration risk has been triggered. We are activating our contingency plan (backup vendor) while continuing to work with the primary vendor. Here is the revised timeline.'; CONTINUE MONITORING PRIMARY VENDOR: the primary vendor may still deliver (3 weeks behind is concerning but not definitive failure); continue weekly status meetings with the primary vendor; set a secondary decision point at Month 6: if primary vendor has recovered or is on track for a manageable late delivery, we may be able to scale back the contingency engagement.
explanations.c: The risk has been triggered — probability assessment is no longer the relevant metric. The contingency plan must be activated based on the trigger event. Updating probability from 40% to 30% while the vendor is already 3 weeks behind is a misapplication of risk management.
explanations.d: When a risk triggers, it transitions from the risk register to the issue log — but this does NOT mean no contingency is needed. The contingency plan is activated BECAUSE the risk has triggered. Closing the risk without activating the contingency wastes the pre-planned response that was developed specifically for this scenario.

questions.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
questions.keyword: Execution phase — tracking and reporting; executive communication; exception reporting
questions.text: A project manager sends a 15-page weekly status report to the project sponsor (a busy C-level executive). The sponsor frequently misses or ignores the reports. Two major issues (a vendor SLA breach and a schedule slip) that were in the report went unnoticed for 3 weeks. How should the PM change their executive reporting approach?

answers.text: Stop sending reports — if the sponsor ignores them, they are useless
Send the report more often — daily reports will ensure the sponsor reads at least one
Ask the sponsor to read the full 15-page report — executives must invest time in governance

Redesign for executive consumption: one-page dashboard (RAG status; key milestone status; top 3 risks; decisions needed); for exception events like SLA breach or schedule slip — send a SEPARATE, concise alert email same day (not buried in a weekly report): subject 'Project Alert: Vendor SLA Breach — Action Needed'; bold the issue, the impact, and the requested decision; follow up verbally for any decision needed within 48 hours
